method: AST evidence and reviewed explanations; five-word Jaccard on article text, cutoff 0.5

rows.title: Citable, specific claims

findings.title: 'Content lacks the specifics AI engines quote'
findings.detail: f'Only {specific} of {len(substantial)} substantial pages contain concrete, verifiable detail (prices, dates, credentials, measurable claims). Answer engines preferentially cite specifics because they are attributable; generic marketing adjectives give them nothing to repeat.'
findings.fix: 'Replace vague claims with facts: real price ranges, the year you started, licence numbers, service-area names, response times, warranty terms.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your copy give AI answers facts to quote?
rows.answer: It looks for numbers backed by words that explain where the claim comes from.
rows.why: A bare promise gives a reader little to check. The test looks for a concrete claim with enough context to understand its basis.

condition.text: The test needs at least 3 indexable pages with at least 250 words each and a supported prose language. A page qualifies as specific only when its prose matches both a number pattern and an attribution pattern. Currency amounts and percentages can supply the number. A bare number needs at least 2 digits, with comma-grouped forms also recognised. Research wording, a start date, a qualification or a version can supply the context. A finding appears when the share of qualifying pages is below 0.3. For example, a 250-word service page can enter the sample when it is indexable and its language is supported.

pages.text: Only substantial pages that can appear in search enter that share. A title alone cannot make a page qualify. Too few pages means this test produces no finding.

reports.text: The report marks a low share of specific claims as medium severity. Pattern matches do not establish that a claim is true, that a source is reliable or that an AI answer will cite it.

fix.text: Read the affected pages and find claims you can support from your own records. Add the measurement, date or source beside the statement it explains. State any limits on what you know. Use numbers only when you can support them. Label estimates clearly.

rows.guide_title: AI search visibility, explained

review.text: Compare a matched passage with the record behind it. A price without context and a dated measurement make different statements, even when both contain digits. Check what the attribution is based on. Limit the claim to what the record supports. Put the source beside it so readers can check it.

faq.question: How much text does a page need for the citable-facts check?
faq.answer: A sampled page needs 250 words or more. The site also needs enough indexable pages and a language the test supports.

faq.question: Does a number alone make my copy a citable fact?
faq.answer: No. Prose needs an attribution pattern as well as a numeric match. A person must still verify the resulting claim.

faq.question: How serious is a lack of specific claims on my pages?
faq.answer: The result has medium severity when too few sampled pages qualify. It does not predict whether an AI service will quote you.

rows.question: Can AI search crawlers read your site?
rows.answer: It separates crawler restrictions you chose from restrictions inherited from a general robots rule.
rows.why: Search access and training permission are separate choices in this code. Keeping them distinct lets you review the rule that caused a finding without being told to remove a restriction you meant to keep.

condition.text: The check reads the saved AI crawler access decisions. An empty access table produces no finding. A robots response with HTTP status 500 or above, or a failed response with a requested robots address, prevents a confident access claim. It separates citation crawlers from training crawlers and distinguishes a named block, an allowlist omission and a wildcard block. The citation group includes OAI-SearchBot, PerplexityBot, Claude-SearchBot and Meta-WebIndexer. For example, a robots response with HTTP status 500 leaves access uncertain even if an earlier copy allowed the crawler.

pages.text: This is a site policy check, based on the saved robots file and its access table. It does not need a set of crawled article pages.

reports.text: Accidental citation blocks can be critical. Named choices, allowlist omissions and training restrictions are notices. The report explains which rule applies. Review it against the access you intended. A robots decision alone cannot prove that a server serves the request.

fix.text: Decide which crawlers should have access, then inspect the named group and the wildcard group that apply to each. Change only the rules that conflict with your policy. Use the linked guide to check the crawler names and retest the file after saving it. Review server access separately when robots allows a request that still fails.

rows.guide_title: How to fix AI crawler access

review.text: Start with the crawler named in the finding and follow the policy that applies to it. A broad wildcard restriction can be deliberate, just as a named allow can be deliberate. Check which choice you intended before editing either group. Keep training preferences separate from search access in your notes, so that a later template update does not silently combine policies you wanted to manage independently.

faq.question: Which AI search crawlers does this robots check name?
faq.answer: Among the citation crawlers are OAI-SearchBot, PerplexityBot, Meta-WebIndexer and Claude-SearchBot. Training access is considered separately.

faq.question: Can a failed robots request prove that AI crawlers are allowed?
faq.answer: No. HTTP status 500 or higher leaves the saved policy uncertain. A failed fetch with a requested robots address also prevents a confident result.

faq.question: Is an intentional AI training block treated like an accidental search block?
faq.answer: No. An accidental citation restriction can be critical. Training restrictions are notices, preserving the distinction between search access and training choices.

rows.question: Do your AI crawler rules still name a real crawler?
rows.answer: It finds retired or unmatchable crawler names in the robots file.
rows.why: A rule can look restrictive while naming a token no crawler sends. The useful distinction is whether your intended restriction still takes effect through another group, which is why the check compares coverage before choosing severity.

condition.text: The test needs a nonempty robots file. It compares crawler names with lists of retired names and names no crawler can match. Restrictions are compared with the wildcard group and any live replacement in the same or a separate group. An old name causes no lost restriction when its replacement already has the same restrictions or stricter ones.

pages.text: The check reads the saved robots groups. It uses the policy text to identify crawler names.

reports.text: A lost restriction is medium severity. Inert names whose restrictions are already covered, or which sit above no restriction, are notices. The report explains whether the old spelling changes the effective policy. It does not assume every retired name makes private pages readable.

fix.text: Find the exact token named in the report and identify its current replacement. Copy the restrictions you intend to keep to the live name, checking for an existing group first. Remove obsolete lines after you have checked the effective policy. Avoid blindly adding another group with a different set of rules.

rows.guide_title: AI crawler directives: which to block, which to keep

review.text: Compare the obsolete group with its replacement before deleting either. Copying a restriction into a new group can be unnecessary when the same rule already applies, while removing an old label alone cannot restore a restriction that never reached the live name. Keep a short record of the intended policy and verify the effective rules after editing, including the wildcard restrictions that may already cover the path.

faq.question: Can an old crawler name stop protecting my pages?
faq.answer: Yes. A retired token can leave a lost restriction when its live replacement has no matching protection.

faq.question: Does every retired crawler rule need a new restriction?
faq.answer: No. Existing restrictions in the wildcard group or a live replacement can already cover the intended policy.

faq.question: How serious is a crawler rule that no longer takes effect?
faq.answer: A lost restriction gets medium severity. An obsolete name with no lost coverage is only a notice.

findings.title: f'{len(contradictions)} AI crawler{plural_s(len(contradictions))} your robots.txt allows {is_are(len(contradictions))} refused by your server'
findings.detail: f"We asked your own server for the homepage as each crawler, with that crawler's documented user-agent, and compared the answer to this audit's own request, which returned {baseline.get('status')}. ' if citation_hit else '') + 'Nothing in robots.txt reports this, because it is not a robots.txt decision. It is a rule in front of your server.' + not_ai_specific
findings.fix: 'Ask whoever runs your CDN or WAF to allow these user-agents. The usual cause is a managed bot-protection rule that challenges or blocks anything not on its known-good list, and AI crawlers are newer than most of those lists. Cloudflare, Fastly and AWS WAF all expose this as a per-user-agent allow rule.\n\n**Checking this yourself takes one extra step.** The same bot protection usually refuses curl and similar tools whatever user-agent they send, so a 403 from `curl -A "GPTBot…"` proves nothing on its own. Send the same request twice (once with the crawler\'s user-agent and once with an ordinary browser one) and compare. If both are refused, your protection is blocking the tool rather than the crawler, and the answer has to come from your CDN\'s own logs. Those logs are the final word either way: Cloudflare and services like it check a real crawler by the address it comes from, so a request from your own computer is not the crawler, whatever user-agent it sends.'

findings.title: 'Crawler access could not be tested: the server asked this audit to slow down' if throttled else 'Your server refused this audit, so crawler access could not be tested'
findings.detail:

This is most often the audit's own doing: crawling a batch of pages and then probing once per crawler is enough to trip a rate limit on many servers. It is not evidence that anything is wrong with the site, and no conclusion about AI crawlers has been drawn from it." if throttled else f"This audit's own request for the homepage returned {base_status or 'no response'}, so every AI-crawler probe returned the same thing and none of it means anything.

This audit identifies itself in its user-agent rather than posing as a browser. Open the same page in your browser: if it loads, the rule is on the user-agent, and allowing this tool is a change in your bot protection rather than on your site. If your browser is refused too, the rule is on the network. Either way it is worth knowing: whatever refuses a reader that names itself will refuse other automated readers that do the same."
findings.fix: "Nothing needs fixing on the site for this. This audit already waited and asked again, and the server was still limiting it, so the AI-crawler answer is missing from this run rather than from your site. To get it, allow this audit's user-agent past the rate limit; real visitors and real crawlers are unaffected." if throttled else "Check the page in your browser first. That tells you whether the rule is on the user-agent or the network. Then allow this audit's user-agent, or the address it runs from, in your bot protection and re-run to get the AI-crawler answer."

Find the crawler rate-limit setting in your platform before looking at your WAF, and raise it for the agents you want indexing you.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your server allow AI crawlers through?
rows.answer: It compares saved server responses with the crawler access your robots file allows.
rows.why: A robots permission does not override a server refusal. Comparing the policy with a real response helps locate the part of the request path that needs attention, while challenges leave room for a real verified crawler to behave differently.

condition.text: The connector must have run and returned data. Its ordinary request must have HTTP status from 200 up to but below HTTP status 400 before crawler refusals can be compared. Payment responses with HTTP status 402 are separated from refusals. Challenges and verifying network edges can make a result untestable. Responses with HTTP status 429 or HTTP status 503 are separated as throttling. Other refusals conflict with policy only when the saved robots decision does not block that crawler. For example, a payment response with HTTP status 402 is handled separately from a crawler access refusal.

pages.text: Saved connector input includes the baseline, search-control request and crawler requests. This is a test of the requested page from the audit's network location, not a complete server log.

reports.text: Untestable, unverifiable and payment results are notices. Throttling is medium severity. A conflicting refusal is critical when a citation crawler is affected and high otherwise. Agreement can produce a pass. The report also records crawlers not asked before the connector's budget expired.

fix.text: Inspect the saved response and the matching firewall or bot rule. Check server logs before relaxing protection. If the server asked for a wait, respect that wait and test again. For a verified-crawler challenge, review the network verification rule rather than assuming that changing the user-agent text proves real crawler access.

rows.guide_title: When your CDN blocks AI crawlers your robots.txt allows

review.text: Match the recorded request with the server rule that answered it. The ordinary request and search-control request help explain whether the response is specific to an AI name, broader crawler handling or the audit's network location. Keep the response status and challenge context together when reviewing logs. Changing a robots rule cannot by itself explain a firewall response, so identify the layer that actually produced the refusal.

faq.question: Can my server block an AI crawler that robots.txt allows?
faq.answer: Yes. A saved server refusal can conflict with the saved robots decision. The check compares policy with the connector's responses.

faq.question: How does the AI server-access check handle rate limits?
faq.answer: Throttling covers HTTP status 503 and HTTP status 429. It gets a different explanation from an ordinary access refusal.

faq.question: Are payment responses counted as AI crawler refusals?
faq.answer: No. Payment responses at HTTP status 402 are kept separate. They produce notices rather than an ordinary conflicting-refusal finding.

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your markup identify your business?
rows.answer: It looks for business identity markup and recognised profile links in sameAs.
rows.why: The distinction between your business and an organisation you discuss matters here. A profile link is useful as an identity statement only when it names the same business, so adding unrelated recognised hosts would make the markup less accurate.

condition.text: The check reads owned identity nodes in JSON-LD from the first 60 indexable pages. It collects sameAs as either a string or a list. If no identity is found there, it checks the wider indexable set for served identity types, other markup and script-built types before reporting absence. With an identity present, an empty sameAs set is reported separately from fewer than 3 recognised profile hosts. For example, an identity with fewer than 3 recognised profile hosts can need review even when sameAs is present.

pages.text: Identity declarations belong to the business described by the page. The check walks owned nodes rather than treating every organisation mentioned in an article as the site's business.

reports.text: Missing business identity can be high severity, absent profile links medium and weak recognised coverage low. A recognised host is a pattern match, not proof that the account belongs to you. Existing identity elsewhere can suppress a claim that the site has none.

fix.text: Review the business node in the served HTML. Give it the correct identity type and link only to profiles your business owns. Keep those links consistent with the accounts shown to visitors. Follow the guide before copying profile URLs, because a platform homepage or another company's account does not identify your business.

rows.guide_title: Not every social link on your site is yours

review.text: Inspect the identity object as a statement about the owner. A useful profile link names a particular account, while a general platform address merely names a service. Check unfamiliar hosts yourself before replacing a valid profile link. Keep linked accounts aligned with the public business name. Remove references that identify an article's subject as the publisher.

faq.question: How many profile hosts does my business identity need in this check?
faq.answer: The weak-coverage case applies below 3 recognised profile hosts. Declare only accounts your business owns.

faq.question: Where does the identity check first look for my business?
faq.answer: It starts with owned JSON-LD identity nodes across the first 60 indexable pages. Broader checks can prevent a false absence claim.

faq.question: Is missing business markup more serious than weak profile coverage?
faq.answer: Yes. The absence of business identity can receive high severity. Weak recognised profile coverage is low.

rows.title: Answer extractability

findings.title: 'Content is not structured as answers to questions'
findings.detail: f'Only {question_pages} of {len(substantial)} substantial pages use question-form headings. AI answer engines assemble responses by lifting self-contained passages; a page organised around questions gives them an obvious passage to lift, and a page of undifferentiated prose does not.'
findings.fix: 'Add H2s phrased exactly as customers ask them, and answer each in the first two sentences underneath before elaborating. Keep the answer complete on its own. The model will quote the paragraph, not the page.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do your pages answer clear questions?
rows.answer: It counts substantial pages with question headings that are specific to the page.
rows.why: A heading can tell a visitor which question the next passage answers. Repeated template questions do not describe the subject of each article, which explains why the code removes headings that occur across the whole sample.

condition.text: The test runs only for a supported prose language. It needs at least 3 indexable pages with at least 300 words each. Headings repeated on every substantial page are removed from consideration. Remaining subheadings qualify when they end in a question mark or match the question-word pattern within its 60-character window. A finding appears when the qualifying page share is below 0.25. For example, a 300-word article with a question subheading can qualify if that heading passes the wording test.

pages.text: Heading tests read subheadings from substantial indexable pages. A shared question in the page template does not count as a distinct answer structure on each page.

reports.text: Low question-heading coverage is medium severity. The test identifies a structure that can be read from headings. It does not grade the answer, confirm its accuracy or promise that an AI service will use it.

fix.text: Find real questions your page already answers. Write a short heading that names the question, then put the direct answer below it before adding detail. Leave headings as statements where that is clearer. Review the body as well as the heading so that punctuation does not become a substitute for a useful answer.

rows.guide_title: Whether an AI answer can be lifted from your page

review.text: Read a qualifying heading together with the passage that follows it. A question mark can satisfy a pattern while leaving a visitor without an answer. Keep the heading specific enough to describe that passage, and put the main answer where it can be read without hunting through unrelated sections. Shared questions about the business can remain useful navigation even when this content-structure test deliberately leaves them out.

faq.question: How long must a page be for the question-heading check?
faq.answer: It needs at least 300 words, must be indexable and must use supported prose. Shorter pages do not enter this comparison.

faq.question: Do question headings repeated in every template count?
faq.answer: No. Questions appearing on every substantial page are set aside. Remaining subheadings must meet the question test.

faq.question: Does low question-heading coverage mean my answers are wrong?
faq.answer: No. The result is medium severity and describes heading structure. Answer accuracy and likely use by AI services remain unmeasured.

rows.title: Dates AI engines can read

findings.title: 'Most pages have no machine-readable date'
findings.detail: f'{len(substantial) - with_iso_date} of {len(substantial)} substantial pages publish no ISO 8601 date in their markup. AI answer engines weight recency heavily and treat undated content as unverifiable, so it loses to dated competitors even when it is better.'
findings.fix: 'Add dateModified (and datePublished where relevant) in ISO 8601 format to your page schema, and refresh it when you update content.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Can a tool read your page dates?
rows.answer: It checks whether substantial pages carry a date in machine-readable markup.
rows.why: A date helps readers understand when an article was written or updated. Attach it to the content it describes. Change an update date when the work has actually changed.

condition.text: At least 4 indexable pages with at least 300 words each are needed. A page counts as dated when it has an article published or modified time in Open Graph, or a matching date in content JSON-LD. The JSON-LD date check excludes site-level types, accepts an ISO-shaped date prefix and stops walking beyond 8 nested levels. A finding appears when the dated share is below 0.3. For example, a 300-word article with a qualifying published date can count toward the dated share.

pages.text: The sample is substantial indexable content. A date on a shared organisation or website node does not stand in for the date of the page being read.

reports.text: The result is low severity. An Open Graph date counts when present. A JSON-LD date also needs the expected format. Review the date yourself to confirm when the content changed and whether it is current.

fix.text: Use the real publication date and change the modified date only after a meaningful edit. Add the matching article time or content schema field, then inspect the served HTML. Keep a visible date consistent with the markup. Do not update the date merely to remove the finding when the underlying page has not changed.

rows.guide_title: How to do a content audit

review.text: Compare the date with the item it describes. A website launch, business start and article update are different events, even when their values use the same date format. Keep the content date attached to its own content node and avoid borrowing a shared template date. After a genuine update, review the visible date and structured date together so that readers and markup receive the same account.

faq.question: Does a date on my website node count as an article date?
faq.answer: No. The date test excludes site-level types. A qualifying date must describe the content itself.

faq.question: How much content is needed for the machine-readable date sample?
faq.answer: At least 4 indexable pages must each contain 300 words or more. Smaller samples do not reach the dated-share test.

faq.question: How serious is missing readable date markup on substantial pages?
faq.answer: It is a low severity result. A detected date still needs review to confirm that it reflects the real work.

rows.title: llms.txt

findings.title: 'No llms.txt file'
findings.detail: "llms.txt is a proposed convention for pointing language models at your key content. Be aware before spending time on it: Google's documentation says you don't need AI text files to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, and nobody has published evidence that the file changes who gets cited. This audit reports its absence for completeness and does not treat it as a defect. Crawler access, server-side rendering and structured data are where the actual gains are."
findings.fix: 'Optional. If you add one, keep it a genuine index of your best pages, not a keyword dump.'

findings.title: 'Whether this site has an llms.txt could not be checked'
findings.detail: f'/llms.txt answered HTTP {ctx.site.llms_txt_status}, so this audit was refused rather than told there is nothing there. Bot protection commonly does this. Nothing is being alleged about the file either way, and this is a file whose absence this audit does not treat as a defect in any case.'
findings.fix: f'Optional, and nothing to do unless you want one. `curl -sI {ctx.site.final_origin or ctx.site.origin}/llms.txt` settles it.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your site have an llms.txt file?
rows.answer: It reports whether the saved site probe found an llms.txt file it could read.
rows.why: The saved probe can answer a narrow file-presence question. It cannot establish that an AI service reads the file or that publishing one changes how the service answers questions about your site.

condition.text: A nonempty saved file ends the check without a finding. The test also stops when the file was skipped under robots rules. A refused response is reported as unreadable rather than absent. Only the remaining missing-file case produces the notice about no llms.txt. It does not test the document's headings, links or usefulness as a content summary.

pages.text: This check uses the site-level file probe. It does not search article bodies for the filename or require the crawler to discover the file through an internal link.

reports.text: This is a notice about an optional file. A refusal leaves the file's presence unknown. Review that response before deciding whether to create or change the file.

fix.text: If you want to publish the file, write a short account of the site with working links to its main content. Check that the root address serves the text and that your policy allows the intended request. When the finding says unreadable, investigate the refusal first instead of creating a second copy of a file that may already exist.

rows.guide_title: What is llms.txt?

review.text: Review a found file as a document in its own right. Presence does not establish that its links still work or that its description matches the site. If a request was refused, preserve that uncertainty until you can inspect the actual response. Keep any decision to publish the file tied to the information you want to provide, rather than treating an optional notice as a failed content page.

faq.question: Does this check grade the contents of the AI summary file?
faq.answer: No. It checks the saved file probe, leaving headings, links and usefulness outside its scope.

faq.question: Does a refused request for the AI summary file mean it is missing?
faq.answer: No. A refused response is unreadable, leaving presence uncertain. Check the refusal before creating another file.

faq.question: Is publishing an AI summary file required to clear a serious error?
faq.answer: The result concerns an optional file and is only a notice. It does not predict changes to AI answers.

rows.title: Content reachable without JavaScript

findings.title: f'{len(js_pages)} page{plural_s(len(js_pages))} {is_are(len(js_pages))} invisible to AI crawlers'
findings.detail: 'These pages return an effectively empty HTML document and build their content with JavaScript. Google eventually renders JavaScript; GPTBot, ClaudeBot and PerplexityBot largely do not. To an AI answer engine these pages are blank, so they can never be quoted or cited.'
findings.fix: 'Server-side render or pre-render, so the headline, body text and links exist in the raw HTML.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Can AI crawlers read your initial HTML?
rows.answer: It finds indexable pages marked as dependent on JavaScript for their content.
rows.why: Browsers can show useful content that a plain document request does not contain. Comparing those views helps explain why a visitor's screenshot and the audit can disagree without either view being fabricated.

condition.text: The check reads which pages the crawler marked as needing JavaScript for their main content. It leaves out addresses recognised as intentionally excluded from search. If no pages remain, there is no finding. It uses the crawler's earlier observations. There is no separate word-count or timing limit here.

pages.text: The check reads initial page content and whether the crawler marked it as needing JavaScript. It uses pages intended for search. Running an AI crawler or confirming a particular service's script support needs a separate test.

reports.text: A finding is high severity and lists the affected URLs. Pages can match even when they work after scripts run. Review the document sent before those scripts run.

fix.text: Open an affected URL and compare the page source with the content visible after loading. Put the main content in the HTML served by the server, using server rendering or a static output where suitable. Retest the actual URL after the change. Keep interactive features, but make the article or product details readable before those features run.

rows.guide_title: How to run a JavaScript SEO audit

review.text: Compare the same address before and after scripts run, using the main text as your reference. A loading screen may contain readable HTML while leaving the article unavailable. Keep the original server response during review. Test each shared page type that delivers its main content differently.

faq.question: Can my page look complete in a browser and still fail the AI HTML check?
faq.answer: Yes. Content marked as needing JavaScript can qualify despite appearing in a loaded browser. Review the original response alongside that view.

faq.question: Are pages deliberately excluded from search counted as unreadable by AI?
faq.answer: No. Pages intentionally excluded from search are set aside before affected content is listed.

faq.question: How serious is main content missing from the initial HTML for AI crawlers?
faq.answer: The result has high severity. It identifies affected URLs without testing a particular AI service's script support.

rows.title: The AI control nothing can detect

conditions.expression: all((access.get(bot) is False for bot in CITATION_CRITICAL)) and access

findings.title: 'One AI visibility control cannot be checked from outside, including by this audit'
findings.detail:
'Google is testing a Search Console toggle that decides whether a site appears in, and helps ground, its generative AI Search features: AI Overviews, AI Mode and AI Overviews in Discover. In Google's words, "sites that opt out will not receive traffic or impressions from our generative AI features", and the control "will not be used as a ranking signal for search results outside of these generative AI Search features".

It publishes nothing. No response header, no robots.txt directive, no markup. A site that has opted out looks identical from the outside to one that has not, so no external audit (this one included) can tell you which you are. It is the only AI visibility input in this report that this audit cannot measure, and it is listed so a clean AI lane is not mistaken for a complete one.

Google began rolling this out to a subset of site owners in the UK before a global release, so it may not be in your account yet.'
findings.fix: 'Open Search Console for this property and look under Settings. If the generative AI control is there, confirm it says what you intend, and check who changed it last if more than one person has access. If it is not there yet, there is nothing to do and nothing is wrong.'
findings.evidence: {'observable_externally': False, 'source_read': '2026-08-07', 'rollout': 'subset of UK site owners, global later'}

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Can an audit see every AI visibility control?
rows.answer: It explains an AI visibility control that cannot be checked from outside the site.
rows.why: An outside audit can only report what it can observe. A provider's private control needs review inside that account. Record the access policy there and use public requests to check the behaviour they can show.

condition.text: This is an explanatory notice rather than a page-content test. It reads the saved access table and suppresses the notice when that nonempty table blocks every citation-critical crawler. Otherwise the notice explains that an outside audit cannot observe the relevant provider-side control. There is no numeric score, content ratio or page-length cutoff in this test.

pages.text: The site access table determines whether the explanation is relevant. Crawled article text cannot reveal the provider-side setting, so a larger sample does not make that setting observable.

reports.text: This result is an explanatory notice. You need account access to check the private setting. A suppressed notice also leaves that setting unmeasured.

fix.text: Review the relevant provider account and its own settings with the person who manages them. Record the policy you intend and check it against the public crawler rules separately. Use public access tests for public access questions. Avoid treating a clean crawl as proof of a private account setting that the crawler cannot read.

rows.guide_title: AI search visibility, explained

review.text: Keep an account-setting review separate from a public request test. A person with access to the provider can confirm a private choice that a crawler cannot observe. Record who checked that choice and what policy it represents without inventing an outside measurement. Revisit the setting through the same account when policy changes, while using public responses only to confirm the access behaviour they can actually expose.

faq.question: Can a public audit read private AI provider settings?
faq.answer: No. A provider-side control is outside what this audit can observe. Account access is needed to review that choice.

faq.question: Why might the private AI control notice be absent?
faq.answer: A nonempty access table blocking every citation-critical crawler suppresses it. That leaves the private setting unmeasured.

faq.question: Does the AI opt-out notice assign a content score?
faq.answer: No. There is no numeric score in this test. The notice explains an observation limit rather than grading your copy.

rows.title: Logo presence and markup

findings.title: "Your logo's alt text does not name your company"
findings.detail: detail.strip()
findings.fix: 'Set the logo\'s alt text to the company name: alt="Acme Roofing", not "logo". It is a name, not a description of an image.'

findings.title: f'No identifiable logo on {len(pages) - identified} of {len(pages)} pages'
findings.detail: 'On most pages no link to your homepage carries a logo image or SVG, no image is marked as a logo, and no link home names the business in text. That usually means the logo is a CSS background image, which nothing reading the markup can see, or that the page has no logo at all.'
findings.fix: 'Put the logo in the page itself, inside the link to your homepage: an whose alt text is the company name, or an inline

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your logo name your business?
rows.answer: It checks how often a readable business identity appears and whether logo text names it.
rows.why: Logo text is also the name of a link for someone who cannot see the image. The check keeps that naming job separate from the choice to use a graphic in the first place.

condition.text: At least 3 successful pages are needed. A page counts as identified when it has a logo or a homepage link whose text contains recognised brand words. Coverage below 0.5 can produce an absence finding when the crawl supports absence claims. Logos with empty or weak alternative text are checked separately. A text link naming the business can count even without an image logo. For example, a site with 3 successful pages has enough pages to begin this comparison.

pages.text: The check reads logos and homepage links from pages the crawl could load. It checks whether they name the business. You still need to review their appearance.

reports.text: Both low identity coverage and weak logo text are low severity. The report does not compare logo artwork, assess a designer's work or require an image when a suitable text identity already exists.

fix.text: Check the header on the affected templates. Give a linked logo useful alternative text that names the business, or keep a clear text link to the homepage. Review the rendered link name before repeating the change across templates. Do not add an image merely because your current identity uses text.

rows.guide_title: What your site says your company is called

review.text: Inspect the name a linked logo supplies when its picture is unavailable. A meaningful text identity can serve the same naming purpose as an image, while a generic logo label may add little. Keep the business name clear without repeating surrounding words unnecessarily. Check the component across templates because a header can differ between the homepage, articles and other sections even when the graphic looks similar.

faq.question: Can a business-name text link count instead of an image logo?
faq.answer: Yes. A text link can identify the business without an image. Its wording must contain recognised brand terms.

faq.question: How many pages does the logo identity comparison need?
faq.answer: The check starts with 3 successful pages or more. It then compares readable business identity across them.

faq.question: Is weak logo alternative text a serious brand error?
faq.answer: The finding has low severity. It asks you to review the link's readable name, without judging the artwork.

rows.title: Brand name consistency

conditions.expression: not any((name in kept or kept in name or name.replace(' ', '') in kept.replace(' ', '') or (kept.replace(' ', '') in name.replace(' ', '')) or _initialism_pair(name, kept, raw_of) for kept in distinct))
any((isinstance(t, str) and t.lower() in wanted for t in types))
any((host and _same_host(host, here) for (_, host) in names))
any((lo <= point <= hi for (lo, hi) in ranges))
not short or len(words) < 2 or len(short) > 8

constants.name: _PAGE_WORDS
constants.expression: frozenset({'home', 'homepage', 'shop', 'store', 'about', 'about us', 'contact', 'contact us', 'blog', 'news', 'press', 'careers', 'jobs', 'pricing', 'prices', 'plans', 'products', 'services', 'support', 'help', 'faq', 'faqs', 'docs', 'documentation', 'login', 'log in', 'sign in', 'sign up', 'register', 'account', 'cart', 'basket', 'checkout', 'search', 'terms', 'privacy', 'privacy policy', 'legal', 'sitemap', 'team', 'our team', 'gallery', 'portfolio', 'reviews', 'testimonials', 'events', 'resources', 'downloads', 'contact form', 'book now', 'menu'})

findings.title: f'Your brand name appears {len(distinct)} different ways'
findings.detail: "Software learns your company name from your title tags, your Organization schema, your og:site_name and your logo's alt text. These disagree, so a knowledge panel, a shared link preview and an AI assistant's citation can each show a different name. Found: " + '; '.join(examples) + '.'
findings.fix: 'Pick the exact string you want to be known by (including capitalisation and whether the legal suffix is part of it) and use it verbatim in the Organization schema `name`, the og:site_name and the suffix of every title tag. The logo link may keep a navigational word: `aria-label="Acme home"` tells a screen-reader user where the link goes, and is not a second brand name.'
findings.evidence: {'variants': [{'name': n, 'seen': variants[n], 'sources': sources[n][:3]} for n in distinct[:6]]}

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your site use a consistent business name?
rows.answer: It compares declared business names while allowing common forms of the same name.
rows.why: Title suffixes and business schema nodes can claim to name the same owner. Reviewing those declarations together helps reveal a template still carrying an earlier name, while the normalisation guards reduce ordinary spelling noise.

condition.text: The check needs at least 3 successful pages and samples the first 40 pages for title, social and logo signals, alongside business schema. Candidate names longer than 60 characters are discarded. Weak variants normally need at least the larger of 2 occurrences or a 0.08 share of the total, while authoritative declarations are retained. Normalisation, writing-system grouping, containment and initialism handling remove apparent differences before distinct names are reported. For example, a name longer than 60 characters is left out of the candidate list.

pages.text: The check uses fields that name the business, such as titles and business markup. Ordinary mentions of other companies in body text are left out. The spelling still needs your review.

reports.text: Remaining distinct names produce a medium-severity finding. A report is a prompt to review the declarations, not an instruction to erase a valid legal name, translated name or trading name without checking its context.

fix.text: Read each cited spelling in its original location. Choose the name that belongs in that field and update stale title suffixes, logo text or business markup. Preserve legal and language distinctions that serve a real purpose. After changing a shared template, check the homepage and an inner page for agreement.

rows.guide_title: What your site says your company is called

review.text: Compare declarations by role before deciding that different spellings conflict. A legal entity, trading name and language-specific name may all have legitimate places. Keep obsolete template values separate from those valid distinctions in your review notes. Update the source component that owns each stale value, then inspect its output again, rather than making unrelated text changes wherever the business happens to be mentioned in an article.

faq.question: Why can a long business name be absent from the name comparison?
faq.answer: Candidate names exceeding 60 characters are discarded. Review a long declaration directly if it falls outside that limit.

faq.question: Does mentioning another company in an article create a name mismatch?
faq.answer: No. Body text mentioning another company is outside the comparison. Business-naming declarations supply the input.

faq.question: How serious are conflicting business-name declarations?
faq.answer: Remaining distinct names lead to a medium-severity finding. Legal, trading and translated names still need review in context.

rows.title: Consistent positioning statement

conditions.expression: any((n * 2 >= len(pages) for (w, n) in vocab.items() if brand not in w and w not in brand))

findings.title: 'No consistent message across your pages'
findings.detail: f'Across {len(pages)} pages with meta descriptions, almost no vocabulary is shared: beyond your own name, hardly a word appears on even half of them. That is the signature of pages written one at a time with no agreed answer to what the company does. A visitor landing on any two of them meets two different businesses, and a language model summarising your site has nothing consistent to say.'
findings.fix: 'Write one sentence naming what you do and who for, then make sure the words in it appear in the description of every significant page. This is not keyword stuffing. It is having a position.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do your page summaries share a clear message?
rows.answer: It checks for shared subject words across page descriptions.
rows.why: Meta descriptions summarise individual pages. Shared terms can show a common subject. Give each description enough detail to explain its own page.

condition.text: The test needs at least 6 indexable pages with nonempty meta descriptions and a supported prose language. It counts meaningful words by page, removing common words and brand terms. Shared words need the larger of 3 appearances or the integer part of a 0.3 share of the sample. At least 2 shared terms suppress the finding. A nonbrand term on at least half the pages also suppresses it. For example, finding 2 qualifying shared terms is enough to suppress this finding.

pages.text: Only descriptions with text enter this comparison. It does not read a positioning document or judge whether every page should use the same sentence.

reports.text: Lack of a shared message produces a medium-severity finding. Shared vocabulary is a clue. Different words can express the same offer, so review the descriptions before deciding that the business message is inconsistent.

fix.text: Compare the affected descriptions with the offer your business actually makes. Keep each summary specific to its page while using clear words for the service or product where they belong. Resolve contradictory claims first. Do not force a repeated keyword into a page whose subject genuinely differs from the rest.

rows.guide_title: When your site stops saying one thing about itself

review.text: Read the descriptions as a group, then return to the purpose of each page. Shared vocabulary can be natural when the pages discuss the same offer. It can also arise from copied summaries. Keep the common subject clear while preserving the detail that distinguishes an individual service or article. Treat the vocabulary result as an editorial prompt, and resolve contradictory statements before trying to increase repeated terms.

faq.question: How many descriptions are needed to compare my site's message?
faq.answer: The sample needs 6 indexable pages or more, each with a nonempty description. Supported prose is also required.

faq.question: How many shared subject terms clear the positioning check?
faq.answer: At least 2 shared terms that meet the frequency rules suppress the finding. Those terms should still make sense for each page.

faq.question: Does matching vocabulary prove my positioning is clear?
faq.answer: No. Shared vocabulary is a clue. A person must decide whether the descriptions express the same real offer.

rows.title: Social profile consistency

findings.title: f'{len(missing)} social profile{plural_s(len(missing))} you link to {is_are(len(missing))} missing from your schema' if declared_anywhere else f'You link to {len(missing)} social profile{plural_s(len(missing))} but declare none in schema'
findings.detail: 'The `sameAs` property in your Organization schema is how Google and AI assistants confirm that this website and those accounts are the same organisation. It is one of the strongest entity signals available and it is free. You are already linking these profiles. They are simply not declared.'
findings.fix: 'Add every official profile URL to the `sameAs` array of your Organization schema on the homepage: "sameAs": [' + ', '.join((f'"{by_platform[p]}"' for p in missing)) + '].'
findings.evidence: {'undeclared': [by_platform[p] for p in missing[:6]], 'declared': sorted(declared)[:6], 'declared_by_script': sorted(scripted)[:6]}

findings.title: f'{len(only_scripted)} social profile{plural_s(len(only_scripted))} {is_are(len(only_scripted))} declared only in markup a script adds'
findings.detail: f"Your schema's `sameAs` names {names}, but that markup is not in the HTML your server sends: a script adds it after the page loads. Google runs the script and reads it. Crawlers that read only the served HTML, which includes the AI crawlers, see no `sameAs` at all, so to them this site and those accounts are not linked."
findings.fix: "Write the JSON-LD block into the page's HTML (the theme template, or your SEO plugin's schema settings) instead of building it in a script. Then open the page source, not the browser inspector, and confirm `sameAs` is there."

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do your social links agree with your markup?
rows.answer: It compares profile platforms linked on the site with those declared in sameAs.
rows.why: Visible links and business markup should describe the identity you intend to publish. A platform-level check can find a gap, but the owner still needs to confirm each account before adding it to a business declaration.

condition.text: The check needs a homepage and at least 3 successful pages. It samples up to 30 pages. A profile is relevant when linked on the homepage or on at least the larger of 2 pages or the rounded-up third of that sample. Content and sharing URLs are excluded. Profile platforms are compared with served sameAs links and script-built declarations. The comparison is by platform rather than exact account URL. For example, a footer profile repeated across the qualifying sample can enter the comparison without a homepage link.

pages.text: The check reads homepage profile links, profiles linked across multiple pages and business markup. You still need to confirm that each account belongs to the business.

reports.text: Missing platforms are low severity when some declarations exist and medium when none do. Script-only declarations can produce a separate notice. The platform comparison does not prove that a linked account and a declared account are the same account.

fix.text: Compare the profile links in your header or footer with the business node. Add the correct owned profiles where missing and remove stale accounts. Inspect script-built declarations in the served document before changing them. Verify the exact account URL yourself, because a matching platform name alone cannot settle ownership.

rows.guide_title: Not every social link on your site is yours

review.text: Compare the actual account addresses as well as their platforms. A platform match can hide a stale account or another organisation's profile, while a missing platform can reveal a declaration gap. Keep only accounts that identify the business in its own markup. Review repeated footer links and served identity nodes together, then inspect any script-built declarations separately before assuming that an initial-source omission means the account was never declared.

faq.question: Does the social-profile check compare exact account addresses?
faq.answer: No. The comparison uses platforms, leaving the exact account URL for you to verify. Matching platforms can still name different accounts.

faq.question: Can a profile linked only in my footer count as relevant?
faq.answer: Yes. Repetition across enough sampled pages can qualify a profile. The test samples up to 30 pages and also considers homepage links.

faq.question: Why can social declarations built by scripts produce a notice?
faq.answer: Script-only declarations are handled separately from served sameAs links. The notice keeps that delivery limit visible.

rows.title: Typography and colour consistency

conditions.expression: all((same(existing, b) for (_, _, existing) in members))
sheets is not None and getattr(sheets, 'ran', False)
len(digits) in (6, 8) and all((c in '0123456789abcdef' for c in digits))
all((0 <= n <= 255 for n in parts))

findings.title: f'{len(fonts)} different typefaces across {len(pages)} pages'

If they are steps in an elevation or shade ramp (a surface and the surface above it) or the same colour tuned for a different theme, such as dark mode or high contrast, that is deliberate and there is nothing to fix; this audit cannot tell that apart from the same colour written twice. presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your site mix too many visual styles?
rows.answer: It counts typefaces and groups nearly identical colours from readable styles.
rows.why: Small differences in style values can be hard to spot by eye while still leaving separate declarations to maintain. The report gives you concrete values to inspect instead of claiming that a count alone proves poor design.

condition.text: The sample needs at least 3 readable pages with font or colour data. Pages left unread because of a stylesheet cap are removed. Too few remaining pages stops the comparison. More than 4 font families produces a low-severity finding. Groups of very similar colours also produce a low finding. Each colour must be within 10.0 RGB distance units and 0.01 opacity units of every other colour in its group. RGB distance is the straight-line distance between the colour channel values. Opacity is measured as a fraction of full opacity. For example, exactly 4 font families stay within the font-count limit.

pages.text: The check counts styles it could read on pages and stylesheets from the same site. When a large enough site has no readable style data, it reports that limit. It leaves the palette unknown.

reports.text: Typeface counts and colour groups are clues for a design review. It does not render screenshots, measure contrast or establish that every close colour pair is accidental. A purposeful colour or font difference can be valid.

fix.text: Compare the listed families and colour groups with your intended styles. Remove unused families and consolidate values that were meant to be identical. Keep deliberate differences such as opacity states. Inspect a representative page after editing the shared stylesheet so that a numerical cleanup does not remove a useful visual distinction.

rows.guide_title: Brand consistency: the question no crawler asks

review.text: Compare the reported style values with your actual design choices. Slightly different colours may be accidental copies or intentional states, and separate fonts may belong to distinct content roles. Keep a value when its purpose is clear. Where duplication was accidental, change the shared declaration and inspect representative content afterwards, including text placed over backgrounds that used the previous colour or typeface choice.

faq.question: How many font families trigger the visual-style finding?
faq.answer: More than 4 font families triggers a low result. The count needs review against the site's intended design.

faq.question: Can unread stylesheets make the site look free of style differences?
faq.answer: A stylesheet cap can leave pages unread and exclude them from the sample. Insufficient readable styles can stop the comparison.

faq.question: Does the visual-style check measure colour contrast?
faq.answer: No. It groups colours and counts fonts; it does not measure contrast. Screenshots are outside its scope.

rows.title: Writing voice consistency

findings.title: 'Your pages are written in noticeably different voices'
findings.detail: f'Average sentence length ranges from {shortest[0]:.0f} words to {longest[0]:.0f} across {len(means)} substantial pages, a spread of {spread:.0f} words. Sentence length is a rough proxy for voice, but a gap this wide almost always means pages written by different people at different times with no shared style, and readers feel it as the site not quite hanging together.'
findings.fix: 'Read the two pages below back to back. If they sound like different companies, that is the finding: write down the three rules that distinguish your voice and bring the outliers in line.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do your pages sound like the same business?
rows.answer: It compares average sentence lengths across substantial pages.
rows.why: Sentence length is a narrow, visible part of writing style. A large spread can help you choose pages to review, while the purpose and audience of those pages still decide whether the difference is a problem.

condition.text: At least 5 indexable pages with at least 250 words and measured rather than estimated word counts are required, together with a supported prose language. Each page needs at least 5 usable sentences. Saved sentence lengths are preferred. The fallback splits up to 20000 characters of prose and keeps sentences with at least 3 words. A population standard deviation below 7.0 words per sentence stops the check. Larger spreads reach the finding. For example, a 250-word article still needs at least 5 usable sentences to enter the comparison.

pages.text: The sample is substantial prose, not short product labels or every successful response. Pages lacking enough usable sentences do not supply an average.

reports.text: The finding is low severity and identifies the shortest and longest sentence-length averages. It does not measure tone, verify authorship or decide whether a technical page should read like a contact page.

fix.text: Read passages from the pages at either end of the comparison. Break dense sentences where a reader would benefit and remove abrupt fragments that obscure meaning. Keep necessary terms and intentional differences between page types. Use the guide to review the whole passage instead of chasing an identical average on every page.

rows.guide_title: When your site sounds like several companies wrote it

review.text: Read the short-sentence and long-sentence pages in their intended context. Instructions, contact details and an explanatory article can have different rhythms without sounding like unrelated businesses. Keep changes focused on passages that are difficult to follow. A shared editing approach can improve clarity, but making every page's arithmetic match would remove useful variety without establishing a consistent tone or a clearer account of the service.

faq.question: How long must pages be for the writing-voice comparison?
faq.answer: Each sampled page needs at least 250 words and enough usable sentences. Estimated word counts are excluded.

faq.question: What sentence-length spread triggers the voice finding?
faq.answer: A standard deviation reaching 7.0 words per sentence can qualify. This compares page averages rather than every sentence individually.

faq.question: Does a voice-consistency finding prove different people wrote the pages?
faq.answer: No. Its low severity reflects a sentence-length clue. The test cannot establish authorship or whether varied page roles justify the difference.

rows.question: Does your copy repeat stock AI phrases?
rows.answer: It flags pages containing multiple phrases from the engine's stock-copy list.
rows.why: Stock wording can say little about the business behind a page. The useful editorial question is whether the affected passage gives the reader information, rather than whether it can be assigned to a particular authoring tool.

condition.text: The check runs for a supported prose language and reads indexable prose. Taxonomy archive URLs are excluded. A page matches when at least 2 distinct entries from the stored phrase list occur in its prose. Repeating the same entry does not create another distinct phrase. The list is a literal set of writing tells, not a model that determines how the text was produced. For example, repeating the same stock phrase still leaves only a single distinct match toward the required 2 phrase matches.

pages.text: Each page supplies its own prose as input. It does not inspect an author's writing history or use a probability score from an AI detector.

reports.text: Matching pages produce a medium-severity finding with the phrases that matched. Their presence does not establish that a machine wrote the page. Review quoted examples and context before rewriting a passage that may be discussing those phrases.

fix.text: Read the marked passage aloud and replace empty claims with an account of what you actually do. Keep real examples, limits and sources close to the statements they support. If the phrase is an example under discussion, review that context before changing it. A phrase list should guide an edit, not decide authorship.

rows.guide_title: Copy that reads as AI-written, and what Check Engine can tell you

review.text: Inspect what the phrase is doing in the passage. A quoted example, a reader's comment and the business's own claim need different editorial treatment. Keep useful information when removing stock wording, and replace vague promises with details you can stand behind. Review the surrounding paragraph after editing so the result reads naturally, rather than substituting a different empty phrase that happens to evade the stored list.

faq.question: How many stock phrases trigger the AI-sounding copy check?
faq.answer: A page must match 2 distinct entries or more from the phrase list. Repetition of a single entry cannot fill that count.

faq.question: Does a stock-phrase match prove an AI wrote my page?
faq.answer: No. The check reports wording patterns with a medium-severity finding. It cannot determine who or what wrote the text.

faq.question: Are taxonomy archives included in the stock-copy phrase test?
faq.answer: No. Taxonomy archive URLs are excluded from the prose sample. The test also requires a language it supports.

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Are different pages making the same promise?
rows.answer: It finds groups of distinct pages whose title subjects overlap after several exclusions.
rows.why: Title overlap can point to pages that promise the same answer. It cannot prove that the pages compete in search, and merging useful pages without reading them could remove a distinction that a short title failed to express.

condition.text: The test excludes the homepage, empty titles and pages with an unambiguous canonical pointing elsewhere. At least 2 usable pages and at least 2 meaningful target words per title are required. Candidate pairs need at least 2 shared meaningful words and an overlap of at least 0.5, calculated as shared title words divided by all distinct title words in the pair. Guards separate products, listings, events, named places, distinct measurements, series entries, section indexes and other distinct subjects before groups are formed. For example, titles sharing fewer than 2 meaningful words cannot form a candidate pair.

pages.text: This comparison uses titles and page context from indexable pages. It is not the body-text duplicate check and does not read search query or ranking data.

reports.text: Groups with different titles produce a medium-severity finding. Identical titles are left to the duplicate-title check. The exclusions are substantial, so a pair sharing ordinary words can still be correctly left out when the pages serve distinct purposes.

fix.text: Read the grouped pages side by side. Make distinct purposes clear in their titles and content. Merge only pages that truly duplicate the same job, then update links and redirects where appropriate. Preserve location, product and series differences when they are useful to visitors, even if some words overlap.

rows.guide_title: Pages competing for the same search

review.text: Compare the jobs performed by grouped pages before merging anything. Similar titles may hide genuinely different products, audiences or questions, while different titles may still lead to almost the same answer. Keep a useful distinction visible in both the promise and the body. If consolidation is appropriate, plan the surviving address and links carefully instead of deleting pages based solely on a title-word relationship.

faq.question: How many shared title words can make pages candidates for overlap?
faq.answer: A candidate pair needs 2 shared meaningful words or more, then meet the overlap limit. Other guards can still keep distinct subjects apart.

faq.question: Can different products with similar titles be excluded from competing-page groups?
faq.answer: Yes. The guards separate products and other distinct subjects before grouping. Shared ordinary words alone do not settle page purpose.

faq.question: Does the competing-pages check use search rankings?
faq.answer: No. It compares titles and page context without reading ranking data. Read the pages before deciding to merge them.

rows.question: Do your articles publish readable dates?
rows.answer: It looks for article pages missing a published or modified date in markup.
rows.why: A date printed for a person and a date attached to an article node serve related readers. The distinction in the report lets you add missing markup without claiming that an already visible date never existed.

condition.text: The sample uses article markup and article-like addresses. A section index with at least 3 child links is left out of address-based selection. At least 3 articles are needed. A finding appears when more than a 0.5 share lacks a machine-readable date. Open Graph article dates and date fields on article objects qualify. A visible date near the start changes severity but leaves the missing markup to fix. For example, a blog section with at least 3 child links can be left out as an index.

pages.text: Indexable article pages supply the comparison. A service page is not automatically an article merely because it contains prose, and a section listing is handled differently from an entry.

reports.text: The finding is low severity if every affected article already shows a visible date, and medium otherwise. It does not compare the date with the age of the facts or verify that a modified date reflects a real edit.

fix.text: Use the true publication and modification dates. Add them to the article markup and show the date clearly near the content when it is useful to readers. Check that the visible date agrees with the structured value. Leave the modification date alone when a rebuild did not change the article itself.

rows.guide_title: How to do a content audit

review.text: Inspect an affected article's opening and its structured dates together. A visible publication date can already tell readers when the article was written. Keep publication and update dates attached to the correct article. Use the date of the actual work when adding or correcting markup.

faq.question: Can a visible article date lower the missing-date finding?
faq.answer: Yes. When every affected article already displays a date, the finding has low severity. Missing markup still needs repair.

faq.question: How many articles are needed to check missing date markup?
faq.answer: The sample needs at least 3 articles. Recognised section listings can be excluded from article selection.

faq.question: Does the article-date check verify that an update date is truthful?
faq.answer: No. The check cannot establish whether an update represents a real edit. Use the date of the actual work.

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your site show who stands behind it?
rows.answer: It checks for trust pages, a route to contact you and article authorship signals.
rows.why: Readers need a way to understand who publishes a page and how to reach them. These observable signals can help with that task, but the code's presence checks do not turn a byline into proof of expertise.

condition.text: The test looks for about and contact pages, an enquiry form with at least 2 fields, and a recognised privacy policy. Missing contact details raise the trust-page finding from low to medium severity. Author names can come from markup or bylines in up to 2000 characters from each of the first 40 successful pages. At least 3 indexable pages with article markup are needed for the missing-author finding. For example, an enquiry form with 2 fields can satisfy the contact-route test.

pages.text: The check reads page addresses, forms, business text and article markup. It looks for who publishes the content and how a visitor can contact them. You need to verify the named people and their roles.

reports.text: Missing authorship is low severity. Trust-page findings name the contact, policy or authorship information the check could not find. An enquiry route can satisfy the contact check without a page named Contact. Review who publishes the content and how visitors can reach them.

fix.text: Publish accurate information about the business and give visitors a working contact route. Attach the real author or responsible organisation to articles. Keep the privacy page linked where people can find it. Check forms and schema before adding duplicate pages merely to satisfy a path-based cue.

rows.guide_title: Trust and authorship signals, and what a crawler can actually see

review.text: Review the contact route as a visitor would use it. A form that looks present can still need a completion test, while an about page can exist without explaining who publishes the material. Keep real identities and responsibilities clear. Add authorship only when it truthfully describes the work, and avoid turning a presence check into an unsupported assertion that every author has expertise the business cannot verify.

faq.question: Can an enquiry form satisfy the trust check without a Contact page?
faq.answer: Yes. An enquiry form can qualify with 2 fields or more. Test the actual route separately.

faq.question: How many marked-up articles are needed for the missing-author test?
faq.answer: It needs at least 3 indexable pages carrying article markup. A smaller article sample does not reach this authorship finding.

faq.question: Does an author name prove expertise in the trust check?
faq.answer: No. Missing authorship is low severity, but a detected byline cannot establish expertise. Confirm the real publisher and their role.

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your content depend on JavaScript?
rows.answer: It reports indexable pages whose initial HTML lacks their main content.
rows.why: Content can be present after loading and absent from the first response. That distinction explains the check without assuming that every reader executes the same scripts or that a missing initial body means the page has no useful content at all.

condition.text: The check reads the crawler's JavaScript-dependent flag and leaves out URLs recognised as intentionally excluded from search. Any remaining affected pages can produce a finding. Severity is high when their share of indexable pages is greater than 0.5, and medium otherwise. The ratio uses the indexable page set, so it does not treat failed responses as readable content. For example, an affected share of exactly 0.5 stays in the medium-severity group.

pages.text: The check uses the crawler's record of pages that need JavaScript. It covers pages intended for search. Script execution time and interactive controls need separate tests.

reports.text: The finding lists affected URLs and their share. A loaded browser view may show text absent from the original response. Inspect both views when reviewing the result.

fix.text: Compare source HTML with the loaded page. Serve the main text, links and essential details from the server or a static build where practical. Test the affected templates after changing their rendering path. Keep scripts for interaction while making the information they enhance available in the first response.

rows.guide_title: How to run a JavaScript SEO audit

review.text: Inspect the main content rather than the presence of script tags. Many pages use scripts while still serving readable text, so scripts alone are not the reported defect. Keep the original response and loaded view side by side during review. A rendering change should preserve the same useful information and working interactions, then make that information available earlier in the response path instead of merely removing visible features.

faq.question: When does JavaScript-dependent content become a high-severity finding?
faq.answer: High severity applies above a 0.5 share of indexable pages. At the boundary, the affected pages stay in the medium group.

faq.question: Do deliberately noindex URLs count toward JavaScript content problems?
faq.answer: The test sets aside pages intentionally excluded from search. Its reported set concerns content meant to be found.

faq.question: Does the JavaScript content check measure interactive controls?
faq.answer: No. Interactive controls need separate tests. This result follows the crawler's record of missing initial content.

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your page declare the language it uses?
rows.answer: It compares a page's declared language with conservative language clues in the text.
rows.why: Your language attribute states how the page should be read. Names, link lists and bilingual passages can confuse a simple text comparison, which is why the code includes guards for each of those patterns.

condition.text: The page needs a language declaration and at least 40 words for language detection. Listing-like text with an anchor share of at least 0.7 is excluded. Name-heavy text is excluded when at least 40 usable words have a capitalised share of at least 0.55. A title favouring the declared language can suppress a mismatch. Bilingual text is accepted when its declared-language share reaches at least 0.4 of the competing language's share. For example, a page with fewer than 40 words cannot enter the language-detection comparison.

pages.text: The check reads page text, titles, language attributes and link labels on pages intended for search. Pages with too little usable text are left out. It leaves their language unknown.

reports.text: Remaining mismatches produce a medium-severity finding. The detector and its language coverage impose limits, so the result needs a human reading of the affected page before a declaration is changed.

fix.text: Read the affected page and confirm the main language. Correct the document language when it is wrong, keeping regional details when they are valid. Review mixed-language sections separately from the page declaration. Use the guide to distinguish a language attribute from alternate-language links, since changing one does not repair the other.

rows.guide_title: hreflang and html lang mismatch

review.text: Ask a fluent reader to review the passage used to detect the language. A list of names or a bilingual passage can be harder to classify than ordinary prose. Keep the declaration tied to the document's main language. Review each translation and retain valid regional forms.

faq.question: How many words are needed to compare declared and detected language?
faq.answer: The text needs 40 words or more plus a language declaration. Shorter passages leave this comparison unmade.

faq.question: Can link-heavy pages be excluded from a language mismatch?
faq.answer: Yes. An anchor share reaching 0.7 can exclude listing-like text. Names and bilingual passages also have guards.

faq.question: How serious is a remaining language mismatch?
faq.answer: It gets a medium-severity finding. A fluent reader should check the text before the document declaration is changed.

rows.title: Language coverage

findings.detail: f"The site's content is in {name}. This audit's checks for calls to action, social proof, contact wording, question-style headings and generic AI-sounding copy all work by matching English phrasing, so they were skipped rather than reporting everything as missing. Treat them as unknown, not as passing.\n\nEverything structural still ran and is fully valid: indexing, canonicals, hreflang, schema, speed, security, links, images and headings do not depend on language. Word counts and title lengths are measured in a script-aware way, so they are comparable to an English site."
findings.fix: 'No action needed. Review calls to action, proof and contact paths by hand, or run the audit against an English version of the site if one exists.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Can this audit judge your site's prose language?
rows.answer: It states when language-dependent copy checks were skipped.
rows.why: Clear limits matter when a report contains a mixture of measured results and withheld judgements. Naming the language limit helps you see where the tool's answer ends and a reader who knows the language must take over.

condition.text: The check asks whether the site's prose language is supported. A supported language ends the test without a finding. Otherwise it names the detected language and explains the limit. It assigns no content-quality score or sentence-length cutoff.

pages.text: This is an audit-scope notice based on the saved language decision. It describes which copy checks can run, rather than inspecting every sentence for a writing fault.

reports.text: The notice names the language limit. Copy checks that need to understand that language are withheld. Checks of status codes, markup and links may still run. Review the text with a fluent reader.

fix.text: Have a fluent reader review the copy using the same questions the skipped checks would ask. Check whether the page says what it does, answers its subject and gives a clear next step. Correct a mistaken language declaration when needed, but keep the site's real language instead of translating it solely to remove this notice.

rows.guide_title: hreflang and html lang mismatch

review.text: Separate a withheld judgement from a clean result in your review notes. A page can have well-formed markup while its prose remains outside the tool's language coverage. Keep a fluent person's review attached to the copy decisions that need it. Changing an attribute to a supported language without changing the actual language would misdescribe the page and would not supply the missing understanding this notice identifies.

faq.question: Does an unsupported prose language mean my content is poor?
faq.answer: No. The notice explains a language limit and assigns no content-quality score. Have a fluent reader assess the prose.

faq.question: Can markup checks run when language-dependent copy checks are skipped?
faq.answer: Yes. Markup and links may be checked independently of prose. Status-code tests can also run when language understanding is unavailable.

faq.question: Does a supported prose language trigger a scope warning?
faq.answer: No. A supported language ends this test without a finding. The notice is reserved for unsupported prose.
