presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Did unfinished text reach your public pages?
rows.answer: It searches for known filler text while excluding many cases where a page discusses it.
rows.why: An unfinished template field can appear outside the main body, including in the text used to describe a page. That is why the check looks beyond visible paragraphs while trying to preserve useful discussions of placeholder examples.

condition.text: The test reads indexable prose and snippet fields. It uses a literal marker list, with separate guards for comments, hidden text, quoted discussion, examples and redaction masks. Context checks use a 160-character window. Short holding-page wording, longer discussions and Latin filler have different guards. The snippet announcement case uses a 12-word limit, while the holding-page test uses 200 words. These are context rules, not a general quality score. For example, short announcement wording in a snippet is assessed with the 12-word limit.

pages.text: Main prose, selected headings, descriptions and social or schema snippet text can supply a match. A marker confined to a hidden or comment area is not automatically treated as the page's own unfinished copy.

reports.text: Confirmed matches produce a high-severity finding. The report still needs context review, especially on documentation that quotes a marker deliberately. A pattern match does not establish that every sentence containing the words is unfinished.

fix.text: Open the cited field and replace actual filler with finished text, or remove the unfinished page from public use until it is ready. Inspect metadata as well as the body. If the text is a quoted example, check its context before editing. Fix the template that supplied it when the same field appears across pages.

rows.guide_title: Mentioning filler is not shipping filler

review.text: Check the field where a marker appeared before changing the page's main text. An unfinished social description and an unfinished paragraph can come from different templates. Keep legitimate examples of filler wording when they are clearly part of an explanation. Repair the source of actual placeholder values and inspect the final served output, since editing a visible paragraph alone may leave the same unfinished text in metadata.

faq.question: How much surrounding text is checked for a placeholder marker?
faq.answer: The search uses a 160-character window. Additional guards distinguish examples and quoted discussion from unfinished copy.

faq.question: Are snippet announcements and holding pages tested with the same word limit?
faq.answer: No. Snippet announcements use a 12-word limit; holding-page checks use 200 words. Each has its own context rules.

faq.question: How serious is a confirmed placeholder in published content?
faq.answer: It receives a high-severity finding. Read the marked passage in context before replacing a legitimate example.

rows.title: Readability

findings.title: f'{len(dense)} page{plural_s(len(dense))} {is_are(len(dense))} hard to read'
findings.detail: f'Average sentence length above 25 words. Worst: {dense[0][1]:.0f} words per sentence on {dense[0][0].url}. Dense prose loses readers and gives AI answer engines nothing short enough to quote.'
findings.fix: 'Break long sentences in two. Aim for 15–20 words on average, and use lists where you are enumerating things.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Are your sentences hard to follow?
rows.answer: It finds substantial pages whose usable sentences are long on average.
rows.why: Long sentences can ask a reader to hold several ideas at once. The code measures their length as a review cue, while a human still decides which ideas belong together and which terms the intended reader needs.

condition.text: The test needs a supported prose language and a page intended for search with at least 200 words. It uses recorded sentence lengths when available. Otherwise it splits the prose into sentences and keeps those longer than 2 words. At least 5 usable sentences are needed. An average greater than 25 words produces a finding. Exactly 25 words per sentence stays within the limit. For example, an average of exactly 25 words per sentence stays within the limit.

pages.text: Only pages with enough prose and usable sentences enter the calculation. It does not assign a school reading age or analyse the meaning of technical terms.

reports.text: The finding is low severity and reports the pages with dense sentence structure. An average can hide both short and long sentences, so use it to choose passages for review rather than treating every sentence on a reported page as a fault.

fix.text: Read the affected paragraphs and put the main point early. Split a sentence when it joins separate ideas, and replace vague phrases with concrete words. Keep a longer sentence when its structure is clear. Review the edited passage for meaning before checking whether the average changed.

rows.guide_title: How to do a content audit

review.text: Read a dense passage for the ideas it asks the reader to hold together. A list, a quotation and a long explanation can affect sentence parsing differently. Keep necessary technical meaning while separating unrelated clauses. After editing, read the whole paragraph again rather than checking the average alone. A shorter sentence can still be confusing if its subject, action or relationship to the previous sentence is unclear.

faq.question: Is an average of 25 words per sentence too long for this check?
faq.answer: No. Exactly 25 words per sentence passes the length comparison. Only a higher average reaches the finding.

faq.question: How much text is needed for the sentence-readability sample?
faq.answer: A page needs at least 200 words and enough usable sentences. Unsupported prose is left out.

faq.question: Does a readability finding mean every sentence needs shortening?
faq.answer: No. It is a low severity result based on an average. Read individual passages to find where the structure becomes hard to follow.

rows.title: Thin content

predicates.expression: sum((1 for w in words if w in anchor_words)) / len(words) >= ARCHIVE_ANCHOR_SHARE

thresholds.expression: sum((1 for w in words if w in anchor_words)) / len(words) >= ARCHIVE_ANCHOR_SHARE

findings.title: f'{len(indexable_boilerplate)} search or utility page{plural_s(len(indexable_boilerplate))} {is_are(len(indexable_boilerplate))} indexable'
findings.detail: 'Site search, cart, login and confirmation pages carry almost no content because that is what they are for. These are indexable, so Google can put them in front of someone searching for your brand, and internal search results in particular are something Google asks site owners to keep out of the index.\n\n' + '; '.join((p.url for p in indexable_boilerplate[:3]))
findings.fix: 'Add `<meta name="robots" content="noindex, follow">` to these pages. Keep `follow` so the links on them are still crawled. Nothing needs writing. These pages are doing their job.'

findings.title: f'{len(empty_archives)} archive page{plural_s(len(empty_archives))} ' + (f"{verb('list', len(empty_archives))} almost nothing" if biggest < VERY_THIN_WORDS else f"{verb('carry', len(empty_archives))} little beyond the headlines {('it links' if one_archive else 'they link')} to")
findings.detail: ('This page is an index' if one_archive else 'These pages are indexes') + ' (an author, tag or category listing), and ' + ('its body text is almost entirely the headlines it links to. ' if one_archive else 'their body text is almost entirely the headlines they link to. ') + (f'The whole page is {biggest} word{plural_s(biggest)} ' if one_archive else f'The longest is {biggest} word{plural_s(biggest)} ') + 'including the list itself, so there is very little for Google to ' + f'rank {them_it(len(empty_archives))} on, and a taxonomy that ' + 'generates hundreds of them puts hundreds of near-empty URLs into ' + 'the index.\n\n' + '; '.join((p.url for p in empty_archives[:3]))
findings.fix: 'Do not delete these. Other pages link to them: an article\'s byline points at its author page, so removing them breaks those links, and author pages are part of how Google assesses who stands behind the writing. Decide instead whether the archive should be generated at all when it has one entry; if it should, add `<meta name="robots" content="noindex, follow">` to the near-empty ones so the links on them are still crawled. Nothing here needs writing.'

findings.title: f'{len(very_thin)} page{plural_s(len(very_thin))} {has_have(len(very_thin))} almost no content' + (' in the HTML as served' if all((p.hydrates_client_side or p.served_heavy_empty for p in very_thin)) else '')
findings.detail: f'Under {VERY_THIN_WORDS} words of body text. Pages this sparse rarely rank for anything and, in volume, drag down how Google assesses the whole site.' + _unrendered_caveat(very_thin)
findings.fix: 'For each: either write real content answering what a customer wants to know, merge it into a stronger related page, or remove it and redirect.\n\nOne exception, and this audit cannot tell it apart from the rest: if a page here is an index (a category listing, an A–Z, a tag or author page), its job is to point elsewhere and a low word count is normal. Judge that one on whether the list is worth having and whether anything links to it, not on its length, and do not delete it.'

findings.title: f'{len(thin)} page{plural_s(len(thin))} {is_are(len(thin))} thin ({VERY_THIN_WORDS}–{THIN_WORDS} words)' + (' in the HTML as served' if all((p.hydrates_client_side or p.served_heavy_empty for p in thin)) else '')
findings.detail: 'There is not enough here to answer a search intent fully, so these pages lose to competitors covering the same topic properly.' + _unrendered_caveat(thin)
findings.fix: "Expand each with the specifics its reader needs: for a commercial page that means what's included, pricing signals, service area and FAQs.\n\nOne exception, and this audit cannot tell it apart from the rest: if a page here is an index (a category listing, an A–Z, a tag or author page), its job is to point elsewhere and a low word count is normal. Judge that one on whether the list is worth having and whether anything links to it, not on its length, and do not expand it into an article."

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does a page have too little useful text?
rows.answer: It separates short content, sparse archives and intentionally indexable utility pages.
rows.why: Short text can mean a missing answer, a useful index or content assembled after loading. Distinguishing those cases matters before adding paragraphs, because extra words cannot repair a rendering fault or make an empty archive useful by themselves.

condition.text: The main cutoffs are fewer than 60 words for very thin content and fewer than 150 words for thin content. JavaScript-dependent pages and useful hubs are treated separately. A hub needs at least 3 child targets. Archive detection uses taxonomy paths or a prose anchor share of at least 0.6 with qualifying anchor phrases of at least 4 words. Utility URLs and archive-like pages are reported differently from ordinary content. For example, a page with exactly 60 words is outside the very-thin group but remains below 150 words.

pages.text: Indexable page prose supplies word counts. The check includes caveats for pages whose browser-built content may be fuller than the served HTML, so the reported count needs to be read with its source view in mind.

reports.text: Ordinary very thin content is high severity. Thin content is medium. Utility and sparse archive findings are low. Use these cutoffs to choose pages for review. Judge whether each page answers its visitor's question before adding text.

fix.text: Decide what the page should help a visitor do. Supply missing information on genuine content pages, improve archive listings where useful and keep utility pages out of search when that is their intended role. Check the browser view before rewriting a page whose text is absent only from the initial HTML.

rows.guide_title: How to fix thin content pages

review.text: Compare the reported word count with what the page is meant to do. A short utility response and a useful service explanation have different jobs. Keep an archive useful through its listings instead of filling it with unrelated prose. If content appears only after loading, address that delivery issue before commissioning replacement text. Review usefulness directly, because crossing a word-count cutoff does not establish that a question was answered.

faq.question: What word count puts an ordinary page in the very-thin group?
faq.answer: Ordinary pages below 60 words enter the very-thin group. Utility pages, useful hubs and script-dependent pages have separate treatment.

faq.question: Does a page with 60 words still count as thin?
faq.answer: Yes. It remains below 150 words, the ordinary thin-content limit. Passing that count alone would not establish usefulness.

faq.question: Are sparse archives treated as severely as very thin articles?
faq.answer: No. Sparse archive findings are low, while ordinary very thin content can be high severity.

rows.title: Topics worth writing about

conditions.expression: not outcome or not getattr(outcome, 'ran', False)

findings.title: 'Tell this audit what this site is about to get topic suggestions' if not_asked else 'This audit could not look up what people search for'

'This audit can list real questions people search for around your subject, and which of them no page here answers. It works the subject out from what your pages say (the words that recur across your titles and headings), and this site did not give it enough to be sure.

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do search suggestions point to missing topics?
rows.answer: It compares saved demand queries with words already used in page titles and headings.
rows.why: Suggestions can expose subjects worth reviewing, but a vocabulary gap is only a starting point. Reading the existing content and checking whether the subject belongs to your business prevents a list of suggestions from becoming an automatic publishing plan.

condition.text: The demand-topics connector must have run. From up to 30 top queries, it filters inferred subjects when present and collects covered words from up to 120 indexable pages. A query is a gap when its meaningful words are not all in the covered set. At most 12 gaps are shown. If topics were unavailable, the code emits a notice explaining the missing input instead of inventing suggestions. For example, a report stops at 12 suggestions even when more queries qualify as gaps.

pages.text: Saved query suggestions and the site's titles and headings supply the comparison. The union of words across pages is used, so it is not a full review of whether a particular page answers a query.

reports.text: Topic gaps are low severity. Unavailable suggestions are notices. It does not supply search volume, prove demand size or confirm that the business should publish on every suggested topic.

fix.text: Read the suggested query and find any existing page that answers it. Improve that page when it already serves the need. Add new content when the subject fits the business and needs an answer. Use only demand estimates you can support. Explain where the suggestions came from.

rows.guide_title: How to do a content audit

review.text: Read the suggested query as a real question and check where the site answers it. A topic can be explained in the body even when its wording is absent from a heading. Base the content decision on the business and the reader's question. Check demand separately before assigning an audience size to a saved suggestion.

faq.question: How many topic-gap suggestions can the report show?
faq.answer: It shows at most 12 suggestions. More eligible queries do not lengthen that displayed list.

faq.question: Can the audit invent topics when the demand connector has no data?
faq.answer: No. The demand-topics connector supplies the input. When suggestions are unavailable, the result explains that limit instead of inventing topics.

faq.question: Do topic-gap suggestions include search volume?
faq.answer: No. The check does not supply search volume or establish demand size. Treat each saved query as a prompt to review existing answers.

rows.title: Published email addresses that cannot receive mail

findings.title: f'Email at {domain} cannot receive mail'
findings.detail: f"{', '.join(addresses[:3])} {('is' if len(addresses) == 1 else 'are')} published on {len(pages)} page{plural_s(len(pages))}, and {domain} {data['reason']}. Anyone writing to that address gets a bounce; you get nothing, and no record that they tried."
findings.fix: (f'Replace the domain in that address with your real one. {domain} is a server address, not a domain name, and no mail can ever be delivered to it: DNS records cannot be published for an IP. An address like this is left behind when a site is moved between servers and the old host is written into the content; search your pages and your theme settings for {domain} and you will usually find links and images pointing at it too.' if looks_like_ip else f'{domain} is not a domain this site appears to control, so there are no DNS records here for you to add. If this address is an example in documentation, nothing needs doing. If it is meant to reach someone, replace it with an address at a domain that receives mail, or a form that posts somewhere.' if not ours else f'Either add MX records for {domain} pointing at a mail host, or replace the address with a channel that works: a form that posts somewhere, or an address at a domain that already receives mail.') + ' Removing it is better than leaving it: a visitor who sees no address looks for another route, and a visitor who emails a dead one believes they have contacted you.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Can your published email addresses receive mail?
rows.answer: It reports published email domains that the saved mail test says cannot accept mail.
rows.why: A visible email link is a route a visitor may use to contact you. Without mail delivery, a domain breaks the contact route even if the link itself is correctly written and the website still loads.

condition.text: The mail-delivery measurement must be available. Domains from mail links on successful pages are joined to saved domain results. Only a result with accepts-mail explicitly false and a published address can produce a finding. A conclusive result on a static host raises severity. Domain validity, IP-like forms and the relationship to the site's own host inform the explanation and suggested fix.

pages.text: The check uses published email links and the recorded domain-level mail test. A result applies to the domain. Checking whether a specific mailbox accepts messages needs a separate test.

reports.text: Severity is high for the conclusive static-host case and medium otherwise. This is a domain delivery test, not a promise that a particular inbox exists or that a person will answer a message.

fix.text: Confirm the intended address with the person who receives enquiries. Correct spelling errors in the link and its visible text. For an address you own, review the domain's mail setup with its provider and retest delivery. Do not replace a valid address merely because an inconclusive network result needs investigation.

rows.guide_title: The contact address that cannot receive mail

review.text: Inspect both the visible address and the hidden mail destination. A working website domain can have a separate mail configuration, and a correctly written link cannot repair that configuration by itself. Keep domain-level delivery details distinct from a mailbox test. When another provider manages enquiries, confirm the intended destination with its owner before replacing a published address or changing records that serve other business mail.

faq.question: Does the mail-link check test whether a particular inbox exists?
faq.answer: No. It uses domain delivery results rather than testing a particular inbox. A domain result cannot promise that someone will answer.

faq.question: When can a published email address produce a dead-contact finding?
faq.answer: The saved result must say accepts-mail explicitly false. Unknown delivery results cannot establish that the published address is unusable.

faq.question: Does a conclusive mail failure on a static host change severity?
faq.answer: Yes. The conclusive static-host case is high severity. Other qualifying failures are medium.

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Can visitors send you an enquiry?
rows.answer: It finds long forms and checks whether key pages offer a contact route.
rows.why: A visitor may need to call, write or book rather than complete a form. Keeping those routes in the check prevents a site with a working off-site booking service from being treated as unable to take enquiries.

condition.text: An enquiry form with 6 or more counted fields is flagged as long. The check also reviews key pages for forms, direct contact links, recognised booking or messaging services and useful contact-page links. If every target lacks a route, it can report no way to make contact. That absence claim needs a supported prose language. Field counting can still run in other languages.

pages.text: Form scanning reads indexable pages. Contact-route review uses the homepage and pages recognised as selling, falling back to up to 5 shallow indexable pages when no such targets are found.

reports.text: Long forms are medium severity. No contact route across the target set is high. The check recognises several routes besides an embedded form and does not judge whether every field is necessary for your actual service.

fix.text: Walk through the real enquiry route from a key page. Remove fields you do not need before the first reply and make the action clear. Keep necessary fields for the service you provide. If the route uses another service, verify the destination and link wording before adding a duplicate form solely to change the report.

rows.guide_title: A form is a call to action

review.text: Follow the enquiry route through to its intended destination, including any booking or messaging service outside the page. A route can be useful without an embedded form. Keep each requested field tied to information needed at that stage. When reviewing a long form, distinguish essential service details from questions that could wait for a reply, then check that the shorter route still supports the business's real workflow.

faq.question: How many fields make an enquiry form long in this audit?
faq.answer: A form reaches the long-form finding at 6 or more counted fields. Review whether each request is needed before the first reply.

faq.question: Can a booking service count as a way to contact my business?
faq.answer: Yes. Recognised booking or messaging services can qualify alongside forms and contact links. An embedded form is not the only route.

faq.question: Is a missing contact route more serious than a long form?
faq.answer: Yes. No route across the target pages is high severity. Long forms are medium severity.

rows.title: Funnel coverage

findings.title: 'The site only serves buyers who are already ready'
findings.detail: f"Missing: {'; '.join(missing)}. Most people searching are not ready to buy on the first visit: they are researching. With nothing for that stage you only capture the small fraction at the very bottom of the funnel, and you compete for the most expensive keywords to do it. This is also where AI answer engines look for content to cite."
findings.fix: "Write the answers to the questions customers actually ask before buying: cost, timelines, what's included, how you compare. One page per question, each linking to the relevant service page."

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your site help people before they buy?
rows.answer: It looks for page paths that suggest educational and comparison content.
rows.why: Someone learning about a problem may need a different answer from someone comparing providers. Those are distinct page jobs, and the check provides a small inventory check for whether the site appears to serve either stage.

condition.text: At least 6 indexable pages are needed. Educational paths include blog, guide, resources, learn, FAQ and related sections. Comparison paths include compare, alternatives, reviews, case studies, testimonials and work examples. Missing both groups produces medium severity. A single missing group produces low severity. This is a path-based presence test, not a reading of the persuasive quality of every page. For example, a site with 6 indexable pages can enter the section-presence check.

pages.text: The check searches the site's page inventory for recognised path shapes. A useful page under an unusual address may not match those shapes even when its content helps visitors make a decision.

reports.text: The finding names the missing content groups. It does not establish that a business needs a large publishing programme or that adding a section will create demand for its services.

fix.text: Review the questions customers ask before an enquiry and while comparing options. Link existing useful answers clearly, including work examples where relevant. Add a page only when it can answer a real question that the current site leaves open. Keep the address and title descriptive without renaming good pages merely to match a path list.

rows.guide_title: Conversion audit

review.text: Compare the apparent content groups with actual customer questions. A path can look educational while holding little help, and a useful comparison may live outside the recognised path list. Keep the decision tied to what the business can explain accurately. Before creating a section, identify a missing answer and the page that should provide it, rather than assuming a larger page inventory is itself a better buying experience.

faq.question: How many pages are needed to check educational and comparison sections?
faq.answer: The site needs at least 6 indexable pages. Recognised educational and comparison paths then supply the clues.

faq.question: Is a missing comparison section as serious as missing both content groups?
faq.answer: No. Missing one group gets low severity. The absence of both educational and comparison groups receives medium.

faq.question: Does the funnel check read whether my guides persuade visitors?
faq.answer: No. The path-based presence test uses addresses as clues. Useful answers under unusual paths can be missed.

rows.title: Title / headline consistency

findings.title: f"{len(mismatched)} page{plural_s(len(mismatched))} {verb('promise', len(mismatched))} one thing in search and another on the page"
findings.detail: f'The title tag and the H1 share almost no words, so a visitor who clicks expecting one thing lands on something that reads as different. Example. Title: "{example.title[:70]}" vs headline: "{example_headline[:70]}"'
findings.fix: 'Make the on-page headline restate the promise from the title. They do not have to match word for word, but they must clearly be about the same thing.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your headline match your page title?
rows.answer: It compares meaningful words in the title with a page-specific main heading.
rows.why: A page title and the headline a visitor reaches should make sense together. The code checks a visible part of that relationship without claiming to know the full intent of a search or the visitor's next action.

condition.text: The check runs for a supported prose language and requires both a title and a nonempty main heading. Common page-kind words, simple plurals and recognised equivalent contact phrases are normalised. On a sample of at least 5 successful pages, headings present on at least a 0.6 share are treated as shared furniture. The first remaining heading is preferred. A meaningful-word overlap below 0.2 produces a finding, except for a title made only of brand words. For example, a meaningful-word overlap of exactly 0.2 does not fall below the mismatch limit.

pages.text: Indexable titles and main headings supply the comparison. Shared headings are identified from successful pages so that a repeated business heading does not automatically replace the page's actual subject.

reports.text: The finding is low severity. Word overlap is a narrow clue and can miss synonyms, so review the title and headline as promises to a reader before changing either field.

fix.text: Read the title as it would appear in a search result, then read the first specific headline. Make both describe the same page job. Preserve useful differences in wording and avoid copying the title mechanically when a clearer headline works. Check a shared template if the wrong heading appears across several unrelated pages.

rows.guide_title: Conversion audit

review.text: Read the title without the headline, then read the headline without the title. Each should make a truthful promise about the content that follows. Keep meaningful differences in phrasing when they help a reader. If a repeated business heading displaced the specific subject, inspect the shared template before rewriting good content, and confirm that the actual page heading remains clear in the served outline after the change.

faq.question: How much title-to-heading overlap avoids a message-match finding?
faq.answer: A meaningful-word overlap of 0.2 passes the comparison. Lower overlap can qualify after the wording guards are applied.

faq.question: Can a repeated business heading be ignored when checking my page headline?
faq.answer: Yes. A heading seen across a 0.6 share of a large enough sample is treated as shared furniture. The comparison prefers a page-specific heading.

faq.question: Does a title-headline mismatch prove my wording misleads readers?
faq.answer: No. The low severity result is a word-overlap clue. Synonyms and page purpose still need a person's review.

rows.title: Calls to action

conditions.expression: all((c.strip().lower() in ('submit', 'send', 'go', 'ok', 'continue', 'next', 'click here') for c in page.ctas))

findings.title: f'{len(without)} key page{plural_s(len(without))} {has_have(len(without))} no clear call to action'
findings.detail: 'No button or link on these pages asks the visitor to do anything: no quote request, no booking, no purchase, no contact. Every visit these pages earn from search or paid campaigns arrives, reads, and leaves. This is the single most expensive gap on the list because it wastes traffic you already have.'
findings.fix: 'Add one primary action per page, phrased as the outcome the visitor wants ("Get a free quote", "Book a callback") rather than the mechanism ("Submit"). Repeat it near the top and again at the bottom of long pages.'

findings.title: f"{len(vague)} page{plural_s(len(vague))} {verb('use', len(vague))} generic button labels"
findings.detail: 'Buttons labelled "Submit" or "Send" describe what the software does, not what the visitor gets. Outcome-led labels reliably convert better because they restate the benefit at the moment of decision.'
findings.fix: 'Rewrite each button as the result: "Get my free estimate", "Book my appointment", "Send my enquiry".'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do your key pages ask for a clear next step?
rows.answer: It checks for an action or useful enquiry form on the pages most likely to sell.
rows.why: An action label tells a visitor what they can do next. A form or link can already serve that job, which is why the presence test allows more than a single style of sales button.

condition.text: The test needs a supported prose language. A recognised call to action or a form with at least 2 fields counts as a next step. Pages without either are reported separately. When actions exist, it checks whether all their labels are generic, such as Submit or Continue. Ordinary links are kept out of that label test. For example, a form with 2 fields can count as a next step without a separate action button.

pages.text: Targets are the homepage and recognised selling pages intended for search. When none match, the check uses up to 5 shallow indexable pages. It reads recorded action labels and forms. Completing a purchase or submitting an enquiry needs a separate test.

reports.text: Missing actions are high severity and weak labels medium. It does not test whether the destination completes a sale, whether an off-site service works or whether a particular button colour attracts attention.

fix.text: Choose the next useful action for each key page. Name it in words that explain the result, and link it to the correct form, booking page or product step. Test that route yourself. Keep labels consistent with what happens after clicking, rather than adding a vague action just to satisfy the presence test.

rows.guide_title: A form is a call to action

review.text: Follow the next step named by the action. A clear label is useful only when the destination carries out the promise, and an enquiry form may already provide an appropriate action. Keep the page's purpose in mind when choosing what to emphasise. Avoid adding several competing buttons simply to increase detected actions. Review whether a new visitor can understand the route and complete it without guessing. After a trial of the route, record where a visitor lands and whether that destination still matches the action label.

faq.question: Can a form count as my page's next step without another button?
faq.answer: Yes. A form containing 2 fields or more can qualify without another action button. Test the destination yourself.

faq.question: Are generic action labels as serious as having no action?
faq.answer: No. Missing actions are high severity, while weak labels are medium. Read the wording in the context of its destination.

faq.question: Which pages are checked for missing calls to action?
faq.answer: The homepage and selling pages are preferred. Otherwise, 5 shallow indexable pages is the fallback cap.

rows.title: Pricing transparency

constants.name: _PRICE
constants.expression: matcher(('$', '£', '€', '¥', '￥', '₩', '₹', '₽', '₺', 'R$', 'CHF', 'kr', 'zł', '円', '元', '원', 'pricing', 'price', 'prices', 'per month', '/mo', 'per year', '/yr', 'free trial', 'starting at', 'from just', 'quote', 'quotes', 'estimate', 'estimates', 'no obligation', 'how much', '価格', '税込', '送料', 'preis', 'prix', 'precio', 'prezzo', 'preço', 'цена', '가격', '价格', '售价'))

findings.title: f'No indication of cost {ctx.scope(30).where()}'
findings.detail: "No prices, price ranges, 'from' figures, or even a free-quote offer appear anywhere. Cost is the first question almost every buyer has, and a site that refuses to address it loses the visitors who assume the answer is 'expensive'. It also removes the strongest thing an AI assistant could cite about you."
findings.fix: "You do not have to publish a rate card. A range ('most repairs are $150–$400'), a starting price, or a clear 'free, no-obligation quote' all answer the question well enough to keep the visitor moving."

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your site explain cost or how to get a quote?
rows.answer: It looks for a pricing route or recognisable cost language.
rows.why: Cost can be explained as a price, a range or a route to an estimate. The check includes quote language because a business can be transparent about the next step without publishing a fixed amount for work that varies.

condition.text: The check runs only for a supported prose language. It first looks for pricing, plans, prices, rates, cost, quote or estimate paths. Across the sample, it also reads up to 6000 characters from each of the first 30 indexable pages for currency, price, trial, quote and estimate signals. A finding appears only when neither a matching page route nor a price-language signal was found. For example, a quote invitation in the first 6000 text characters of a sampled page can satisfy the wording test.

pages.text: The check uses the page list and sampled text. A quote invitation can qualify. You still need to review whether the visitor can understand the cost or the steps to get a quote.

reports.text: The absence finding is medium severity. A detected currency symbol or quote word can satisfy the check, so a clean result does not establish that visitors receive a complete or clear account of cost.

fix.text: Read the main buying pages as a new visitor. Explain the real cost where it is known, or say how to request a quote and what information is needed. Keep any stated amount current. Link the cost explanation from the relevant page and check that the visible wording gives more help than an isolated currency sign.

rows.guide_title: Conversion audit

review.text: Inspect the cost explanation in the context of the service. A quote request can be appropriate for variable work, while a fixed offer may need a clear amount and conditions. Keep the explanation honest about what is known. Verify any published amount against the business's current source before editing it, and make sure the route to further pricing information is easy to understand from the relevant buying page.

faq.question: Can a quote invitation satisfy the cost-information check?
faq.answer: Yes. The quote and estimate signals can qualify, so the test does not require every business to publish a fixed price.

faq.question: How far into page text does the pricing check read?
faq.answer: It searches up to 6000 characters on each sampled page. Important cost wording beyond that sample can be missed.

faq.question: Does a clean pricing result prove my costs are clearly explained?
faq.answer: No. A currency symbol can satisfy the test. Read the full offer and its terms to decide whether the explanation helps.

rows.title: Social proof

constants.name: _PROOF
constants.expression: matcher(('testimonial', 'testimonials', 'review', 'reviews', 'rated', 'rating', 'ratings', '5 stars', 'five stars', 'trusted by', 'customers say', 'clients say', 'case study', 'case studies', 'success story', 'as seen in', 'featured in', 'award', 'awards', 'award-winning', 'certified', 'accredited', 'guarantee', 'guaranteed', 'money back', 'satisfaction guaranteed', 'trustpilot', 'google reviews', '★', 'licensed and insured', 'licensed & insured', 'licensed, insured', 'licensed and bonded', 'licensed, bonded', 'bonded and insured', 'fully licensed', 'fully insured'))

findings.title: 'No social proof on any conversion page'
findings.detail: 'No testimonials, reviews, ratings, case studies, client logos, certifications or guarantees appear on the pages meant to convert. Proof is what closes the gap between interest and action for a visitor who has never heard of you, which describes almost everyone arriving from a campaign.'
findings.fix: 'Put two or three specific customer quotes near each call to action, with a real name and location. Add your review rating, any certifications, and a guarantee if you offer one. Specific beats glowing.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do your selling pages show reasons to trust you?
rows.answer: It looks for recognised proof language on key conversion pages.
rows.why: A visitor may want to see work examples or real customer experiences before making contact. Check the truth and relevance of any claim you publish. The phrase test can only locate wording for you to review.

condition.text: The test requires a supported prose language and a nonempty target set. Each target is searched across up to 8000 characters of text plus its subheadings for the stored proof phrases. A finding appears only when every target lacks a match. The phrase set includes review, testimonial, certification, guarantee and work-example language. It does not verify the underlying claim or count satisfied customers. For example, a work example beyond the first 8000 text characters needs a qualifying subheading to be found by this search.

pages.text: Targets are the indexable homepage and selling pages, or up to 5 shallow indexable pages when the site has no recognised selling targets.

reports.text: The finding is medium severity. You need to review each phrase in context and check its basis. The phrase list may also miss genuine examples written in other words.

fix.text: Publish only reviews, qualifications, guarantees and work examples you can support. Put them near the offer they describe. Keep the source clear and get any permission needed. Review each claim again when the service changes.

rows.guide_title: Conversion audit

review.text: Review each proof statement for its basis and relevance to the offer beside it. A recognised review word may describe the topic of a discussion. Keep the source and permission record for published reviews. State qualifications accurately and confirm their current scope. Check that approved examples still apply when an offer changes.

faq.question: How much text is searched for testimonials and work examples?
faq.answer: Each target contributes up to 8000 characters plus subheadings. Wording outside that text window may be missed.

faq.question: Does the social-proof check verify that a testimonial is true?
faq.answer: No. It looks for stored proof phrases, leaving the underlying claim unverified. Keep your own source and permission records.

faq.question: When does missing proof language trigger a selling-page finding?
faq.answer: The result requires that every target lacks a match. A qualifying proof phrase on a target can prevent the absence finding.

rows.title: Phone links that will not dial

conditions.expression: len(part) == 2 and part.isalpha() or (len(part) == 3 and part.isdigit())

findings.title: 'Phone links contain letters and will not dial'
findings.detail: f'{len(nums)} phone number{plural_s(len(nums))} {is_are(len(nums))} linked with letters in the href ({_example(nums)}) on {pages} page{plural_s(pages)}. RFC 3966 does not support vanity notation because the mapping from letters to digits is not uniform internationally, so tapping the link on a phone dials nothing. The printed number{plural_s(len(nums))} can stay as {they_are(len(nums))}; the link{plural_s(len(nums))} behind {them_it(len(nums))} cannot.'
findings.fix: 'Keep the memorable number as the visible text and put digits in the href: YOUR MEMORABLE NUMBER.'

findings.title: 'Phone links write an extension in a way the tel: standard does not define'
findings.detail: f"{len(nums)} phone number{plural_s(len(nums))} {is_are(len(nums))} linked with an extension written as a letter and digits ({_example(nums)}) on {pages} page{plural_s(pages)}. The letter is a dialer's pause or extension marker, and RFC 3966 has no such character inside a number: it writes an extension as ;ext=. Depending on the phone, tapping the link may dial the main line, the whole string, or nothing."
findings.fix: 'Write the extension the standard way, after the number: YOUR NUMBER, ext. EXTENSION. Or link the main number and print the extension beside it.'

findings.title: 'A phone link contains HTML instead of a number'
findings.detail: f'{len(nums)} phone number{plural_s(len(nums))} {has_have(len(nums))} an HTML tag inside the href where the number should be ({_example(nums)}) on {pages} page{plural_s(pages)}. A whole link was pasted into a field that expects a phone number. **The page still looks right**: the number a visitor reads is fine, and only the link behind it is broken, so tapping it on a phone dials nothing.'
findings.fix: 'Open the phone-number field in your CMS and look at what is actually stored in it. Clear it and type the number by itself (digits and separators only, no <a> tag) and let the template build the link around it.'

findings.title: 'A phone link is a placeholder'
findings.detail: f"{len(nums)} phone number{plural_s(len(nums))} {is_are(len(nums))} a placeholder, a repeated digit or a row of X's ({_example(nums, 30)}), on {pages} page{plural_s(pages)}. A template that was never filled in. Anyone tapping {them_it(len(nums))} reaches nobody."
findings.fix: 'Replace it with the real number, or remove the link.'

findings.title: 'Phone links are not in international format'
findings.detail: f"{len(nums)} phone number{plural_s(len(nums))} {is_are(len(nums))} linked with no country code and no phone-context parameter ({_example(nums, 30)}) on {pages} page{plural_s(pages)}. RFC 3966 says all phone numbers must use the global form unless they cannot be represented that way. {('It dials' if len(nums) == 1 else 'They dial')} correctly from inside the country and incorrectly from outside it." + (" This site's hreflang names more than one country, so it is asking for visitors who would be dialling from outside." if international else ' This site offers pages in more than one language, and a language is not a country: if any of those readers call from abroad, the number will not dial for them.' if any((p.hreflang for p in ctx.ok_pages)) else '')
findings.fix: 'Prefix the country code and a plus in the href, leaving the visible text alone: YOUR PHONE NUMBER, spaced as you print it.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Will your phone links dial the right number?
rows.answer: It checks phone-link destinations for forms that are placeholders or not defined by the link standard.
rows.why: A visible phone label can look correct while its hidden destination contains different text. Checking that destination matters because tapping a link uses the destination, not the words displayed beside it.

condition.text: The check decodes phone-link destinations and separates pasted markup, placeholder runs, written extensions, other letters and missing international context. Repeated identical digits are placeholders when there are at least 7 digits. A local-format number without a leading plus or phone-context parameter is reported separately. At least 2 recognised hreflang regions raise that last case from low to medium severity. Extension and placeholder patterns have their own exact formats in the source. For example, a phone target made of at least 7 identical digits can be flagged as a placeholder.

pages.text: The check reads phone links on pages the crawl could load. It validates their written format. You need to test the intended contact route yourself.

reports.text: Pasted markup, letters and placeholders can be high severity. Written extensions are medium. Missing international context is low, or medium when language-region declarations suggest a wider audience. The check validates the written link format. Test the intended line separately.

fix.text: Inspect the full link target and compare it with the intended number. Remove pasted tags, replace placeholders and use a valid extension parameter where needed. Include an international number or the required phone context. Test the destination on a suitable device without making an unwanted call during automated checks.

rows.guide_title: Phone links that will not dial

review.text: Compare the display label with the decoded destination, including any extension or context parameter. A number can look normal on the page while its target still contains template markup. Keep call and text routes appropriate to the service offered. Review international context for the audience that uses the page, and validate the link format without placing automated calls or assuming that format validation proves a working line.

faq.question: When do repeated digits look like a placeholder phone link?
faq.answer: A run containing 7 identical digits or more can qualify. The hidden destination is inspected independently of the label.

faq.question: Can a local phone link need international context?
faq.answer: Yes. A local-format target without a plus prefix or phone-context parameter can qualify. Regional declarations can raise severity.

faq.question: Does the phone-link check prove the line works?
faq.answer: No. It validates the written link format. Confirm the intended contact route separately.

rows.title: Above-the-fold value proposition

conditions.expression: home is None or not home.ok

findings.title: f'{subject} does not state what the business does'
findings.detail: 'There is no headline and supporting line that a first-time visitor can read to understand the offer. Visitors decide whether to stay in a few seconds, and campaign traffic arriving with no context is the least forgiving of all.'
findings.fix: 'Put a plain-language headline at the top: who you help, what you do for them, and what makes you the obvious choice. One sentence underneath for the detail.'

findings.title: f'{possessive} headline talks about you, not the customer'
findings.detail: f'''The opening copy is written entirely in the first person and never addresses the visitor. Visitors are asking "can this solve my problem?" Copy about the company's history answers a question nobody asked. Currently: "{hero[:140]}…"'''
findings.fix: 'Rewrite so the first line names the visitor\'s problem or desired outcome. "We are a family-run firm established in 1998" becomes "Get your boiler fixed today. Family-run, and in business since 1998."'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your homepage say what you do?
rows.answer: It reviews the saved opening text for an absent or inward-looking statement.
rows.why: The opening passage gives a visitor an early account of the page's purpose. Counting pronouns can suggest a passage to review, but a clear statement of the offer matters more than adding a customer pronoun to an unclear sentence.

condition.text: The test requires a supported prose language and a successful homepage or audited page. Missing opening text, or fewer than 25 characters, produces the absent-value finding. Otherwise the code counts inward terms such as references to the company and outward terms addressing the customer. At least 3 inward matches with no outward match produce a separate medium-severity finding. It does not measure the physical fold of a rendered screen. For example, opening text shorter than 25 characters is reported as missing an offer explanation.

pages.text: Saved opening text from the homepage supplies the input. In a single-page scope, the explanation names the audited page instead of asserting that the root homepage was read.

reports.text: An absent statement is high severity. Inward-only statements are medium. Phrase counts do not establish whether the offer is useful or whether the language fits the audience.

fix.text: Read the opening text without the rest of the site. Say what the business provides and who it helps in concrete terms. Keep the statement accurate and let supporting detail follow it. Review the rendered page after editing so that decorative headings or repeated brand text do not hide the actual explanation.

rows.guide_title: Conversion audit

review.text: Read the opening passage as someone unfamiliar with the business. A company name or a decorative slogan may be clear to the owner while leaving the offer unstated for a visitor. Keep the useful claim concrete and accurate. Review customer-directed wording for meaning rather than pronoun count, because inserting a customer word into an unclear headline cannot by itself explain what is provided or who the page serves.

faq.question: How short can my opening text be before the offer is treated as absent?
faq.answer: Opening text below 25 characters reaches the absent-value finding. The test uses saved text rather than screen position.

faq.question: Can an opening statement about only the company produce a finding?
faq.answer: Yes. At least 3 inward matches and no outward match can trigger the separate medium result. Adding pronouns alone will not clarify an offer.

faq.question: Does the value-proposition check measure what is above the fold?
faq.answer: No. The physical fold is outside this check. Saved opening text supplies the measured wording.

rows.title: Broken pages (4xx/5xx)

conditions.expression: not any((ch.isspace() for ch in path))

predicates.expression: 'did not respond in time' in (getattr(page, 'error', '') or '')

constants.name: _SCHEMELESS_NOTE
constants.expression: '. One of these is a link written as "{href}" with no https:// in front of it. A reference with no scheme is a relative path, so browsers ask for it underneath the current folder, which is why {host} appears twice in the address above. This audit did not build that URL; the link did.'

findings.title: f"{len(server_errors)} internal page{plural_s(len(server_errors))} {verb('return', len(server_errors))} a server error"
findings.detail: 'Server errors on crawlable URLs cost crawl budget and drop pages out of the index.'
findings.fix: 'Check the server logs for these URLs and fix the underlying error.'

findings.title: f'{len(rejected)} page{plural_s(len(rejected))} {is_are(len(rejected))} rejected by your own server'
findings.detail: f'These URLs are linked from the site and answered with HTTP {shown}. That is the server refusing the request rather than saying the page is gone, so it will not show as a 404 in any report that only counts those, and a search engine asking for the same URL gets the same refusal.\n\nThe usual causes are a rule that rejects a query string or a header, a URL the application cannot parse, or a request size limit.'
findings.fix: "Request one of these URLs yourself and read the server's own log line for it. If the URL should not exist, return 404 or 410 so it is understood as gone; if it should, fix what is rejecting it. Either is better than a refusal, which tells a search engine nothing."

findings.title: f"{len(forbidden)} page{plural_s(len(forbidden))} {verb('return', len(forbidden))} 401/403"
findings.detail: 'These URLs are linked but refuse access. Three causes, and they need different answers: a firewall or bot-protection rule catching crawlers along with visitors, a page that should not have been linked at all, or content deliberately behind a login or subscription.'
findings.fix: 'If they should be public, allowlist search-engine crawlers in the WAF. If they are gated on purpose, keep the links and mark the pages up as paywalled content (`isAccessibleForFree: false` with a `cssSelector` for the gated part) so Google indexes them without treating the teaser as cloaking. Only remove the links if the pages should not have been linked at all.'

findings.title: f'{len(malformed)} link points to something that is not an address' if len(malformed) == 1 else f'{len(malformed)} links point to something that is not an address'
findings.detail: 'These are links whose destination is not a URL, so no request was ever made and nothing here is a DNS, TLS or availability problem. The usual cause is text pasted into a link field in a site editor.\n\n' + '; '.join((_short(p.url) for p in malformed[:3]))
findings.fix: 'Open the page that contains each link and replace the destination with a real address, or remove the link.'

findings.title: f'{len(turned_away)} URL{plural_s(len(turned_away))} stopped accepting connections partway through the crawl'
findings.detail: f'The server closed the connection on these requests after answering {len(answered)} others normally, so this is rate limiting rather than an outage. Nothing here points at DNS, TLS or availability. This audit slowed down when it started; these are the requests that were still refused afterwards.\n\n' + '; '.join(sorted({p.error for p in turned_away})[:2])
findings.fix: "Nothing needs fixing on the site for this. If you want a complete crawl, allow this audit's user-agent past the rate limit, or re-run the audit when the server is less busy. Real visitors are unaffected."

findings.title: f'{len(dead)} URL{plural_s(len(dead))} could not be reached at all'
findings.detail: 'Connection failures, DNS errors or certificate problems: ' + '; '.join(sorted({p.error for p in dead})[:3])
findings.fix: 'Check DNS, TLS and server availability for these hosts.'

findings.title: f'{len(timed_out)} URL{plural_s(len(timed_out))} did not answer before the crawl gave up'
findings.detail: f'These {len(timed_out)} URL{plural_s(len(timed_out))} were not read, because the server had not begun replying within the time allowed. That is not the same as being unreachable: a page that answers eventually is live, indexable and visible to a visitor patient enough to wait, and Googlebot is not that patient.\n\nWhatever else this audit says about the site, it did not see these pages, so nothing here describes them.'
findings.fix: "Treat this as the same problem as the site's response time rather than a separate one. Fix that and these read normally. A visitor and Googlebot are waiting exactly as long as this audit did."

findings.title: f"{len(linked)} page{plural_s(len(linked))} linked from your own site {verb('do', len(linked))} not exist"
findings.detail: 'Broken internal links waste crawl budget, leak link equity, and are a direct bad experience for visitors. Linked from: ' + ', '.join(sources[:5]) + (_SCHEMELESS_NOTE.format(href=doubled[0][0], host=doubled[0][1]) if doubled else '')
findings.fix: 'Add https:// to the link' + plural_s(len(doubled)) + ' that ' + verb('name', len(doubled)) + ' the domain without it, then update any remaining link to the correct URL or 301-redirect the dead URL to its replacement.' if doubled else 'Update each link to the correct URL, or 301-redirect the dead URL to its replacement.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Which pages failed during the crawl?
rows.answer: It separates server errors, missing pages, refusals and requests that could not finish.
rows.why: Different failures need different fixes. Separating a missing address from a server rejecting requests avoids telling you to delete a useful page when the real issue is access or crawl pressure.

condition.text: Responses marked as challenges are excluded from the main status groups. Server responses with HTTP status from 500 up to but below HTTP status 600 are critical. Missing responses with HTTP status 404 or HTTP status 410 are separated from refusals with HTTP status 401 or HTTP status 403 and other rejected client requests. A zero status with an error is divided into timeouts, malformed links, connection refusals on otherwise answering hosts and hard failures. Prose-like URL paths are guarded against misleading missing-page claims. For example, a refusal with HTTP status 403 needs a different review from a missing-page response with HTTP status 404.

pages.text: The check uses response statuses, errors and incoming links from the crawl. Refused or challenged requests may leave the destination unchecked. Keep those outcomes in view when deciding which link to change.

reports.text: Severity ranges from medium for several refusal or timeout cases to high for hard failures and broken internal links, and critical for server errors. A refusal means the audit could not read the page. It is not automatically proof that a visitor sees a missing page.

fix.text: Open the cited source link and review the saved response. Correct a malformed destination, restore genuinely missing content or redirect an obsolete address to a relevant replacement. Investigate server errors and request refusals with logs. Retest timeouts before declaring the page dead, especially when other pages on the same host still answer.

rows.guide_title: 'Could not be reached' is not a diagnosis

review.text: Trace a reported destination back to the link or discovery source that supplied it. A real page returning an access refusal needs a different response from an address containing pasted prose. Keep the saved error category alongside the URL during review. For intermittent failures, compare server logs and a later request before removing content, while correcting a clearly malformed internal link at the template or page that published it.

faq.question: Is an HTTP 403 response the same as a missing page?
faq.answer: No. HTTP status 403 represents a refusal here, while HTTP status 404 represents a missing response. Access restrictions need their own review.

faq.question: How serious are server errors in the failed-page check?
faq.answer: The result is critical for server errors. Missing addresses, refusals and timeouts have separate treatment.

faq.question: Are challenge pages treated as ordinary broken-page responses?
faq.answer: No. Responses marked as challenges are kept outside the main status groups. They can leave the destination unchecked.

rows.title: Googlebot's 2MB fetch limit

findings.title: f"{len(over)} page{plural_s(len(over))} {verb('exceed', len(over))} Googlebot's 2MB fetch limit"
findings.detail: f"Googlebot fetches at most 2MB of any URL, HTTP headers included, and everything after that is never fetched, rendered or indexed. These pages are larger: the biggest is {('at least ' if biggest.body_truncated else '')}{mb(biggest.html_bytes):.1f} MB{(' (this audit stops reading there, so the page is larger)' if biggest.body_truncated else '')}, so their tail is being discarded silently. Nothing Google requires is past the cutoff today, which means this is costing you content rather than indexation, and the margin will not survive the page growing."
findings.fix: 'Trim the page below 2MB. Inlined base64 images and large inline CSS or JavaScript are the usual causes, and moving them into linked files removes them from this budget entirely: referenced resources each get their own.'

findings.title: f"{len(losing)} page{plural_s(len(losing))} {verb('push', len(losing))} required markup past Googlebot's 2MB cutoff"
findings.detail: f"Googlebot fetches at most 2MB of any URL, HTTP headers included, and hands what it got to indexing as if it were the whole file. On these pages, markup Google needs sits after that cutoff, so it is not late: it is absent. {detail_lines}. The largest page here is {('at least ' if biggest.body_truncated else '')}{mb(biggest.html_bytes):.1f} MB{(' (this audit stops reading there)' if biggest.body_truncated else '')}."
findings.fix: 'Move the affected markup into the <head>, and cut what is inflating the page. The usual causes are base64 images inlined into the HTML, large inline CSS or JavaScript blocks, and navigation that renders thousands of links before the content. Referenced files do not count: each resource has its own separate 2MB budget, so moving inline blocks into linked files fixes this outright.'
findings.evidence: {'cap_bytes': GOOGLEBOT_BYTE_CAP, 'pages': [{'url': p.url, 'bytes': p.html_bytes, 'bytes_is_floor': p.body_truncated, 'lost': lost} for (p, lost) in losing]}

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does important markup fall beyond the fetch budget?
rows.answer: It compares decompressed HTML size and important markup offsets with a fixed byte budget.
rows.why: A large document can put important tags beyond the read budget. The check compares their recorded positions with that budget. Review the actual document order before choosing what to reduce.

condition.text: The cap is 2097152 bytes, with 1024 bytes reserved for headers. Successful HTML pages larger than the remaining budget are checked. Important tags found strictly beyond that budget produce high severity. An oversized document with no identified tags beyond it produces medium severity. The header allowance is fixed for every response. For example, the same 1024-byte header allowance applies to each measured HTML response.

pages.text: Successful HTML responses supply document size and recorded offsets of important markup. Images, stylesheets and other separate files are not added to this HTML-byte comparison.

reports.text: Important markup beyond the read budget is high severity. An oversized document without identified lost markup is medium. A truncated response leaves its full size unknown. Keep the saved limit beside the size when reviewing it.

fix.text: Inspect the document source and the locations named in the finding. Reduce excessive inline scripts, style blocks or repeated markup, and keep essential head tags early. Retest the decompressed HTML after changing the template. Review the actual source order rather than relying on the visual location of content in a browser.

rows.guide_title: Googlebot stops reading at 2MB

review.text: Inspect the actual document order around the recorded cutoff. A tag can appear visually near the top of a page while its source arrives much later, and separate resource sizes do not describe the HTML budget. Keep the byte unit and fixed header allowance visible in your notes. After reducing markup, compare the new offsets with the saved ones instead of assuming that a smaller file moved every important tag equally.

faq.question: What is reserved for headers in the HTML fetch budget?
faq.answer: Each response has 1024 bytes set aside for headers. The remaining budget is compared with decompressed HTML and tag positions.

faq.question: Are images included in the HTML byte-cap comparison?
faq.answer: No. The document comparison leaves out other separate files, including images and stylesheets. It measures decompressed HTML.

faq.question: Is oversized HTML worse when important markup lies beyond the budget?
faq.answer: Yes. Important markup beyond the limit is high severity. Without identified lost tags, the oversized-document result is medium.

rows.title: Canonical tags

conditions.expression: host and origin_host and (host.lstrip() != origin_host) and (not _same_reg(host, origin_host))
target is not None and (not ctx.is_indexable(target))
not any((phrase in text for phrase in _SYNDICATION_PHRASES))

constants.name: _SYNDICATION_PHRASES
constants.expression: ('co-published with', 'copublished with', 'co-published by', 'originally published by', 'originally published on', 'originally published in', 'first published by', 'first published on', 'first appeared on', 'first appeared in', 'republished from', 'in partnership with', 'produced in partnership with', 'this story was produced by')

findings.title: f'{len(missing)} page{plural_s(len(missing))} {has_have(len(missing))} no canonical tag'
findings.detail: 'Without a canonical, any URL variation (tracking parameters, trailing slashes, uppercase paths) can be indexed as a separate page competing with the original.'
findings.fix: 'Add a self-referencing canonical tag to every indexable page template.'

findings.title: f"{len(conflicting)} page{plural_s(len(conflicting))} {verb('declare', len(conflicting))} more than one canonical URL"
findings.detail: 'Each of these pages carries two or more rel=canonical tags naming different URLs, so the page contradicts itself about where it really lives. This audit does not guess which one a search engine honours. The point is that the declaration cannot do what either tag intends. The usual cause is a template that adds a self-canonical on top of one a plugin or syndication partner already set.'
findings.fix: "Leave exactly one rel=canonical per page. If this is syndicated content, note that Google does not recommend the canonical element for avoiding duplication by syndication partners (see the reference), so blocking indexing on the partner's copy is usually the better arrangement."

findings.title: f"{len(syndicated)} co-published page{plural_s(len(syndicated))} {verb('give', len(syndicated))} the canonical to a partner"
findings.detail: f"{len(syndicated)} page{plural_s(len(syndicated))} canonicalise{('s' if len(syndicated) == 1 else '')} to " + ', '.join(named) + f", and say so in the page itself: the byline names the same outlet. This is a co-publishing arrangement, not a stray tag, so this audit is not calling it a mistake.\n\nWhat it costs is still worth knowing: the canonical hands the ranking for {('these stories' if len(syndicated) > 1 else 'this story')} to the partner's domain, so searches for your own reporting can land on their copy rather than yours."
findings.fix: 'Nothing here is broken. If the arrangement is what you intend, leave it. If you would rather keep the ranking, Google does not recommend the canonical element for syndication (see the reference), and asking the partner to noindex their copy, or agreeing which outlet takes the canonical story by story, are the two arrangements that work.'

findings.title: f"{len(off_site)} page{plural_s(len(off_site))} {verb('canonicalise', len(off_site))} to a different domain"
findings.detail: 'These pages tell Google the real version lives on another site, which hands the ranking to that domain. This is almost always an accident: a copied template, or a staging URL left in place. ' + _offsite_targets(off_site, off_site_hosts, origin_host)
findings.fix: "Change the canonical to point at this site's own URL."

findings.title: f"{len(to_noncanonical)} page{plural_s(len(to_noncanonical))} {verb('canonicalise', len(to_noncanonical))} to a noindex page"
findings.detail: 'The canonical points at a page that is itself blocked from indexing, so the signal is contradictory and both URLs risk being dropped.'
findings.fix: 'Point the canonical at an indexable page, or remove the noindex from the target.'

findings.title: f"{n} page{plural_s(n)} {verb('name', n)} another spelling of {('its' if n == 1 else 'their')} own address as canonical"
findings.detail: f'{example.url} declares its canonical as {example.canonical}, the same page under its index-file name. Nothing is handed to another page, so this is not a cross-canonical. ' + (f"On {seen} of {('them' if n > 1 else 'it')} this audit followed that address and it redirected back to the page, so the canonical points at a redirect: the tag names a URL that does not serve the page, and search engines have to resolve the difference themselves." if seen else 'A canonical should be the address that answers with the page itself, not another spelling of it.')
findings.fix: f"Make each canonical the page's own final address, the one that answers 200, such as {example.url}. Usually a one-line change in the template that builds the tag."

findings.title: f"{len(non_self)} page{plural_s(len(non_self))} {verb('canonicalise', len(non_self))} to a different URL"
findings.detail: 'Cross-canonicals are correct for genuine duplicates (paginated views, filtered variants) and a mistake everywhere else: the page will not rank on its own.'
findings.fix: 'Confirm each of these is a deliberate duplicate. If the page has unique content, make the canonical self-referencing.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do your canonical tags name the right pages?
rows.answer: It checks missing, conflicting, off-site and unusable canonical targets.
rows.why: A canonical is a statement about which address should represent content. Checking the actual target matters because a syntactically valid tag can still name another domain, an excluded page or an address that redirects back to the source.

condition.text: The check reads canonical declarations from indexable pages. Distinct target strings after trailing-slash handling identify conflicts. It separates off-site targets from hosts whose last 2 domain labels match, recognises declared syndication, and checks saved targets for indexability. Redirect aliases and default-index spellings are treated differently from a genuinely different page. A non-self canonical can produce a low-severity result when a stronger target problem was not already reported. For example, hosts sharing their last 2 domain labels receive different handling from an unrelated off-site host.

pages.text: The check compares canonical tags, redirects, measured target pages and selected wording about republished content. An uncrawled target can remain unknown. Check the intended destination before changing a declaration.

reports.text: Missing canonicals are medium, conflicts and noindex targets high, and unrelated off-site targets critical. Declared syndication is medium. Spelling aliases and other non-self targets are low. These cases preserve the difference between a deliberate relationship and a template mistake.

fix.text: Choose the intended representative URL for the content. Make the HTML declaration consistent, use the final address where appropriate and check that the target can be indexed. Preserve intentional syndication after confirming the agreement. Fix shared templates before editing individual pages when the same wrong host appears throughout the site.

rows.guide_title: How to fix conflicting canonical tags

review.text: Compare the canonical target with the intended relationship between the pages. An alias, a syndicated article and an accidental off-site template value need different decisions. Keep details of redirects and target directives together. When the destination was not crawled, inspect it before assigning a status or indexing judgement. Update shared host settings carefully so that a correction on ordinary pages does not erase an intentional partner relationship.

faq.question: Is an off-site canonical always treated as a critical error?
faq.answer: No. Declared syndication is medium. Unrelated off-site targets get critical severity, so review the intended relationship first.

faq.question: Can a canonical pointing to a noindex page be high severity?
faq.answer: Yes. The report rates noindex targets high, along with conflicting canonicals. Check whether the intended representative page can be indexed.

faq.question: Does the canonical check treat trailing slashes as distinct targets?
faq.answer: The comparison applies trailing-slash handling before checking distinct target strings. Other address differences can still need review.

rows.title: Conflicting canonical tags

findings.title: f"{len(conflicts)} page{plural_s(len(conflicts))} {verb('declare', len(conflicts))} two different canonical URLs"
findings.detail: f"The canonical in the HTML and the canonical in the HTTP Link header point to different URLs. Google treats multiple conflicting canonicals as an unreliable signal and may ignore both, choosing its own. This is invisible when reviewing the page source, because the HTML looks correct. Example: {url} declares '{html_target}' in HTML but '{header_target}' in its Link header."
findings.fix: 'Pick one and remove the other. Most sites want the HTML tag; the header is usually left over from a CDN rule, a plugin or a reverse proxy.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do your HTTP and HTML canonicals disagree?
rows.answer: It compares a canonical in the response header with the canonical in the HTML.
rows.why: Separate configuration layers can make separate claims for the same response. A correct-looking tag in page source does not reveal a conflicting HTTP header, which explains why looking at the browser document alone can miss this test.

condition.text: The page must be intended for search and have a canonical in both its HTTP Link header and its HTML. Its header address is resolved against the page URL. Both targets have trailing slashes removed before comparison. Different targets produce a conflict. A page with only an HTML canonical produces no conflict here.

pages.text: The check reads the saved HTTP headers and HTML canonical values. A server or proxy may add a header separately from the page template. Inspect both places before editing.

reports.text: Conflicts are high severity. The report gives a source page and both targets so that the server configuration and page template can be reviewed together instead of guessing which layer supplied the wrong value.

fix.text: Choose the intended canonical destination. Align the server or proxy header with the HTML tag. Check every layer that can add a declaration. Request the page again and inspect both values in the new response.

rows.guide_title: How to fix conflicting canonical tags

review.text: Inspect the complete response, including headers, before editing the document template. A proxy or server can add a declaration independently of the page generator. Keep both target values in the review until the intended owner of the policy is clear. After changing the responsible layer, request the page again and compare the resulting header with the served document, rather than relying on a local source file alone.

faq.question: Can a response header conflict with the canonical in my HTML?
faq.answer: Yes. A canonical in the HTTP Link header is compared with the document declaration. Different destinations can trigger the conflict.

faq.question: Does having only an HTML canonical trigger a header conflict?
faq.answer: No. Both declarations must exist for this comparison. A page carrying only an HTML canonical has no conflict here.

faq.question: How serious is disagreement between header and HTML canonicals?
faq.answer: The conflict gets high severity. Both targets and the saved source page help locate the configuration needing repair.

rows.title: Click depth and orphans

findings.title: 'Click depth could not be measured on this crawl'
findings.detail: 'How many clicks a page sits from the homepage is measured along the links this crawl could read, and this one could not read them: either the navigation was not in the HTML or too much of the site was left unfetched. A depth of four here would be a distance through a menu this audit never saw, so no depth claim is made either way.'
findings.fix: 'Re-run without a page limit (`-n 0`) and without a depth limit (`-d 0`). If the navigation is built by JavaScript, the link graph cannot be read from the HTML at all and no crawl setting will fix it.'

findings.title: 'Orphan pages could not be checked on this crawl'
findings.detail: f"Whether anything links to a page can only be answered by fetching the pages that might link to it, and {len(ctx.crawl.skipped)} URL{plural_s(len(ctx.crawl.skipped))} discovered here {('was' if len(ctx.crawl.skipped) == 1 else 'were')} never fetched. Any of them could carry the missing links, so no orphan claim is made either way."
findings.fix: 'Re-run without a page limit (`-n 0`) to get an answer, or raise the limit past the number of URLs the site declares.'

findings.title: f"{len(deep)} page{plural_s(len(deep))} {verb('sit', len(deep))} 4+ clicks from the homepage"
findings.detail: 'Pages buried deep in the structure get crawled less often and are read as less important. Anything commercially valuable should be within three clicks.'
findings.fix: 'Add internal links from higher-level pages: hub pages, related-content blocks, or the main navigation.'

findings.title: f'{len(orphans)} orphan page{plural_s(len(orphans))} {has_have(len(orphans))} no internal links pointing to {them_it(len(orphans))}'
findings.detail: 'These pages appear in the sitemap but nothing on the site links to them. Orphans receive almost no ranking signal and are often forgotten content.'
findings.fix: 'Link to each from a relevant parent or hub page, or remove it if it is obsolete.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Are useful pages hard to reach through links?
rows.answer: It reports deep pages and sitemap pages with no observed internal links.
