rows.why: A sitemap can reveal a URL without showing how a visitor reaches it from another page. The graph requirement protects that distinction and prevents incomplete discovery from being presented as a confirmed absence of links.

condition.text: Indexable pages at a depth of 4 clicks or greater enter the deep-page test. Orphans are indexable sitemap entries with no internal inlinks, excluding the homepage. When the crawl cannot support link-graph claims, the code reports that depth or orphan status could not be checked instead of asserting the defect. A sufficiently complete graph allows the corresponding depth and orphan findings. For example, a page at a depth of 4 clicks enters the deep-page review.

pages.text: The check uses measured click depth, internal links and the saved sitemap list. An incomplete crawl can leave the result unknown. Review what the crawl covered before moving pages or adding links.

reports.text: Deep pages are low severity, confirmed orphans medium and withheld measurements notices. The result describes the graph the audit could establish. It does not prove how every user navigates or that every deep page needs a place in the main menu.

fix.text: Review the route to useful affected pages. Add relevant links from pages where a visitor would expect them, and repair links that point to obsolete addresses. Keep intentional utility pages separate from useful public content. If the finding says the graph was incomplete, improve crawl coverage before making structural changes based on that uncertainty.

rows.guide_title: Click depth and orphan pages

review.text: Trace a route from a known entry page to the affected content. Sitemap discovery alone does not show that route, and a partial crawl can miss a valid source link. Keep the coverage warning attached to any structural conclusion. Add links where they help visitors follow the subject, then check the graph again, instead of putting unrelated pages into a menu simply to lower a reported click count.

faq.question: How many clicks make an indexable page deep in this audit?
faq.answer: A measured depth of 4 clicks qualifies. That distance follows the internal links the crawl could actually read.

faq.question: Can an incomplete crawl prove a page is an orphan?
faq.answer: No. Without support for link-graph claims, orphan status is withheld. Improve coverage before treating absent links as a confirmed defect.

faq.question: Are confirmed orphan pages more serious than deep pages?
faq.answer: Yes. Confirmed orphans are medium, while deep pages have low severity. Both results still need a review of page purpose.

rows.title: Duplicate pages

conditions.expression: not langs or not all(('-' in lang for lang in langs))

predicates.expression: max((p.word_count for p in group), default=0) <= _SUBSTITUTE_MAX_WORDS

thresholds.expression: max((p.word_count for p in group), default=0) <= _SUBSTITUTE_MAX_WORDS

findings.title: f'{len(g)} unrelated URLs returned the same short page'
findings.detail:
f'{len(g)} URLs across {len(sections)} different sections of the site all returned an identical body of about {shared} words. Pages this unrelated do not normally share their text, so the likeliest explanation is that the server returned one stand-in page (a shell, a holding page, or a response to load) rather than the content of each URL.

This audit has not judged the content of these pages, because what it received is not their content. They are NOT reported as duplicate content: redirecting or canonicalising them to each other would merge pages that are genuinely different.

Sections affected: ' + ', '.join(sections[:8])
findings.fix: 'Open two of these URLs in a browser and compare them. If they differ, the crawl was served a stand-in and nothing here needs fixing on the page itself: check whether a cache, a CDN rule or a rate limit returns a shared response to automated requests, since search engines would receive it too. If they genuinely are identical, then they are duplicates and want one canonical URL between them.'

findings.title: f'{total} page{plural_s(total)} {has_have(total)} identical content across {len(groups)} group{plural_s(len(groups))}'
findings.detail: f'These URLs serve the same body text. Google picks one and ignores the rest, and the choice is not yours. Examples: {sample}' + (' Each of these already declares itself canonical, so the tag is not missing. It is telling Google that pages with identical text are different pages, which is the claim being ignored.' if self_canonical else '') + scheme_note + regional_note
findings.fix: "Keep each page's canonical pointing at itself, and add hreflang annotations that link the regional versions to each other, with an x-default. Each country then keeps its own page in its own results. Do not canonicalise them to one URL. That removes the other countries from search. If you already declare hreflang in a sitemap, this audit did not read it: check that it lists these pages." if regional_note else 'Point the canonical on each of these at one chosen URL instead of at itself, or give them body text that differs. If they are product variants a customer can still buy, canonicalise them to the parent product. Do not redirect them.' if self_canonical else 'Redirect http:// to https:// site-wide first. That is one server rule and it resolves these groups without a canonical tag on any of them; adding tags per group instead is a great deal of work for the same result. Re-check afterwards for any group that is left.' if redirect_is_the_fix else 'Pick one canonical URL per group and either 301-redirect the others or add a canonical tag pointing at the chosen one.' + (' Start with a site-wide http-to-https redirect, which closes the groups that are only a scheme apart.' if both_schemes else '')
findings.urls: [p.url for g in groups for p in g][:25]

findings.title: f"{len(affected)} page{plural_s(len(affected))} {verb('share', len(affected))} a duplicated title tag"
findings.detail: f'{len(dupe_titles)} title{plural_s(len(dupe_titles))} {is_are(len(dupe_titles))} used on more than one page. Duplicate titles make pages compete with each other and give searchers no way to tell the results apart. Most repeated: ' + repr(max(dupe_titles.values(), key=len)[0].title.strip()[:80])
findings.fix: 'Write a unique, specific title for each page. Lead with what makes that page different.'

findings.title: f"{len(affected)} page{plural_s(len(affected))} {verb('share', len(affected))} a duplicated meta description"
findings.detail: 'Duplicate descriptions get rewritten by Google, so you lose control of the snippet.'
findings.fix: "Write a distinct description per page describing that page's specific offer."

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do different URLs repeat the same content?
rows.answer: It groups identical page bodies, titles and descriptions after checking canonical agreement.
rows.why: Identical bodies can appear because of duplicate publishing, multiple address forms or a server serving a substitute response. Understanding which case applies is necessary before deciding whether to merge content or repair delivery.

condition.text: Body comparison ignores pages with fewer than 50 words and hashes lowercased text with normalised whitespace. Groups sharing a single nonempty canonical are excluded. A separate substitution case needs at least 5 pages across at least 4 sections with no page above 200 words. Duplicate titles and descriptions are grouped independently. Redirect scheme splits and regional alternatives change the explanation rather than turning all identical text into the same diagnosis. For example, a page with exactly 50 words is long enough for the body-text comparison.

pages.text: The check reads body text and metadata from pages with usable content. Body matching ignores capitalisation and extra spaces, then compares the resulting text exactly. A separate test compares the subjects suggested by titles.

reports.text: Duplicate bodies are high severity, titles medium and descriptions low. Repeated short responses across unrelated sections are medium. The report distinguishes a shared error or substitute response from normal pages that genuinely contain the same text.

fix.text: Compare the saved bodies with the expected pages. Fix substitute responses at the server or template level. For real duplicate addresses, select the intended canonical or redirect where appropriate. Write distinct titles for distinct pages. Preserve valid regional alternatives and review their language annotations before treating them as accidental copies.

rows.guide_title: Identical content is not always duplicate content

review.text: Compare the saved text with the content expected at each address. Identical responses across unrelated sections can indicate a shared substitute page rather than duplicated editorial work. Keep that delivery case separate from genuine alternate URLs. When titles alone repeat, inspect the page purposes before rewriting them, and preserve a real canonical agreement that already describes duplicate content instead of creating contradictory address policies during cleanup.

faq.question: How many words are needed for the duplicate-body comparison?
faq.answer: A page needs at least 50 words. Shorter responses are left out of the ordinary body-hash comparison.

faq.question: Can identical pages with the same canonical be excluded from body duplicates?
faq.answer: Yes. A group can be excluded when its members share a single nonempty canonical. That declaration should still describe the right relationship.

faq.question: Are duplicate descriptions as serious as duplicate page bodies?
faq.answer: No. Body duplication gets high severity. Titles have medium severity and descriptions low.

rows.title: Client-side redirects

findings.title: f"{len(hops)} page{plural_s(len(hops))} {verb('redirect', len(hops))} with a meta refresh"
findings.detail: detail
findings.fix: 'Prefer a server-side 301 where your hosting can issue one: it is faster, it passes ranking signals unambiguously, and a link checker can see it. On static hosting that cannot return a 301 (GitHub Pages and most object storage), a refresh stub with noindex and a canonical to the destination is the correct available answer, and no change is needed.'
findings.evidence: {'targets': {p.url: p.meta_refresh for p in hops[:5]}, 'max_delay_seconds': max((p.meta_refresh_delay for p in hops))}

findings.title: f"{len(js_hops)} URL{plural_s(len(js_hops))} {verb('redirect', len(js_hops))} with JavaScript"
findings.detail: f"{len(js_hops)} URL{plural_s(len(js_hops))} {is_are(len(js_hops))} an empty page whose only job is a script that sends the visitor elsewhere. It answers 200, so nothing reading status codes sees a redirect, crawlers that do not run JavaScript never follow it, and Google follows it later and less surely than a server redirect. This audit has not judged these pages' titles or content: they have none, because they are redirects."
findings.fix: 'Replace each with a server-side 301 to its destination. Where the hosting cannot issue one, a meta refresh stub with noindex and a canonical to the destination works without JavaScript and is the better fallback.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your page redirect through the browser?
rows.answer: It separates JavaScript redirects from HTML meta refresh redirects.
rows.why: A page can answer successfully and still send a browser elsewhere. That makes a status-only review incomplete, which is why this test examines document instructions separately from HTTP redirect responses.

condition.text: A successful page with a recorded JavaScript redirect produces a low finding. Meta refresh instructions produce a notice. Delays greater than zero are collected to explain when visitors must wait. The check reads redirect instructions from the document. It can find them even when the server returned a successful response.

pages.text: The check reads successful responses and their recorded JavaScript or meta refresh redirects. These instructions run after the initial response. Server-side redirects are checked elsewhere.

reports.text: JavaScript redirects are low severity and meta refresh results notices. The report identifies the mechanism and any delay. It does not establish whether the destination is relevant or whether a deliberate delay is justified for the page.

fix.text: Check the source URL, destination and reason for the move. Use a server redirect for a permanent address change when suitable. Preserve intentional browser flows only after reviewing their purpose and delay. Test the source response and the final destination after editing so that a replaced redirect does not leave a second client-side hop behind.

rows.guide_title: Meta refresh: the redirect your tools cannot see

review.text: Review the redirect mechanism and destination together. A successful response followed by a document instruction can be intentional, but it is different from the server moving the request immediately. Keep a deliberate waiting message separate from a permanent address move. After replacing a browser redirect, inspect the served HTML as well as response headers so that an old instruction does not remain and send visitors through another move.

faq.question: Can a successful page response still contain a redirect instruction?
faq.answer: Yes. A recorded JavaScript redirect can be reported even after a successful response. Document instructions and server status are separate observations.

faq.question: Are JavaScript redirects and meta refresh given the same severity?
faq.answer: No. JavaScript redirects have low severity, while meta refresh results are notices. Review whether the mechanism fits the page.

faq.question: Does the document-redirect check judge whether the destination is useful?
faq.answer: No. It reports the mechanism and any delay. The relevance of the destination needs a separate review.

rows.title: Pages blocked from indexing

conditions.expression: home is not None and ctx.homepage_is_root and (home in blocked)

findings.title: 'Your address redirects to a page set to noindex' if moved else 'The homepage is set to noindex'
findings.detail: f'{ctx.site.start_url} redirects to {home.url}, a different host, which carries a noindex directive ({directive}). Anyone who enters your address there, and every search engine following it, lands on a page Google is told to drop. If that host is a checkout, account or staging host, the noindex is right and the redirect is what is wrong.' if moved else f'{home.url} carries a noindex directive ({directive}). Google will remove it from search results.'
findings.fix: f'Point the address at your real homepage, the page you want people and search engines to arrive at, rather than at {home_host}. If {home_host} IS your homepage, remove its noindex.' if moved else 'Remove the noindex directive from the homepage template or the X-Robots-Tag header.'

findings.severity: Severity.HIGH if len(blocked) > len(ctx.ok_pages) * 0.2 else Severity.MEDIUM
findings.title: f'{len(blocked)} page{plural_s(len(blocked))} {is_are(len(blocked))} blocked from indexing'
findings.detail: 'These pages return HTTP 200 and are linked internally, but carry a noindex directive. If any of them are meant to rank, they currently cannot.' + aside
findings.fix: 'Review the list. Legitimate noindex targets (cart, checkout, thank-you, internal search results) are fine. Anything else should have the directive removed.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Are useful pages marked to stay out of search?
rows.answer: It checks noindex directives while excluding several intentional and sitemap-only cases.
rows.why: The directive expresses an indexing choice. Reviewing the page's purpose before removing it avoids exposing a confirmation, account or search-results page merely because it appeared in a crawl.

condition.text: Successful pages with a noindex directive enter the initial set. A root homepage marked noindex is critical, with separate wording when the starting host moved elsewhere. Utility URLs and tag or author archives are excluded from the ordinary blocked-page count. Pages found only in the sitemap without observed links are also separated. Remaining blocked pages are high severity above a 0.2 share of successful pages and medium otherwise. For example, a blocked-page share of exactly 0.2 stays within the medium group after the exclusions.

pages.text: The check reads meta and HTTP-header directives, homepage status, sitemap entries, redirects and observed links. A utility page can be deliberately excluded from search. Confirm the page's purpose before removing a directive.

reports.text: The report separates an accidental exclusion of important content from pages commonly kept out of search. A successful HTTP response alone does not cancel a noindex directive, and a noindex flag alone does not establish that you intended the page to rank.

fix.text: Confirm which affected pages should be public search entries. Remove unintended noindex directives from those pages in both HTML and response headers. Keep deliberate exclusions and remove inappropriate sitemap entries. Check the root homepage separately, then request the page again to confirm the served directive changed.

rows.guide_title: Site search and cart pages that ended up in Google

review.text: Check the page's intended audience before removing an exclusion. A confirmation or account page may be public enough to crawl while still being deliberately absent from search. Keep the homepage case separate from those utility roles. Where a page should be indexed, inspect both the document and response-header directives, then verify the served result so that a hidden header does not preserve the exclusion after a template edit.

faq.question: Is a noindex directive on the root homepage serious?
faq.answer: Yes. Homepage noindex is critical. The explanation accounts for an audited host that moved elsewhere.

faq.question: Are utility pages included in the ordinary blocked-page share?
faq.answer: No. The count excludes tag or author archives along with utility URLs. Sitemap-only discoveries are separated too.

faq.question: When does noindex coverage move from medium to high severity?
faq.answer: High severity applies when blocked pages exceed a 0.2 share after exclusions. The denominator is successful pages.

severity.expression: Severity.HIGH if len(blocked) > len(ctx.ok_pages) * 0.2 else Severity.MEDIUM

rows.title: Redirect problems

findings.title: f'{len(loops)} URL{plural_s(len(loops))} {is_are(len(loops))} stuck in a redirect loop'
findings.detail: 'These URLs redirect back to themselves, so no crawler or visitor ever reaches content.'
findings.fix: 'Trace the redirect rules for these paths and break the cycle.'

findings.title: f"{len(chains)} URL{plural_s(len(chains))} {verb('redirect', len(chains))} more than once before resolving"
findings.detail: 'Every hop is a round trip the visitor waits for before anything renders. A chain is also a set of rules that must all keep working: remove or change one of the intermediate redirects and the whole path breaks, usually without anyone noticing. Example: ' + _redirect_example(chains[0])
findings.fix: 'Point the first URL in each chain straight at the final destination, in one hop.'

findings.title: f"{len(internal_redirected)} internal link{plural_s(len(internal_redirected))} {verb('point', len(internal_redirected))} at a redirect"
findings.detail: 'Internal links should point at the final URL so crawlers reach content in one request.'
findings.fix: 'Update these internal links to their destination URL.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do your redirects make unnecessary stops?
rows.answer: It finds redirect loops, longer chains and internal links pointing at a redirect.
rows.why: Each recorded hop is another request before the destination is reached. A loop has a different effect from a successful move, so the code keeps the most disruptive case separate from routine link cleanup.

condition.text: A recorded redirect loop produces a critical finding. Chains with at least 2 hops produce a medium finding. Exactly 1 hop with internal links to its starting address produces a low finding. For example, a menu link that redirects once can need an update to its final URL. These tests use recorded server redirects.

pages.text: The check reads redirect history from the full page set. Incoming links show which old addresses the site still links to. Repair those links at the page or template that supplies them.

reports.text: The report distinguishes a loop that prevents resolution from a working chain and a working redirect still used by internal links. A valid address move can remain intentional even when the links pointing to its old location need updating.

fix.text: Resolve loops first by choosing a final destination and removing rules that send requests back. Shorten chains where an old address can point directly to that destination. Update internal links to the final relevant URL. Retest both the original address and the destination to catch rules that vary by scheme or host.

rows.guide_title: How to fix redirect problems

review.text: Follow the saved chain in order and identify who controls each rule. A correct legacy redirect can still be linked unnecessarily from a current template. Keep working old-address support while updating sources you control. For a loop, compare host and scheme rules as well as paths, since individually plausible moves can send a request back to an earlier address when applied together by different layers.

faq.question: How many redirect hops count as a chain finding?
faq.answer: At least 2 hops reaches the medium chain result. A working move still needs review before changing a useful redirect.

faq.question: Can a single redirect be reported when my menu uses the old address?
faq.answer: Yes. Exactly 1 hop can trigger the low result when internal links still point to its start. Update links you control.

faq.question: How serious is a redirect loop?
faq.answer: A recorded redirect loop is critical. It is kept separate from a working chain or an outdated internal link.

rows.title: robots.txt blocks the whole site

findings.title: f"robots.txt blocks {', '.join(blocked)} from the entire site"
findings.detail: f"The robots.txt this audit received from {site.robots_url} contains a rule that disallows all crawling for {', '.join(blocked)}. If search engines receive the same file, the site cannot appear in them at all. No amount of other SEO work will help."
findings.fix: "Remove the site-wide `Disallow: /` from the affected user-agent group. If this was left over from a staging environment, delete it now. Recovery takes weeks after the rule is removed. If you are sure your site is indexed, check Search Console's robots.txt report, which shows the file Google fetched: a few large sites serve verified search crawlers a different file from everyone else, and this audit, which does not pose as one, sees only the one everyone else gets."

findings.title: f'robots.txt returns {site.robots_status}'
findings.detail: 'When robots.txt returns a server error, Google stops crawling the site entirely rather than assuming it is allowed. A persistent 5xx here will drop the whole site out of the index.'
findings.fix: 'Fix the server error, or return a 404. A missing robots.txt is safe, a broken one is not.'

findings.title: 'robots.txt has syntax problems'
findings.detail: '; '.join(robots.parse_errors[:5])
findings.fix: 'Clean up the malformed lines. Directives before the first `User-agent:` line are ignored entirely.'

findings.title: 'This audit did not wait the Crawl-delay your robots.txt asks for'
findings.detail: f'robots.txt asks crawlers that honour it to wait {site.robots_crawl_delay:g} seconds between requests. You chose to skip that wait for your own site, so this audit read it at its normal pace; every Disallow rule was still followed. Google does not read Crawl-delay at all, so this says nothing about how Google crawls the site.'
findings.fix: 'Nothing to do. Leave the option off when auditing a site that is not yours.'

findings.title: f"robots.txt blocks {', '.join(blocked)} from the entire site"
findings.detail: f"The robots.txt this audit received from {site.robots_url} lets {', '.join(admitted)} crawl the site and disallows all crawling for {', '.join(blocked)}. Googlebot is let in, so this does not keep the site out of Google; it keeps it out of results that depend on {them_it(len(blocked))}. This is usually a robots.txt that lists the crawlers it admits by name and closes with `User-agent: *` and `Disallow: /`, so any crawler left off the list is shut out."
findings.fix: f"If you want to appear where {', '.join(blocked)} {is_are(len(blocked))} used, add {('a `User-agent:` line' if len(blocked) == 1 else '`User-agent:` lines')} for it to the group that admits the others, so it gets the same rules. If leaving it out is deliberate, there is nothing to do."

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does robots.txt block a whole search crawler?
rows.answer: It checks whole-site search restrictions and problems reading the robots policy.
rows.why: Robots rules state where a crawler may go. A site-wide restriction can prevent crawling when that was never intended. Check that the file loaded successfully before treating its absence or unreadability as a deliberate policy.

condition.text: The check uses the saved robots file's access rules for search crawlers. A response with HTTP status 500 or above leaves the policy unreadable and produces a critical server-error finding. Blocking Googlebot across the site is critical. Bingbot blocks are high, and another supported crawler block is low. Syntax problems are low. A crawl-delay wait skipped by the audit produces a notice. For example, a robots response with HTTP status 500 produces the server-error result and leaves the policy unreadable.

pages.text: This site-wide test reads the robots response, its rules and the saved crawl-delay result. It does not need article pages to run. A failed robots request can leave the intended policy unknown.

reports.text: The report distinguishes policy restrictions, parsing problems and an audit that did not honour the requested wait. A failed robots request cannot prove which individual allow or disallow rule would apply if the file were readable.

fix.text: Inspect the root robots response and the exact applicable group. Remove a whole-site block only when it conflicts with your intended policy. Repair server errors before interpreting missing rule data. Correct syntax in place, then check the saved access result again. Review crawl-delay handling as an audit setting rather than changing your public policy solely to speed a test.

rows.guide_title: What is robots.txt?

review.text: Read the applicable crawler group and the wildcard rules alongside the saved response status. A server unable to deliver the policy is not the same as an owner deliberately excluding a crawler. Keep that distinction when discussing the finding. Repair delivery before interpreting missing access data, and check the policy after editing syntax so that a cleaner file still expresses the access choice the business intended.

faq.question: Is blocking Googlebot across the site more serious than blocking Bingbot?
faq.answer: Yes. The Googlebot case is critical, while Bingbot blocks are high. Review the intended crawler policy before changing either.

faq.question: Can a robots.txt server error leave search policy unknown?
faq.answer: Yes. HTTP status 500 or higher leaves robots policy unreadable and gets a critical server-error result.

faq.question: Does an ignored crawl-delay request mean the site blocks every crawler?
faq.answer: No. The crawl-delay wait concerns a notice about audit behaviour. It is separate from a policy blocking search crawlers.

rows.title: XML sitemap

conditions.expression: refused and (not any((c == 404 for c in statuses)))

predicates.expression: 'did not respond in time' in (getattr(page, 'error', '') or '')

findings.title: 'No XML sitemap found'
findings.detail: 'No sitemap was declared in robots.txt and none was found at the usual locations. Sitemaps are how search engines discover pages that are linked shallowly or not at all.'
findings.fix: 'Publish a sitemap at /sitemap.xml listing every indexable URL, then declare it in robots.txt. Most CMS platforms generate one automatically.'

findings.title: f'{len(broken)} declared sitemap{plural_s(len(broken))} {is_are(len(broken))} unreachable'
findings.detail: 'robots.txt points at sitemaps that return an error: ' + ', '.join(broken[:3]) + (f'\n\nThis audit found a working sitemap at {working[0]} and crawled from that instead, so this report is not limited to what links alone reach.' if working else '')
findings.fix: f'Point robots.txt at {working[0]}. The file is not missing, the declared address is wrong.' if working else 'Fix the sitemap URL in robots.txt, or restore the missing file.'

findings.title: f"{len(nested)} sitemap URL{plural_s(len(nested))} {has_have(len(nested))} the site's address written twice"
findings.detail: f"These entries carry a full address after the site's own (for example {nested[0]}). That is not a page anyone can reach: a server reads everything after the first host as a path, so the entry usually answers 404 or a stand-in, and search engines are told to crawl it by your own sitemap. The generator is putting the site's address in front of a value that is already a full URL."
findings.fix: "Fix the sitemap generator so each entry is written once, either as the full URL or as the site's address plus a path, then regenerate. This audit has not requested the repaired address, so open one to confirm it loads."

findings.title: f'{len(dead)} sitemap URL{plural_s(len(dead))} {is_are(len(dead))} broken'
findings.detail: 'The sitemap lists URLs that return errors. Google treats a sitemap full of dead URLs as a quality signal.'
findings.fix: 'Regenerate the sitemap so it only contains live, indexable, canonical URLs.'

findings.title: f'{len(refused)} sitemap URL{plural_s(len(refused))} could not be checked'
findings.detail: 'These URLs answered ' + ', '.join((str(c) for c in codes)) + ' to this audit, which is a refusal rather than a verdict: they may serve Google perfectly well. 429 in particular means the server asked this crawler to slow down, and a large crawl can provoke it. Nothing here says the URLs are broken, only that this audit could not see them.'
findings.fix: "Open a couple of these in a browser. If they load, nothing is wrong with them and they are simply missing from this run: this audit already slowed down and was still turned away. If you want them crawled, allow this audit's user-agent in your bot protection or rate limit."

findings.title: f"{len(redirecting)} sitemap URL{plural_s(len(redirecting))} {verb('redirect', len(redirecting))} instead of serving a page"
findings.detail: f'A sitemap is the list of URLs you want indexed, and these are not those URLs: each one redirects somewhere else. Every engine that reads the file spends two requests to reach one page, and has to decide which of the two URLs you meant. Example: {example}'
findings.fix: 'Regenerate the sitemap from the destination URLs. If it is generated from a stored base URL, that setting is usually the cause: an http:// or non-www base produces a whole sitemap of redirects.'

findings.title: f'{len(noindexed_in_sitemap)} noindex page{plural_s(len(noindexed_in_sitemap))} {is_are(len(noindexed_in_sitemap))} listed in the sitemap'
findings.detail: 'The sitemap asks Google to index pages that then tell it not to. The mixed signal wastes crawl budget.'
findings.fix: 'Exclude noindex URLs from the sitemap. If any of them are meant to rank, remove the noindex instead.'

findings.title: f'{len(missing_from_sitemap)} indexable page{plural_s(len(missing_from_sitemap))} {is_are(len(missing_from_sitemap))} missing from the sitemap'
findings.detail: f'{listed_sentence} Pages absent from the sitemap rely entirely on internal links to be discovered.'
findings.fix: 'Regenerate the sitemap from the live URL list rather than maintaining it by hand.'

findings.title: 'Whether this site has a sitemap could not be checked'
findings.detail: f"robots.txt declares no sitemap, and every address this audit tried refused the request (HTTP {', '.join((str(c) for c in sorted(set(refused))))}). That is a fact about this crawl, not about your site: bot protection commonly refuses automated requests while serving Google normally. This audit will not say a file is missing when it was not allowed to look."
findings.fix: f'Check it yourself: `curl -sI {origin}/sitemap.xml` should return 200 if one is published. If it is, declare it in robots.txt so crawlers do not have to guess.'

findings.title: f'{len(malformed)} sitemap URL{plural_s(len(malformed))} {has_have(len(malformed))} an empty path segment'
findings.detail: f'These URLs contain a doubled slash (for example {malformed[0]}), and most servers answer them with the same page as the clean form. That is two URLs for one page, published by your own sitemap, and it is where duplicate-content findings about URLs nobody typed usually come from. The cause is almost always a template joining a base path that already ends in a slash to a path that starts with one.'
findings.fix: 'Fix the sitemap generator so it does not emit empty path segments, then regenerate. Adding a canonical to the clean version is worth doing too, but the sitemap is what is advertising the duplicate.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your sitemap list usable current URLs?
rows.answer: It checks sitemap discovery, responses, URL quality and coverage against the crawl.
rows.why: A sitemap is a list of addresses, so its value depends on the addresses it actually names. Comparing it with measured responses can reveal stale entries without mistaking a temporary refusal for proof that a page no longer exists.

condition.text: The check separates missing or refused sitemap probes, broken declared files, malformed paths, dead entries, refused entries, redirects and noindex pages. A declared file response with HTTP status 400 or above is broken only outside the refusal set. Missing indexable entries are reported when their count exceeds the larger of 3 entries or a 0.15 share of crawled indexable pages. Redirects become medium rather than low when they exceed the larger of 1 entry or half the listed entries. For example, exactly 3 missing entries cannot exceed a threshold that is at least 3 entries.

pages.text: Saved sitemap files and entries are joined to crawled pages using the current URL and redirect history. Timeouts and connections refused on otherwise answering hosts are guarded against false dead-entry claims.

reports.text: Broken files are high severity. Missing files and dead entries are medium. Several coverage or indexing problems are low. Unreadable results are notices. Keep the response status beside the reported URL during review.

fix.text: List final public indexable URLs. Remove obsolete, redirected and intentionally excluded entries after checking their purpose. Repair the sitemap generator if malformed paths repeat. Investigate refusals and timeouts before deleting entries, then fetch the file again and compare it with a fresh crawl of the affected pages.

rows.guide_title: When 'regenerate your sitemap' is wrong

review.text: Compare entries with the final addresses that actually serve public content. A redirecting sitemap URL and a temporarily refused page are different cases, even when neither supplied a fresh body to this crawl. Keep entries until their role is understood. Repair repeated malformed paths in the generator, and review omitted content against the measured crawl rather than assuming the sitemap must contain every address the application can produce.

faq.question: Can exactly three missing sitemap entries trigger the coverage finding?
faq.answer: No. The threshold is at least 3 entries and the count must exceed it. Larger crawls can raise that threshold through the share rule.

faq.question: Are refused sitemap requests treated as missing files?
faq.answer: No. Missing and refused sitemap probes are separated. An unreadable result is a notice because file presence may remain unknown.

faq.question: Are broken sitemap files more serious than missing sitemap files?
faq.answer: Yes. Broken files get high severity; missing files get medium. Inspect the saved response before deciding which repair applies.

rows.title: Soft 404 handling

findings.title: 'Missing pages return HTTP 200 instead of 404'
findings.detail: 'A deliberately invalid URL returned a success status. Every mistyped or stale link then becomes an indexable page, and Google cannot tell real content from a placeholder.'
findings.fix: 'Configure the server or CMS to return a real 404 status for unknown URLs. The error page can still be branded and helpful.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do missing pages return a proper error status?
rows.answer: It reports the saved site probe for a missing page that answered as successful content.
rows.why: Successful statuses and not-found messages communicate different outcomes. The check highlights that disagreement so you can review the route handling rather than assuming that the visual error page alone defines the response.

condition.text: The check uses the crawl's saved missing-page test result. A positive result produces a medium finding for a missing page returning HTTP status 200 instead of HTTP status 404. This check uses that earlier test. It does not make a new request or compare every article's text.

pages.text: The check reads the site's saved missing-page test result. It needs no article sample or percentage of failed pages. Review the tested address and response before changing error handling.

reports.text: The finding is medium severity. A false flag produces no finding from this check, which is narrower than proving that all possible missing addresses on the site return the correct response.

fix.text: Request a genuinely nonexistent address and inspect its response status as well as its appearance. Make the missing-page handler return the appropriate error while keeping useful navigation for the visitor. Avoid sending every unknown address to the homepage as successful content. Recheck the original probe case after changing the server or application route.

rows.guide_title: How to fix soft 404s

review.text: Inspect a genuinely nonexistent address without treating its visual design as the response status. A helpful error page can still return the wrong success response. Keep the missing-page route separate from valid content routes when changing the application. After repair, confirm that a real page still succeeds and the nonexistent address still provides useful navigation while returning the intended error, rather than replacing every unknown path with the homepage.

faq.question: What does the saved missing-page probe flag as a soft 404?
faq.answer: The saved probe can identify HTTP status 200 on a missing page where HTTP status 404 was expected. This mismatch gets a medium result.

faq.question: Does the site-level soft-404 check make a fresh request?
faq.answer: No. The missing-page test result was saved earlier. This check reviews that record without another request.

faq.question: Does a clear site-level soft-404 result prove every missing URL works correctly?
faq.answer: No. A false flag only clears this saved test. Other missing addresses may need separate response checks.

rows.title: Soft 404 pages in the crawl

conditions.expression: any((marker in haystack for marker in _NOT_FOUND_MARKERS))

constants.name: _NOT_FOUND_MARKERS
constants.expression: ('page not found', 'page cannot be found', '404 error', 'error 404', "we can't find that page", 'we cannot find that page', "page doesn't exist", 'page does not exist', 'no longer exists', 'page you requested', 'oops! the requested page', 'sorry, that page', 'nothing found here', 'the page you are looking for')

findings.title: f"{len(offenders)} page{plural_s(len(offenders))} {verb('show', len(offenders))} an error message but return HTTP 200"
findings.detail: f"These URLs serve a 'page not found' message with a success status code. {len(linked)} of them are linked from elsewhere on the site. Google treats this as a soft 404: the page is dropped from the index anyway, but the crawl budget and link equity spent reaching it are lost, and visitors hit a dead end."
findings.fix: 'Return a real 404 (or 410) status for these URLs, and fix or remove the internal links pointing at them.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do successful pages show a not-found message?
rows.answer: It finds short successful pages containing one of the stored missing-page messages.
rows.why: Missing-page messages and successful statuses tell readers' software different things. An internal link to that response also gives you a source to repair. Review the message and the linking page together.

condition.text: The test reads successful pages and skips any with more than 250 words. It searches the title plus the first 1500 characters of text for the literal not-found markers. Matching pages are separated according to whether another crawled page links to them. The presence of an observed source link raises severity from medium to high. Matching words alone leave the cause of the response unknown. For example, a page above 250 words is left out even if it discusses a not-found message.

pages.text: Crawl records supply successful responses, short page text, titles and incoming links. This test does not use the separate site-level probe of a nonexistent address.

reports.text: The finding reports a conflict between a successful response and an error-like body. A short article discussing an error message can need review before being treated as a missing page, because the check is a phrase test with a length guard.

fix.text: Open the affected URL from its source link. Restore the intended content if it should exist, or return a proper missing-page status if it does not. Fix internal links that still lead there. If the page is a genuine explanation of an error, verify its content and response before changing it solely because a phrase matched.

rows.guide_title: How to fix soft 404s

review.text: Read the short page and the source link together. A real error response disguised as success differs from an article explaining an error message. Keep the page's purpose in view before deleting it. If the content should exist, restore it. For an obsolete address, correct the response and the links that point there. Retest the served document so that an old substitute body does not remain behind a successful status.

faq.question: How long can a page be and still enter the error-body check?
faq.answer: Pages above 250 words are skipped. Short successful responses can be searched for stored not-found wording.

faq.question: Does an internal link to an error-like page raise severity?
faq.answer: Yes. An observed source link moves the result from medium to high. The text still needs review before calling the page missing.

faq.question: How much text is searched for not-found markers on successful pages?
faq.answer: It searches the title and first 1500 characters. A matching phrase leaves the cause uncertain until the response is inspected.

rows.title: URL structure

findings.title: f"{len(session_ids)} URL{plural_s(len(session_ids))} {verb('contain', len(session_ids))} a session ID"
findings.detail: 'Session IDs in URLs create a new, unique URL for every visit, an effectively infinite duplicate-content space.'
findings.fix: 'Move session state into cookies and strip the parameter from crawlable URLs.'

findings.title: f"{len(uppercase)} URL{plural_s(len(uppercase))} {verb('contain', len(uppercase))} uppercase characters"
findings.detail: 'URL paths are case-sensitive on most servers, so /About and /about can both be indexed as separate pages.'
findings.fix: 'Standardise on lowercase URLs and 301-redirect the mixed-case versions.'

findings.title: f"{len(spaces)} URL{plural_s(len(spaces))} {verb('contain', len(spaces))} encoded spaces"
findings.detail: 'Spaces in URLs are ugly when shared, break in plain-text contexts, and are frequently mis-copied.'
findings.fix: 'Use hyphens between words in URL slugs.'

findings.title: f'{len(very_long)} URL{plural_s(len(very_long))} {is_are(len(very_long))} longer than 115 characters'
findings.detail: 'Long URLs get truncated in search results and shared links.'
findings.fix: 'Shorten slugs to the two or three words that describe the page.'

findings.title: f"{len(params)} URL{plural_s(len(params))} {verb('carry', len(params))} multiple query parameters"
findings.detail: 'Faceted or parameterised URLs multiply into large numbers of near-duplicate pages and consume crawl budget that should go to real content.'
findings.fix: 'Add a canonical on each parameterised URL pointing at the clean version, and leave those URLs crawlable so the canonical can be read. Do not also disallow the parameters in robots.txt: a URL Googlebot cannot fetch is a canonical it cannot see, and the URL can still be indexed with no content behind it. Use robots.txt only for parameter spaces you never want crawled at all (session ids, infinite filter combinations), and do not bother canonicalising those, because nothing will read it.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do your URLs contain avoidable clutter?
rows.answer: It checks address spelling, length, query parameters and session identifiers.
rows.why: Different spellings and session data can make an address harder to manage consistently. A parameter can also be necessary, so the check identifies a pattern to inspect instead of proving that every matching part should be deleted.

condition.text: The check looks for uppercase URL paths, encoded spaces and addresses longer than 115 characters. A query with at least 2 ampersands joins the multiple-parameter group. That group is reported only above the larger of 3 pages or a 0.25 share of indexable pages. Known session names are checked in queries and path parameters. Each type has its own finding and severity. For example, an address exactly 115 characters long is outside the long-URL group.

pages.text: The check reads the address itself. It does not decide whether every parameter is needed. Review the destination and its use before changing the URL.

reports.text: Session identifiers are high severity, multiple-parameter findings medium, uppercase and spaces low, and long URLs notices. These are review categories rather than a claim that every long or parameterised address is broken.

fix.text: Review which URL parts identify content and which only track a session or view. Keep stable public addresses and update links when changing them. Use redirects or canonicals deliberately for real alternatives. Test query-dependent pages before removing parameters so that cleanup does not erase filters or other useful page states.

rows.guide_title: SEO URL structure best practice, minus the folklore

review.text: Inspect the role of each parameter or path segment before simplifying it. A useful filter and a session identifier do not make the same public address statement. Keep stable content identifiers while removing values that should not persist in public links. Plan redirects for changed addresses where appropriate and review generated navigation, because editing a displayed URL cannot correct the template that keeps publishing the old form.

faq.question: How long must a URL be for the long-address notice?
faq.answer: It must exceed 115 characters. Equality does not enter the long-address group.

faq.question: How many ampersands put a URL query in the multiple-parameter group?
faq.answer: At least 2 ampersands qualifies the query. The group must also clear the page-count or share requirement before it is reported.

faq.question: Are session identifiers as minor as uppercase URL paths?
faq.answer: No. Session identifiers have high severity, while uppercase paths are low. Long addresses receive notices.

rows.title: www / apex canonicalisation

findings.title: 'The site is reachable on both www and non-www without redirecting'
findings.detail: f'{ctx.site.www_note}. Search engines see two complete copies of the site and split every ranking signal between them.'
findings.fix: 'Pick one hostname and 301-redirect the other to it, site-wide, preserving the path.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do your www and bare addresses agree?
rows.answer: It reports the saved result for host canonicalisation.
rows.why: A consistent public host gives the site a clear address policy. The useful question is whether the alternate address leads to the intended one, rather than which spelling a tool happens to prefer.

condition.text: The check uses the saved test of www redirects. If that test failed, it produces a high finding for a site reachable with and without www, without the expected redirect. It does not choose the preferred host or inspect every internal link. Review the measured host responses before changing server settings.

pages.text: The check uses the earlier host test. It does not assign a content-duplication percentage or a ranking effect to either host spelling. You choose the preferred address for the business.

reports.text: The finding is high severity. It describes the observed host setup and does not mean that using www is inherently better or worse than using the bare domain.

fix.text: Choose the host your site should use and configure the alternate host to redirect to it. Keep the path and query where appropriate. Align internal links, canonicals and sitemap addresses with that choice. Test both host variants over the relevant schemes after editing server rules, since a working homepage rule may not cover inner paths.

rows.guide_title: www vs non-www: does it still matter?

review.text: Test the alternate host on an inner path as well as the root. A homepage move alone may not explain how the rest of the site behaves. Keep the intended path and query through the redirect where they identify real content. Inspect how the alternate host handles a meaningful inner destination before deciding that its root response represents the whole route. Align canonical and sitemap addresses with the chosen host, while preserving valid external links through a working alternate-host route instead of making those older links fail.

faq.question: Does the www check choose which host spelling I should use?
faq.answer: No. Choosing the preferred host is left to you. The test reads the saved www redirect result.

faq.question: How serious is a failed www-to-preferred-host setup?
faq.answer: It gets high severity. Inspect the saved host responses to decide which redirect setting needs repair.

faq.question: Does a www finding mean the bare domain is inherently worse?
faq.answer: No. The bare domain and www can both be valid choices. What matters here is the observed host setup and expected redirect.

rows.title: hreflang language codes

conditions.expression: not raw or raw.lower() == 'x-default' or raw in seen
