findings.title: f'{len(bad)} invalid hreflang code{plural_s(len(bad))}'
findings.detail: f'''An hreflang value is a language, optionally a script, optionally a country. A value a search engine cannot resolve is silently dropped: the tag is simply ignored, with no error anywhere to tell you. Example: hreflang="{code}": {reason}. The most common instance of this is 'en-uk': the United Kingdom's country code is GB, so 'en-uk' does nothing at all. Capitalisation is not one of these problems: 'af-za' and 'af-ZA' are the same tag, and this audit does not report either.'''
findings.fix: 'Correct the codes to valid language-country pairs, and use x-default for the fallback version.'
findings.evidence: {'invalid': [{'code': c, 'reason': r} for (_u, c, r) in bad[:10]]}

findings.title: f"{len(codes)} hreflang code{plural_s(len(codes))} use{('' if len(codes) > 1 else 's')} a superseded language subtag"
findings.detail: "These are well-formed and name a real language by an old code. IANA's language subtag registry marks them deprecated and gives the value to use instead: " + '; '.join((f"'{l}' is the old code for {name}, now '{pref}'" for (l, pref, name) in pairs[:4])) + f'. Example here: hreflang="{first[1]}". Whether a given search engine still honours the old form is not something this audit can test from outside, so this is a tidy-up rather than a fault, but the registry is unambiguous about which one is current.'
findings.fix: 'Replace the language subtag with the current one, keeping the region and the URL exactly as they are: ' + ', '.join((f'{l}- becomes {pref}-' for (l, pref, _n) in pairs[:4])) + '. Update the return tags on the target pages in the same change, or the pair stops matching.'
findings.evidence: {'superseded': [{'code': c, 'use': pref} for (_u, c, _l, pref, _n) in superseded[:10]]}

findings.title: f'{len(regions)} hreflang region code{plural_s(len(regions))} Google does not support'
findings.detail: f"These tags are correct. BCP 47 allows a UN M.49 numeric area code where a country code would go, so {', '.join(regions[:8])}{('…' if len(regions) > 8 else '')} {('are' if len(regions) > 1 else 'is')} well-formed there, and other consumers may honour {('them' if len(regions) > 1 else 'it')}, as written here, in {examples[0]}{(f' and {len(examples) - 1} other tag' if len(examples) > 1 else '')}{(plural_s(len(examples) - 1) if len(examples) > 2 else '')}. Google is not one of them. Its hreflang documentation says only ISO 639-1 languages and ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 regions are supported, and names es-419 as an example of a code that is not. Google discards the annotation, so the alternate it points at goes unlinked, which is worth knowing, because a numeric area code is something you only write on purpose."
findings.fix: 'If the audience really is a multi-country region, there is no single tag for it: name the countries you care about, one hreflang each, all pointing at the same page: es-MX, es-AR, es-CO. Keep x-default for everyone else. If only the language matters, drop the region and use the bare language tag.'
findings.evidence: {'unsupported_region': [{'code': c, 'region': r} for (_u, c, r) in unsupported_region[:10]]}

findings.title: f'{len(regions)} hreflang region code{plural_s(len(regions))} this audit does not recognise'
findings.detail: f"These are well-formed, and the language part is fine. It is the country part this audit cannot place. This audit checks regions against IANA's language subtag registry, which is the ISO 3166-1 country codes plus the UN M.49 numeric areas that BCP 47 allows. Not recognised here: {', '.join(examples[:8])}{('…' if len(examples) > 8 else '')}. A code that is not in the registry is almost always a typo, and a search engine will drop the tag, but this audit's copy of the registry has a date and ISO 3166-1 does occasionally assign a new code, so this is reported as something to look at rather than as a fault, and it does not affect your score."
findings.fix: "Check each region against the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 list. If the code is correct and simply newer than this audit's table, nothing needs changing; if it is a typo, correct it on this page and in the return tag on the page it points at, or the pair stops matching."
findings.evidence: {'unrecognised_region': [{'code': c, 'region': r} for (_u, c, r) in unknown_region[:10]]}

findings.title: f'{len(codes)} hreflang language code{plural_s(len(codes))} this audit does not recognise'
findings.detail: f"These are well-formed and may be perfectly valid. This audit's language table covers the common ISO 639-1 codes and does not include every language that BCP 47 allows, including three-letter codes for languages with no two-letter form. Not recognised here: {', '.join(codes[:8])}{('…' if len(codes) > 8 else '')}. This is a limit of the tool, not a fault in your markup, so it does not affect your score."
findings.fix: 'Nothing to do unless one of these is a typo. Check any you do not recognise against the IANA language subtag registry.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Are your hreflang codes recognised?
rows.answer: It separates malformed, superseded, unsupported and unrecognised language-region codes.
rows.why: A language code states which audience an alternate page serves. Keeping unknown values separate from known mistakes avoids replacing a legitimate declaration on the strength of an incomplete lookup table.

condition.text: The sample uses successful pages with hreflang. Empty values, x-default and repeated values are skipped. The format allows 2 language letters or 3 language letters, an optional 4-letter script and an optional region of 2 letters or 3 digits. Known region mistakes, private-use regions, numeric regions, old language codes and unknown values receive different explanations. A value missing from a recognition table stays unrecognised until it can be checked. For example, a 4-letter script subtag can appear between the language and region.

pages.text: The check reads declared alternate-language codes. It does not judge translation quality or inspect an unavailable target's language. Review each declaration against its intended audience.

reports.text: Malformed codes are medium severity. Superseded languages and unsupported regions are low, while unrecognised regions or languages are notices. The report distinguishes a known defect from a limit in the audit's own reference tables.

fix.text: Review the exact code and the audience it should identify. Correct known typos and use a supported language-region form where needed. Verify unfamiliar values against the relevant registry before changing them. Check the target page and return tags after fixing the code, since spelling alone cannot establish a complete alternate-language relationship.

rows.guide_title: hreflang values that are not valid language codes

review.text: Compare the reported code with the language and region of the target page. A familiar-looking region suffix can still be a known typo, while an unfamiliar registered value may simply exceed the audit's table. Keep uncertainty separate from a confirmed format error. After correcting declarations, review the whole alternate group so that a local spelling edit does not leave related pages using inconsistent codes for the same audience.

faq.question: Can a hreflang code contain a script subtag?
faq.answer: Yes. An optional 4-letter script can sit between language and region. The full value must still match the allowed format.

faq.question: Does an unrecognised hreflang region always mean the region is invalid?
faq.answer: No. Unrecognised regions or languages receive notices. A missing reference-table entry is kept separate from a known defect.

faq.question: Are empty hreflang values and x-default checked as ordinary language codes?
faq.answer: No. Empty values, x-default and repeats are skipped. The format comparison uses the remaining values on successful pages.

rows.title: hreflang return tags

conditions.expression: target == source or target not in crawled

findings.title: f'{len(broken)} hreflang link{plural_s(len(broken))} {is_are(len(broken))} not reciprocated'
findings.detail: f'hreflang only works when the link goes both ways: if page A declares B as its alternate, B must declare A in return. Google ignores one-way declarations entirely, so the wrong language version keeps being served. This is invisible in the page source: every tag is present and correct in isolation. Example: {source} points to {target}, which does not point back.'
findings.fix: 'Make every page in the set list every other page in the set, including itself. Generating the block once and including it on all versions is the only reliable way to keep it symmetrical.'
findings.evidence: {'pairs': [{'from': s, 'to': t} for (s, t) in broken[:10]]}

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do your language alternatives link back?
rows.answer: It checks reciprocal hreflang declarations between pages the crawl successfully read.
rows.why: An alternate-language relationship is meant to connect versions of content. Comparing both directions reveals a partial template update that looking at either page in isolation can miss.

condition.text: At least 2 successful pages with hreflang are needed. Source and target addresses are compared without trailing slashes. Self-links and targets not in the successful crawl set are skipped. For each remaining declaration, the target must declare the source in return. A missing return relationship enters the finding. It is not inferred for an alternate URL whose page was never available to compare. For example, with 2 successful alternate pages, each can be checked for a return link to the other.

pages.text: The check compares alternate-language declarations on successful pages. Targets that could not be loaded are skipped. No missing return link is claimed for those unchecked pages.

reports.text: Missing return links are high severity. The result names a source and target pair, while incomplete target coverage limits which relationships the audit can judge.

fix.text: Open the source and target declarations together. Add the intended reciprocal link with the correct language code and final URL, then check the rest of the same group for consistency. Keep the self-reference where appropriate. Crawl the target before treating a relationship outside the measured page set as confirmed broken or confirmed complete.

rows.guide_title: How to fix hreflang return tags

review.text: Inspect both pages in a reported pair. A declaration on the source does not establish what the target publishes, and a target outside the successful crawl remains outside this comparison. Keep the intended alternate group consistent when updating templates. After adding a return relationship, check the current page's self-reference and the final target addresses too, rather than treating reciprocity as proof that every part of the group is correct. Record which language variants belong together before editing templates, and compare the served declarations again after the shared change is built.

faq.question: How many pages are needed to check alternate-language return links?
faq.answer: At least 2 successful pages carrying hreflang are needed. Both sides must be available for the relationship to be judged.

faq.question: Can an uncrawled translation be called missing a hreflang return link?
faq.answer: No. A target outside the successful crawl set is left unchecked. Its return declaration cannot be inferred from an unavailable page.

faq.question: How serious is a confirmed missing hreflang return link?
faq.answer: It has high severity. Review the reported source and target together before updating the alternate declarations.

rows.title: hreflang self-reference

findings.title: f'{len(missing)} page{plural_s(len(missing))} {has_have(len(missing))} hreflang tags but no self-reference'
findings.detail: 'Each page in an hreflang set must include an entry pointing at itself. Without it Google cannot tell which language version the current page is, and typically discards the whole set, so the tags do nothing.'
findings.fix: 'Add a self-referencing hreflang entry to every page in the set.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does each language page include itself?
rows.answer: It looks for a self-reference in pages that already declare hreflang alternatives.
rows.why: An alternate set should describe the page being read as well as its alternatives. A self-reference gives the same kind of address declaration for the current version that the markup gives for the others.

condition.text: The check selects successful pages with hreflang. For each page, it builds the declared target set and compares the page's own URL after removing trailing slashes. A page missing from its own target set enters the finding. Sites with no hreflang pages produce no finding here, so this test does not require a single-language site to add alternate-language markup.

pages.text: Only existing alternate-language declarations are reviewed. It does not infer a translation from similar text or decide which language code the page should use.

reports.text: Missing self-references are medium severity. The target comparison is address-based, so an alias that differs beyond a trailing slash needs review rather than being silently treated as the page's final URL.

fix.text: Inspect the page's alternate-language group. Add the current page under its correct language code and use the intended final address. Apply the same group consistently to related versions where appropriate. Review return links and target health separately, because a self-reference does not prove that the rest of the group is usable.

rows.guide_title: How to fix hreflang return tags

review.text: Compare the self-reference with the page's final public address. A nearby alias may describe the same content to a person while still being a different target string to this test. Keep the declared language accurate and use a consistent alternate group. Review the resulting markup on the current page and its alternatives after a template change, since adding a self-link alone cannot establish that the other pages return the relationship.

faq.question: Must a page appear in its own hreflang target set?
faq.answer: Yes. Each qualifying page should belong to its declared target set. The address comparison ignores trailing slashes.

faq.question: Does a single-language site need hreflang to pass the self-reference check?
faq.answer: No. With no hreflang pages, there is nothing for this comparison to test. It reviews existing declarations rather than requiring new ones.

faq.question: How serious is a missing hreflang self-reference?
faq.answer: The result receives medium severity. Address aliases beyond trailing-slash differences still need review.

rows.title: hreflang target health

findings.title: f'{len(targets)} hreflang target{plural_s(len(targets))} could not be reached'
findings.detail: f'This audit got no response at all from these URLs: not an error page, nothing. That is usually a network problem at this end rather than anything wrong with the target, so they are reported here instead of counted as broken. Example: {targets[0]}. Whether the hreflang cluster is intact is simply unknown for these.'
findings.fix: 'Open one of them in a browser. If it loads, nothing needs doing and a re-run will clear this. If it does not, the hreflang pointing at it is broken and worth fixing.'

findings.title: f"{len(dead)} hreflang tag{plural_s(len(dead))} {verb('point', len(dead))} at unusable URLs"
findings.detail: f'hreflang must reference the live, final, indexable URL of each version. Targets that 404, redirect, or carry a noindex break the cluster for every page in it. Example: {target} {reason}.'
findings.fix: 'Point each hreflang at the final destination URL, and make sure that URL is indexable.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do your language links point to usable pages?
rows.answer: It checks measured hreflang targets for errors, redirects and noindex directives.
rows.why: A correctly written alternate link can still name an address that does not serve an indexable page. Checking the measured destination adds details beyond code spelling and reciprocal tags.

condition.text: Targets are matched to saved pages using the exact address and trailing-slash alternatives. Unmeasured targets are skipped. Refused responses and zero-status failures are reported as unchecked rather than dead. Other responses with HTTP status 400 or above, addresses known to redirect away and pages carrying noindex can enter the unusable-target finding. The code uses saved redirect history to recognise an alternate address that was not the final page. For example, a measured HTTP status 400 can enter the unusable-target finding after refusal handling.

pages.text: Successful pages supply the alternate-language links. The wider crawl supplies responses for their destinations. An unmeasured destination stays unknown and needs a separate review.

reports.text: Unusable targets are medium severity and unchecked targets notices. The distinction prevents a blocked request or failed fetch from being presented as certain proof that a translation no longer exists.

fix.text: Use the final intended URL for each alternate. Repair genuinely missing pages or remove obsolete alternatives, and review unintended noindex directives. Investigate refused requests before replacing a valid translation. Retest the target and the source declaration together after a change so that the markup names the address that actually serves the content.

rows.guide_title: Why an hreflang target is reported as dead

review.text: Inspect the measured destination and its redirect history before replacing an alternate. A refusal leaves the target unchecked. Keep confirmed errors and noindex directives in the change list with their recorded statuses. Use the intended final address. Check its language and return links after repairing the response.

faq.question: Can an alternate-language target returning an error be unusable?
faq.answer: Yes. After refusals are handled, HTTP status 400 or higher can qualify. Redirects and noindex targets have their own qualifying cases.

faq.question: Are refused translation requests reported as dead hreflang targets?
faq.answer: No. Refused responses are unchecked. They receive notices because the saved request cannot establish that the translation is gone.

faq.question: Does the hreflang-target check judge translations it never measured?
faq.answer: No. Unmeasured targets are skipped. Inspect those destinations separately when the crawl did not save a usable result.

rows.title: Broken outbound links

conditions.expression: p.endswith('/') or not rest or (not rest[0].isalnum())

findings.title: f'{len(broken)} outbound link{plural_s(len(broken))} {is_are(len(broken))} broken'
findings.detail: f"Checked {len(statuses)} of the site's outbound links (a sample, not every outbound link on the site{_per_host_note(ctx)}{_left_out_note(ctx)}) and {len(broken)} failed. Dead outbound links are a small quality signal and a direct annoyance for visitors. Example: " + next(iter(broken))
findings.fix: 'Update or remove each dead link. If the destination moved, link to its new home.'

findings.title: f'{len(malformed)} link{plural_s(len(malformed))} {has_have(len(malformed))} the address written twice'
findings.fix: 'Delete the duplicated scheme from each href. This audit has not requested the repaired address, so open one to confirm it loads before publishing the change.'

findings.title: f'{len(own_broken)} link{plural_s(len(own_broken))} to your own subdomain{plural_s(len(own_broken))} {is_are(len(own_broken))} broken'
findings.detail: f"{len(own_broken)} link{plural_s(len(own_broken))} on this site {verb('point', len(own_broken))} at a host of your own that did not answer. These are not outbound links. They are yours, so this is a service of yours that is down or gone rather than someone else's page moving."
findings.fix: 'Check whether the subdomain is still meant to exist. If it is, it is down; if it is not, remove the links to it.'

findings.title: f'{len(refused)} outbound link{plural_s(len(refused))} could not be checked'
findings.detail: f'{len(refused)} of the {len(statuses)} outbound links sampled refused an automated request: 400, 401, 403, 429 and similar, or a server that closed the connection without answering. That is a statement about this crawler, not about the link: the pages may be perfectly fine in a browser. They are neither reported as broken nor counted as working. Example: ' + next(iter(refused))
findings.fix: 'Open a couple in a browser if you want certainty; nothing here needs fixing on the strength of this check.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do your outbound links still work?
rows.answer: It separates broken external destinations from refusals, sharing links and malformed addresses.
rows.why: Broken and untestable destinations need different decisions. Keeping those outcomes separate helps you repair actual address errors without deleting a useful source because its server rejected an automated request.

condition.text: The test uses saved external statuses, excluding image probes and recognised share-intent links. Doubled-scheme addresses are reported separately. Links to related own hosts are separated from third-party links. HTTP status 400 or above, or a zero status, can be broken only after refusal handling. Known refusal codes, HTTP statuses at or above 600 and recorded hangups are treated as unverified instead. Source links are collected for the remaining broken targets. For example, HTTP status 600 or above stays unverified under this test.

pages.text: The saved external-link measurement determines coverage. Per-host caps and time limits can leave links unchecked, so this test is not a promise that every outbound URL on every page was tested.

reports.text: Broken links and malformed or own-subdomain cases are low severity. Unverified destinations are notices. A destination refusing the audit may still work for a visitor, which is why the code avoids calling every unsuccessful request a dead link.

fix.text: Open the destination and inspect the cited source link. Correct doubled schemes and obsolete addresses, or replace a dead source with a relevant working one. Review refusals manually and respect rate limits. Check the source page after editing so that both the visible label and the hidden destination still describe the resource you intended.

rows.guide_title: How to fix broken outbound links

review.text: Follow the cited source link and inspect the destination's response in context. A sharing endpoint is designed for a different request from an ordinary reference page, and a server may reject automated checks while serving visitors. Keep unverified links in a review list rather than deleting them as certainly dead. Where an address is genuinely wrong, correct the source component so the same malformed destination does not return on the next build.

faq.question: Is an external link refusing the audit definitely broken?
faq.answer: No. Known refusal codes are treated as unverified. A visitor may still be able to reach the destination.

faq.question: Can a doubled-scheme external address get its own finding?
faq.answer: Yes. Doubled-scheme addresses are separated from ordinary third-party failures. Inspect the original source link for the malformed target.

faq.question: How serious are confirmed broken external links?
faq.answer: They receive low severity. Unverified destinations receive notices so that blocked requests are not presented as proven dead links.

rows.title: Insecure internal links

findings.title: f"{len(offenders)} page{plural_s(len(offenders))} {verb('link', len(offenders))} to your own site over plain http://"
findings.detail: f'The site runs on HTTPS but some of its own links point at http:// addresses. Each one costs a redirect to reach the secure page on every click and every crawl. Where nothing redirects, it sends the visitor to the insecure copy. Example: {example}'
findings.fix: 'Update these links to https://.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your secure site link to plain HTTP pages?
rows.answer: It finds internal links written with an insecure scheme on a site served over HTTPS.
rows.why: A secure page can still send a visitor through a plain-scheme address in its links. Reviewing the source link makes it possible to align the site's own navigation with its intended secure address policy.

condition.text: The check stops when the site is not served over HTTPS. On a secure site it scans indexable pages for internal links beginning with http. Pages with such links enter a low-severity finding, with an example destination. Even a working redirect can leave the site's own links using the older scheme. Those links can qualify without a failed destination.

pages.text: The check uses the site's security status and internal links read from pages intended for search. It compares the URL schemes. You need to review the response and final destination separately.

reports.text: The finding is low severity. It describes the spelling of internal destinations, not proof that the final page remains insecure after redirects or that every visitor receives an error.

fix.text: Update internal destinations to the correct secure final URLs. Check shared menus and templates before editing repeated links individually. Confirm that the destination works over HTTPS and preserve paths and queries that identify the content. Review the redirect policy separately so that old external links still reach the intended page.

rows.guide_title: How to redirect http:// to https://

review.text: Compare the written destination with the site's final secure address. A redirect may rescue the old spelling, but the internal source can still be updated. Keep legacy redirect support for visitors arriving through links you do not control. Review the shared navigation and stored content separately, because the same plain-scheme link can be generated by a template or copied into an individual article's body.

faq.question: Can an HTTP internal link be reported even when it redirects successfully?
faq.answer: Yes. A failed destination is not required. An HTTP link on a secure site can qualify even when a redirect reaches the right page.

faq.question: Does the HTTP internal-link check run on an HTTP-only site?
faq.answer: No. This test applies to a site served over HTTPS. Plain-HTTP sites do not enter the internal-scheme comparison.

faq.question: How serious are HTTP internal links on an HTTPS site?
faq.answer: The finding has low severity. It reports the address spelling rather than establishing that the final response remains insecure.

rows.title: Internal links into and out of each page

conditions.expression: weak and len(weak) > len(ctx.content_bearing) * 0.3 and ctx.crawl.supports_link_graph_claims

findings.title: f"{len(isolated)} page{plural_s(len(isolated))} {verb('link', len(isolated))} out to almost nothing"
findings.detail: 'Pages with two or fewer internal links are dead ends. They hold ranking signal instead of passing it on, and they give visitors nowhere to go next.'
findings.fix: 'Add contextual links from the body copy to related services or articles, as well as the navigation links.'

findings.title: f'{len(weak)} page{plural_s(len(weak))} {has_have(len(weak))} only one internal link pointing to {them_it(len(weak))}'
findings.detail: 'Internal links are how ranking signal flows through a site and how Google judges which pages matter. Pages reachable from only one place read as unimportant, however good they are.'
findings.fix: 'Link to your commercially important pages from several places: the main nav, relevant body copy, and related-content blocks.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do useful pages have enough internal links?
rows.answer: It checks sparse outgoing links and widespread pages with a single observed incoming link.
rows.why: Outgoing links and incoming links describe different routes through a site. A page can link to plenty of content while being difficult to discover from elsewhere, which explains why the code checks both directions.

condition.text: At least 5 pages with readable content are needed. A page other than the homepage with at most 2 outgoing internal links can be flagged as sparse. Below the root, a page other than the homepage with exactly 1 incoming internal link joins the weak-link group. That group is reported only above a 0.3 share of readable pages and with enough crawl coverage to judge links. Incoming and outgoing links are checked separately. For example, a page with exactly 2 outgoing internal links can enter the sparse-link group.

pages.text: The check reads pages with usable content and the internal links observed by the crawl. Missing coverage can prevent a finding. Review which sections were crawled before adding site-wide links.

reports.text: Sparse outgoing links are low severity. Widespread single-inlink pages are medium. A count alone does not tell you whether a link is relevant, so adding unrelated links merely to increase the total would miss the page's purpose.

fix.text: Review the affected page in its section. Add useful contextual links to related information and link important pages from places where visitors expect to find them. Repair obsolete destinations before adding more links. If the graph is incomplete, improve coverage before treating an apparent lack of incoming links as a confirmed structural problem.

rows.guide_title: Internal link equity, measured

review.text: Review the source pages as well as the affected destination. An incoming-link count describes discovery routes, while an outgoing-link count describes choices offered from the page itself. Keep both directions in your notes. Add links that belong in the reader's journey and use accurate labels, then inspect the graph after recrawling rather than assuming a repeated footer link supplies the same context as a useful reference in related content.

faq.question: How few outgoing links make a page sparse in this audit?
faq.answer: A non-homepage can qualify with 2 outgoing internal links or fewer. Add useful routes rather than unrelated links.

faq.question: How many readable pages does the internal-link volume check need?
faq.answer: The comparison starts with at least 5 pages that have readable content. Insufficient graph coverage can withhold incoming-link claims.

faq.question: Are widespread single-inlink pages treated like sparse outgoing links?
faq.answer: No. The sparse-link result has low severity. A widespread single-inlink pattern can receive medium severity when coverage supports the claim.

rows.title: Internal links to the pages that sell

findings.title: f"{len(weak)} page{plural_s(len(weak))} that {verb('sell', len(weak))} {has_have(len(weak))} only one internal link pointing to {them_it(len(weak))}"
findings.detail: 'Internal links are how ranking signal flows through a site and how Google judges which pages matter. These are the pages a visitor buys, books or gets in touch on, and each is reachable from exactly one place on the site, so they read as incidental rather than central.'
findings.fix: 'Link to each of these from several places: the main navigation, the body copy of related pages, and any related-content block. A page you want ranked should be reachable the way a visitor would look for it.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Can visitors find the pages that sell?
rows.answer: It finds non-homepage selling pages with exactly a single observed internal inlink.
rows.why: A service or product page needs a route from other useful parts of the site. The check gives extra attention to pages recognised as selling, while leaving the owner to decide which specific pages matter to the business.

condition.text: Enough crawl coverage is needed to judge internal links. The check selects pages with readable content and a recognised selling-page address, leaving out the homepage. Exactly 1 observed incoming link qualifies. For example, a service page linked only from its menu can qualify. Business importance still needs your review.

pages.text: The check uses readable pages, selling-page addresses and observed internal links. A browser-only menu or limited crawl can leave links unseen. Check that coverage before treating the count as complete.

reports.text: The finding is medium severity. Its scope is the recognised selling pages with a measured single source, rather than a complete inventory of every URL that can contribute to an enquiry or purchase.

fix.text: Find the page's place in the site's navigation and related content. Add relevant links from category pages, useful articles or other routes that naturally lead to the offer. Use labels that explain the destination. Keep the page's purpose clear and avoid adding repeated irrelevant links solely to change a graph count.

rows.guide_title: Fix the pages that make you money first

review.text: Compare the detected selling role with the page's actual business purpose. URL patterns help select candidates but cannot replace the owner's knowledge of which services matter. Keep relevant routes from section pages and supporting explanations clear. Review those source links after editing so that they lead to the current offer, rather than adding generic links from unrelated pages merely to increase the number of observed sources.

faq.question: How many incoming links trigger the weak selling-page finding?
faq.answer: The qualifying count is 1 observed incoming link on an eligible selling page. Enough graph coverage is also required.

faq.question: Is the homepage included in the weak selling-page link check?
faq.answer: No. The check selects selling pages while leaving out the homepage. It also requires readable content and enough crawl coverage.

faq.question: How serious is a selling page with only one measured source link?
faq.answer: The result has medium severity. Confirm that the recognised address really serves an important selling role before adding links.

rows.title: Navigation reachable without JavaScript

findings.title: headline
findings.detail: detail
findings.fix: 'Render the navigation server-side, or output real <a href> elements in the initial HTML and let JavaScript enhance them. A menu built from <div onclick> or injected after load is not a link. Test it the way this audit did: fetch the page with JavaScript disabled and look for <a href> in the source.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Is your navigation present before scripts run?
rows.answer: It checks the saved navigation-in-HTML result across successful HTML pages.
rows.why: Sitemaps can expose addresses without supplying the navigation links between pages. Reading the initial document shows whether those routes are available before browser code adds them.

condition.text: At least 3 successful HTML pages are needed. If the saved crawl flag says navigation is present in HTML, the check stops. Otherwise it counts internal links, calculates links per page and reports the missing navigation, with separate wording when the total is zero. Sitemap counts and unlinked pages support the explanation. The registered condition does not use an average-link cutoff to decide whether the navigation flag is true. For example, 3 successful HTML pages are enough to begin the navigation check.

pages.text: The check uses successful HTML responses and the crawler's record of whether navigation is in the HTML. Its claim concerns links in the server response. Review loaded-browser navigation separately.

reports.text: The finding is high severity. A browser can display a menu that was absent from the document the crawler read, so visual inspection after loading answers a different question from this source check.

fix.text: Compare the menu visible in the browser with links in the served source. Render real navigation links in HTML on the server or during the static build. Keep script enhancements for opening and styling menus as needed. Retest several inner pages as well as the homepage, because a shared navigation fix should reach the templates it is meant to serve.

rows.guide_title: Fixing navigation that only exists after JavaScript runs

review.text: Inspect links in the initial source without judging the menu only after it opens. Text can be readable while the routes between pages are assembled later by scripts. Keep the content-rendering question separate from the navigation question. Test a representative inner page after changing the menu component, and confirm that its anchors carry real destinations even before optional browser interactions enhance their appearance or behaviour.

faq.question: How many HTML pages are needed to check missing source navigation?
faq.answer: The sample needs 3 successful HTML pages or more. A saved navigation flag and link records then supply the result.

faq.question: Can a menu visible after loading still be absent from the HTML crawl?
faq.answer: Yes. A menu can appear in a loaded browser despite missing source navigation. The finding has high severity.

faq.question: Does a low average link count alone decide whether navigation is missing?
faq.answer: No. An average-link cutoff does not decide the saved flag. The check uses the crawler's navigation-in-HTML observation.

rows.title: Outbound link handling

findings.title: f'Every outbound link points to {top_host}' if top_count == total_external else f'{top_count / total_external:.0%} of outbound links ({top_count}) point to {top_host}'
findings.detail: f'{top_count / total_external:.0%} of outbound links go to a single domain. That pattern is normal for a booking or payment provider, and is also what injected spam links look like, so it is worth confirming which this is.'
findings.fix: 'If these links are intentional (a booking system, a partner), no action is needed. If not, your site may be compromised. Check the footer and any recently modified templates, and scan for injected content.'

findings.title: 'Nearly every outbound link is nofollow'
findings.detail: 'Blanket nofollow on all outbound links was an old hoarding tactic. It has no upside now and slightly weakens the impression of a well-sourced page.'
findings.fix: 'Remove nofollow from genuine editorial citations. Keep it for paid, sponsored and user-generated links, where it is required.'

findings.title: 'The site links out to nothing'
findings.detail: 'No outbound links at all. Citing credible external sources is a mild trust signal and, for AI answer engines, part of how a page is judged to be well-sourced.'
findings.fix: 'Where you make a factual claim, link to the source: a standards body, a regulator, a manufacturer spec.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: How does your site handle outbound links?
rows.answer: It checks whether external links are absent, dominated by a host or almost all nofollow.
rows.why: A concentrated link pattern can come from a shared template or a deliberate relationship. Looking at the actual destinations and labels gives the context a ratio alone cannot supply.

condition.text: The check counts external links on indexable pages after excluding related own hosts. No outbound links on at least 8 indexable pages produces a notice. A host needs more than 20 links and more than a 0.6 share of all external links for the dominance finding. More than 10 total external links with a nofollow share above 0.9 produces a separate notice. Each comparison uses strict greater-than where stated. For example, exactly 20 links to a host do not exceed the host-dominance count limit.

pages.text: The check counts external destinations and nofollow links read from pages intended for search. It does not inspect every target's quality or commercial relationship. Those decisions need your review.

reports.text: Host dominance is medium severity. No-outbound and near-universal nofollow results are notices. These patterns can have valid explanations, so they are review cues rather than a command to add links to unrelated sites.

fix.text: Review repeated external links and their purpose. Remove abandoned widgets or stale relationships where appropriate, and keep useful references. Apply nofollow according to the relationship of the link rather than automatically across every external destination. Recheck shared templates when a repeated host accounts for much of the total.

rows.guide_title: How to fix broken outbound links

review.text: Group repeated destinations by purpose before removing them. A shared attribution, a tool integration and an editorial source can create different link patterns even when their hosts repeat. Keep useful references and review the relationship behind nofollow choices. If a template supplies most of the repeated links, inspect that component directly rather than editing unrelated articles, and verify that the remaining labels still explain where each external link leads.

faq.question: How many links to one external host trigger the dominance finding?
faq.answer: The count must exceed 20 links to a host, and its share must exceed 0.6 of external links. Both requirements apply.

faq.question: Does a site with no outbound links always get a warning?
faq.answer: The no-outbound result needs at least 8 indexable pages. It is a notice rather than proof that unrelated links should be added.

faq.question: When does near-universal nofollow use get reported?
faq.answer: The sample must exceed 10 total external links. A nofollow share greater than 0.9 then qualifies for a notice.

rows.title: Pagination handling

findings.title: f"{len(collapsed)} paginated page{plural_s(len(collapsed))} {verb('canonicalise', len(collapsed))} back to page 1"
findings.detail: 'Pages 2 and beyond declare page 1 as the canonical version, so Google treats them as duplicates and may stop crawling them, along with everything only linked from them.'
findings.fix: 'Make each paginated page self-canonical. Google no longer uses rel=prev/next, so self-canonical plus clean internal links is the correct pattern.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do your paginated pages name their own content?
rows.answer: It looks for numbered listing pages whose canonical points to a non-paginated address.
rows.why: Different listing pages can contain different entries. A canonical that names an unnumbered page can make a different statement from the content the visitor is reading, which is the relationship this test asks you to inspect.

condition.text: At least 2 successful pages with recognised numbered pagination URLs are needed. The patterns cover page path segments and page or p query parameters. A paginated page enters the finding when it has a canonical whose address does not match one of those pagination patterns. The test checks the shape of the canonical target, not whether the target contains the same list items. For example, a numbered listing needs at least 2 successfully crawled pages before this comparison can run.

pages.text: The check reads successful numbered-page URLs and their canonical tags. It compares address patterns. Review the list items yourself before choosing a canonical destination.

reports.text: The finding is medium severity. It reports a likely collapse of separate listing content, but a real duplicate page or an intentionally different design still needs review before the canonical is changed.

fix.text: Compare the listed entries on the numbered page with those on the canonical target. Use the intended canonical for genuinely distinct listing content, and keep links between listing pages readable. Preserve a canonical relationship only when it accurately describes duplicate content. Retest the final URLs and tags after changing the pagination template.

rows.guide_title: Canonical pagination: which URL should each page use?

review.text: Compare the content on the numbered page with the canonical destination. Distinct listing entries deserve a deliberate address policy, while a true duplicate may justify sharing a representative URL. Keep navigation between listing pages understandable. After changing the pagination template, inspect the source tags on later pages as well as the initial list, since a correct first-page declaration does not establish what the rest of the sequence publishes.

faq.question: How many numbered listing pages are needed for the pagination check?
faq.answer: The sample requires 2 successful pages or more with recognised numbered addresses. Smaller sets do not enter this comparison.

faq.question: Does the pagination check compare the items on each listing?
faq.answer: No. The canonical target is compared with address patterns. Whether the target repeats the same listing items needs review separately.

faq.question: How serious is a numbered page canonical pointing outside a pagination pattern?
faq.answer: It receives medium severity. Review whether the destination is intentional before changing the canonical.

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Should local business checks run on your site?
rows.answer: It checks whether your public business details call for local business tests.
rows.why: Local requirements depend on what the site actually represents. A scope decision helps avoid asking an online-only product for a map while still allowing useful checks on a site that publishes real local business data.

condition.text: The check looks for business markup, physical addresses, contact and location links, and local wording. It accounts for software sites and addresses belonging to listed people or businesses. If no pages load successfully, or all need scripts for their main content, local status can stay unknown. Otherwise it explains whether the site appears local. For example, a directory can list physical shops while its publisher operates entirely online.

pages.text: The check reads the site's business context and readable contact details. A directory may publish other businesses' addresses. Review whose premises each address describes.

reports.text: Applicable and not-applicable outcomes are passes. An undetermined outcome is a notice. A pass here describes scope, not a judgement that every local business detail is complete or correct.

fix.text: Read the details behind the scope result. Correct misleading business markup or location text if it describes the wrong organisation. If the site is a browser-built shell, improve readable content before expecting a confident scope decision. Review individual local findings separately once the business context is established.

rows.guide_title: Where an audit looks for your address

review.text: Read the result as a description of what the site represents. A directory may list premises that belong to someone else. Keep the local decision attached to the business being reviewed. If useful text was unavailable, make it readable and repeat the review before deciding how local checks apply.

faq.question: Can a directory list shops without being a local business itself?
faq.answer: Yes. The test considers listed people or businesses separately from the publisher. A directory can operate online while listing physical locations.

faq.question: Can local-business applicability remain unknown?
faq.answer: Yes. If no pages load successfully, local scope can remain undetermined. Script-dependent main content can also limit the decision.

faq.question: Does a local-business applicability pass mean my contact details are complete?
faq.answer: No. It is a scope result. An undetermined outcome gets a notice rather than establishing that contact details are complete.

findings.detail: 'The number appears as plain text. Most local searches happen on a phone, and a non-tappable number turns a one-tap call or text into a copy-and-paste.'
findings.fix: 'Wrap every phone number in a tel: link, or in an sms: link if the number takes texts rather than calls.'

findings.title: 'No map embed on the contact page'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Can local customers call, write or find you?
rows.answer: It checks tappable contact routes, maps and enquiry forms where local checks apply.
rows.why: The routes a customer can use depend on the service. Separating calls, texts, physical visits and forms keeps the suggested change tied to the contact choice the business actually offers.

condition.text: The check requires supported prose and local-business applicability. Across the first 40 indexable pages, it looks for phone or text-message links when plain numbers are present. A map can be recognised from iframe hosts or a saved map flag. The missing-map case needs a contact page and a locally served market. Form absence is checked across all indexable pages, rather than only the initial sample. For example, a phone printed only outside the first 40 sampled pages can be missed by the tappable-number test.

pages.text: The check reads published phones, link targets, map resources, contact paths and form counts. A business that only accepts texts can use message links. Check the offered contact method before changing a link to invite calls.

reports.text: An untappable number is medium severity. Missing maps and forms are low and require full-crawl support for their absence claims. A business that does not welcome physical visits should not add a misleading map solely to change the report.

fix.text: Make published numbers link to the route they support, whether calling or texting. Add a useful contact form when appropriate, and provide location help only for a place customers should visit. Check existing off-site routes before duplicating them. Test links and form completion manually after changing a shared contact template.

rows.guide_title: How to fix inconsistent name, address and phone

review.text: Review the contact method the business actually offers. A text-only route should not be rewritten to invite calls, and a service-area business should not invent a place for customers to visit. Keep maps, forms and phone links aligned with those real choices. Inspect the shared contact component after editing and verify the destination or form behaviour independently from the audit's presence flags.

faq.question: How many pages are sampled for tappable phone numbers?
faq.answer: The first 40 indexable pages are sampled. A printed number outside that window may be missed by this part of the check.

faq.question: Does the missing-map check apply to every local business?
faq.answer: No. A locally served market is required, together with a contact page. Avoid a map implying visits your business does not accept.

faq.question: Is an untappable number as minor as a missing map?
faq.answer: No. An untappable number gets medium severity, while a qualifying missing-map result is low.

rows.question: Does your local content say where you work?
rows.answer: It checks place names in titles and postal codes for a local market.
rows.why: A local page needs to make sense to someone checking whether the service reaches them. The market gate narrows that question so that an irrelevant office location is not forced into every title.

condition.text: Local-business status and a local market are required. The check searches address text from the first 40 indexable pages, using up to 4000 characters each. It reads all indexable titles for recognised place names and the business's own places. At least 4 titled pages with no location mention produce medium severity. No recognised postal code produces low severity. For example, 4 titled local pages with no recognised place mention can reach the title finding.

pages.text: The check reads titles, address text, footer details and places declared for the business. An office address alone does not explain where an online product is sold. Review the audience and service area.

reports.text: The report identifies missing location cues rather than proving the site cannot serve a place. Place and postcode recognition have limits, so inspect the actual address and audience before changing useful wording.

fix.text: State the real service area where it helps a visitor decide. Include a complete address or appropriate service-area information in a clear contact location. Use accurate place names in relevant titles without adding towns you do not serve. Review the displayed footer and markup when the report missed an address already published.

rows.guide_title: Where an audit looks for your address

review.text: Compare place wording with the area the service really covers. A town in an office address may be less relevant than the customer's service area. Keep titles useful to readers and avoid adding places solely to satisfy a recogniser. Review address text and structured location values together, especially when the visible footer already contains the information that a limited text sample did not establish.

faq.question: How many local-page titles without place names trigger the title finding?
faq.answer: The result can apply with 4 titled pages or more lacking a location mention. Local applicability and market requirements must also be met.

faq.question: How much address text is searched for local place clues?
faq.answer: The first 40 indexable pages contribute up to 4000 characters each. All indexable titles are read separately for the title check.

faq.question: Does missing postal-code recognition prove my service area is absent?
faq.answer: No. Postcode recognition and place matching can miss valid wording. Inspect the address and intended audience directly.

rows.question: Are your business contact details consistent?
rows.answer: It reviews phone numbers and addresses while allowing genuine multiple locations.
rows.why: A business may have several valid departments or premises. Group numbers and addresses by the place or team they belong to. Then look for conflicting details about the same contact route.

condition.text: The site must qualify for local business tests. Contact details are sampled across up to 60 pages intended for search. Several phone checks need at least 7 digits. More than 2 different phone numbers can produce an inconsistency finding unless multiple locations are recognised. A set with more than 3 address variants can produce a low finding when they describe a single place. Missing-phone and missing-address claims also depend on language, coverage and service area. For example, exactly 2 varying phone numbers stay within the count limit for the inconsistency test.

pages.text: The check uses address text, phone markup, published numbers, contact-page roles and available browser output. It tries to identify which details belong to the business. Review any listed person's or listed business's contact details separately.

reports.text: Missing phones are high severity. Absent addresses and inconsistent phones are medium. Inconsistent addresses are low. Different departments or locations may explain valid differences. Review each cited value before deleting it.

fix.text: Confirm the intended numbers and locations with the business. Update stale templates and business markup. Preserve valid location and department details. Explain any service-area policy where customers cannot visit an office. Compare the visible page, dialling links and structured fields after editing.

rows.guide_title: How to fix inconsistent name, address and phone

review.text: Group contact details by the location or department they belong to. Different numbers and address abbreviations may all be valid. Keep a clear main contact route and useful location details. Check the displayed number, its hidden link target and the business markup when repairing an old value.

faq.question: How many different phone numbers can trigger local contact inconsistency?
faq.answer: The count must exceed 2 different phone numbers. Multiple recognised locations can explain that variation and suppress the case.

faq.question: How many address variants can be flagged for a single place?
faq.answer: A count exceeding 3 address variants can qualify. Confirm that the values describe a single location before removing one.

faq.question: Is a missing phone more serious than an inconsistent address?
faq.answer: Yes. Missing phones are high severity. Inconsistent addresses are low, with other contact findings handled separately.

rows.question: Does your local site show real customer reviews?
rows.answer: It looks for customer reviews and for item reviews that could need markup.
rows.why: Real customer experiences can help a visitor understand a service. The wording needs context and a sound source. Finding a review phrase leaves its authenticity for a person to verify.

condition.text: The test needs a supported prose language and a site that qualifies for local business checks. It reads up to 3000 text characters from each of the first 25 pages intended for search. Review markup is checked across all indexable pages. It checks whether review phrases are negated or supported by other details. A business identified as LocalBusiness with no recognised reviews can receive a medium finding. Visible reviews of supported items without review markup can receive a low finding. Check eligibility before marking up ordinary business testimonials. For example, wording outside the first 3000 text characters can be missed in a sampled page's review search.

pages.text: The check reads review and rating markup, sampled text and review-page context. It cannot verify the writer's identity or whether a review is authentic. You need to confirm the source.

reports.text: Missing business reviews and missing item-review markup describe different issues. Read what the review is about before adding ratings. The visible review and declared subject need to match.

fix.text: Publish reviews only with a sound basis and permission where needed. Keep the review attached to the business or item it actually describes. Add suitable markup only when the visible content and type support it. Review negative statements and examples before changing a page that merely discusses reviews.

review.text: Read each review phrase in its surrounding passage. A page discussing reviews may contain no customer testimony. Check whether a rating belongs to the business or a supported item. Before adding markup, confirm its subject and values against the visible review and its source.

faq.question: How much text is sampled for local review wording?
faq.answer: Each of the first 25 sampled pages contributes up to 3000 text characters. Review markup is inspected across the wider indexable set.

faq.question: Does every business testimonial need review markup?
faq.answer: No. Ordinary business testimonials need an eligibility review before markup is added. The declared subject must match the review.

faq.question: Can missing local reviews and missing item-review markup have different severity?
faq.answer: Yes. The LocalBusiness case can receive a medium finding when reviews are unrecognised. Missing markup on a supported item review can get low severity.

rows.question: Does your local business markup fit the business?
rows.answer: It checks local identity markup and important fields while respecting business type and ownership.
rows.why: A business type is a claim about what the site represents. Accurate values matter more than adding empty keys, and a different legitimate identity type can be the correct choice for a physical organisation.

condition.text: After local applicability, the check reads owned and listed local nodes, preferring the business's own nodes. It reviews address, telephone or phone, hours, coordinates or map, URL, image or logo, and price range. Empty values count as missing. The most complete candidate supplies the gap list. Script-built types, organisation-with-address cases and specialised identity types can suppress or change a missing-LocalBusiness claim.

pages.text: The check compares business markup and declared types. A directory entry may describe someone else's premises. Keep that entry attached to the business it names.

reports.text: Missing or incorrectly broad identity can be high severity. Incomplete owned nodes are medium, while incomplete listed-business nodes are low. Presence of a field key alone does not establish a useful value.

fix.text: Choose the identity type that matches the organisation. Fill applicable fields with real details and keep them aligned with visible contact information. Do not add invented opening hours or prices to complete a list. Review whether each node describes your business or someone listed on the site before changing shared markup.

rows.guide_title: When a field is there and still missing

review.text: Inspect who each business node describes before filling gaps. A directory entry, a publisher and the business accepting enquiries can be separate entities. Keep fields attached to the correct subject and use real values only where they apply. If the type is wrong, correct that claim rather than inventing details to complete its expected field list, then compare the result with the public contact information.

faq.question: Do empty LocalBusiness properties count as complete?
faq.answer: No. Empty values count as missing. Fill applicable fields with real information rather than adding empty keys.

faq.question: Which local-business node supplies the list of missing details?
faq.answer: The gap list comes from the most complete candidate. Owned nodes are preferred over those describing listed businesses.

faq.question: Are incomplete owned and listed local-business nodes equally serious?
faq.answer: No. Owned-node gaps get medium severity. For incomplete listed-business nodes, the result is low.

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Are your advertising pixels present and active?
rows.answer: It distinguishes detected pixels, staged pixels and incomplete page coverage.
rows.why: Pixel scripts can exist without being able to run. Keeping that state separate from total absence helps you inspect loading and consent setup before adding another copy of the same tag.

condition.text: The check combines tracking code found in server responses with available browser output. Code present but unable to run can produce a high finding. No pixels or staged code produces a notice, with separate wording for a tag manager. For pixels in server responses, coverage below a 0.7 share of successful pages produces a medium finding. Pixels seen only after scripts run are excluded from that coverage claim. For example, directly served pixel coverage of exactly 0.7 stays within the coverage limit.

pages.text: The check reads detected trackers and available browser output. It cannot access an advertising account. Use the platform's own tools to confirm that an event arrived.

reports.text: Staging, absence and partial coverage mean different things. A tag-manager container can hide configuration from this audit, and a rendered-only observation cannot establish which unrendered pages carry the same code.

fix.text: Confirm which advertising tools you actually use. Inspect staged markup and the relevant consent or loading rule, then test the intended events with the platform's own tools. Add coverage only to pages that need it. Remove abandoned tags rather than installing pixels simply to turn an informational notice into silence.

rows.guide_title: Marketing tag audit

review.text: Compare a detected script with the event it is intended to send. A staged value can be present in markup without being executable, while a rendered-only observation has a narrower coverage scope. Keep consent choices intact when repairing loading. Use the advertising platform's own validation for event delivery, and remove duplicate installations only after identifying the template or manager that owns each copy.

faq.question: What served-pixel coverage avoids the partial-coverage finding?
faq.answer: A share of 0.7 passes the coverage limit. The comparison uses pixels found in server responses.

faq.question: Are pixels seen only after scripts run included in served-code coverage?
faq.answer: No. An observation made only after scripts run is outside the served-code share. It cannot establish the code on unrendered pages.

faq.question: Can advertising pixel code be present but unable to run?
faq.answer: Yes. That pattern can produce a high finding. It differs from absence, staging or incomplete coverage.

findings.title: 'Analytics tags are managed through Google Tag Manager'
findings.detail: 'GTM is installed, but the tags inside a GTM container are injected by JavaScript at runtime, so this audit cannot see which ones are configured without running a browser. Analytics and advertising tags may well be present and working. This is the normal way to deploy them.'
findings.fix: 'Verify directly rather than assuming: open your GTM container and check the tag list, or load the site with the Google Tag Assistant browser extension. Confirm GA4 is receiving data in its Realtime report.'

findings.title: f'{names} is configured but loads only after consent'
findings.detail: f"The pages declare a container ID for {names}, but the vendor's script is not in the HTML the server sent, the normal sign that a consent platform injects it once the visitor agrees. This audit reads the HTML as delivered and does not accept consent banners, so it cannot confirm the tag fires."
findings.fix: 'Verify directly rather than assuming, in either direction: accept the banner on your own site and check the tag loads, and confirm the property is receiving data in its realtime report. If it is not, the consent configuration is dropping the tag for everyone who agrees.'

findings.title: 'No third-party analytics tag; Squarespace records visits itself'
findings.detail: "No Google Analytics, Tag Manager or similar appears on any crawled page. This site is built on Squarespace, and Squarespace's own Traffic panel counts unique visitors, visits and pageviews on every plan, without a tag. A third-party tag adds what those reports do not, for example the same data in Google Analytics beside your ad accounts."
findings.fix: "Check the Traffic panel in Squarespace's Analytics first. If you need more, such as GA4 for ad conversions, add it through Squarespace's settings."

findings.title: 'No third-party analytics tag; Wix records visits itself'
findings.detail: "No Google Analytics, Tag Manager or similar appears on any crawled page. This site is built on Wix, and Wix's own analytics records unique visitors and sessions and how visitors find and move around the site, in the site's dashboard, without a tag. A third-party tag adds what Wix's reports do not, for example the same data in Google Analytics beside your ad accounts."
findings.fix: "Check Wix's traffic reports in your site's dashboard first. If you need more, such as GA4 for ad conversions, add it; Wix's help explains how it connects on your plan."

findings.title: 'No analytics tag on any page this audit could see'
findings.detail: 'No Google Analytics, Tag Manager, Plausible, Fathom, Matomo, PostHog or similar appears on any crawled page. If that is right, nothing about visitor numbers, traffic sources, or which pages generate enquiries is being recorded, and no campaign can be judged as working or not.\n\nOne way this can be wrong, and it is worth ten seconds of your time: a tracker installed as an npm package is compiled into your own JavaScript bundle, so nothing in the HTML names the vendor. This audit reads the HTML your server sends ' + bundled_caveat
findings.fix: "First confirm you do not already have it: open your site, and in the browser's Network tab filter for the vendor's domain, or check whether the property shows traffic in its realtime report.\n\nIf it really is absent, install analytics before spending anything further on marketing. GA4 is free; Plausible and Fathom are paid but simpler and avoid most consent complexity. Install via Google Tag Manager so future tags do not need a developer."

findings.title: f'{_named(core)} {is_are(len(core))} missing from {len(missing)} of {len(scope)} pages'
findings.detail: f"{_named(core)} {verb('appear', len(core))} on {len(tagged)} of the {crawled}, and no other analytics tag was found anywhere.\n\nThe tracking code is not on every page, so sessions break when a visitor moves through an untagged page. Traffic gets misattributed to 'direct', conversion paths look shorter than they are, and bounce rate is overstated. The reports still look reasonable, which is what makes this expensive."
findings.fix: 'Move the tag into the shared site template or header include so no page can be missed. Verify with Google Tag Assistant.'

findings.title: 'A retired Universal Analytics tag is still loading'
findings.detail: f"Universal Analytics stopped processing data in 2023, so this tag collects nothing. It is a request on every page for no return. Your measurement is not affected: {names} {('is' if len(others) == 1 else 'are')} also installed."
findings.fix: 'Remove the Universal Analytics snippet. Nothing reads what it sends.'

findings.title: 'Only the retired Universal Analytics tag is installed'
findings.detail: 'Universal Analytics stopped processing data in 2023. This tag collects nothing. If this is your only analytics, you have had no data since then.'
findings.fix: 'Install GA4 (or a privacy-friendly alternative) and remove the dead UA tag.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Can your analytics tags cover the pages you need?
rows.answer: It separates missing analytics, consent-gated tags, opaque containers and measured coverage gaps.
rows.why: Finding a tag in HTML shows that it was installed. Event delivery and data quality need their own checks inside the analytics service. Use the named tag to decide what to test next.

condition.text: The check uses trackers found in server responses and available browser output. Tag-manager-only setups, tags waiting for consent and recognised built-in analytics receive their own explanations. Comparable readable pages are checked for a tagged share below 0.85. Uneven browser coverage can prevent a fair comparison. Retired Universal Analytics tags are checked separately, with different wording when another analytics tool is present. For example, comparable tagged coverage of exactly 0.85 does not fall below the gap threshold.

pages.text: The check uses detected tags, code waiting to load, platform clues and measured browser coverage. It cannot access an analytics account. Check visits and conversions inside the intended service.

reports.text: Several missing-tag or coverage findings are high severity. Unclear containers or platform limits can produce notices. A retired tag can be low when another tool is present. Read which tag was found and where it was found.

fix.text: Confirm the analytics tool the business intends to use. Review the named tag and affected templates, checking consent and rendering before adding scripts. Use the tool's own live or debug view to verify events. Remove obsolete tags carefully and retest representative page types after changing shared code.

rows.guide_title: 'You have no analytics' is a claim about a list

review.text: Compare the tag named in the report with the tool the business actually uses. A container can be installed while its analytics tags still wait for configuration or consent. Review each state before adding code. After changing templates, verify event delivery and check for duplicates inside the intended service.

faq.question: What analytics coverage avoids the missing-tag share finding?
faq.answer: Comparable tagged coverage at 0.85 passes. Browser coverage must be fair enough for the comparison to be made.

faq.question: Can uneven browser coverage stop an analytics comparison?
faq.answer: Yes. Uneven browser coverage can make pages incomparable. The audit should not infer missing tags from unequal observations.

faq.question: Are retired analytics tags always a high-severity problem?
faq.answer: No. When another tool is present, a retired tag can receive low severity. Review the named tracker and where it appeared.

findings.title: 'Advertising or session-recording tags run with no consent mechanism'
findings.detail: f"Detected: {', '.join(sorted((_label(t) for t in invasive)))}. No cookie or consent banner was found. Under GDPR (EU/UK) these require consent before they fire, and several US state laws now require an opt-out. findings.fix: "Add a consent management platform (Cookiebot, CookieYes, Osano, or Google's own consent mode) and gate the advertising and session-recording tags behind it. Analytics with IP anonymisation is treated more leniently in most jurisdictions, but check your own obligations."

findings.title: 'Tracking is installed but there is no privacy policy'
findings.detail: 'The site collects visitor data through tracking tags with no privacy policy page. This is a legal requirement in most jurisdictions, and both Google Ads and Meta require one before they will run your ads.'
findings.fix: 'Publish a privacy policy naming each tool you use, what it collects, and how to opt out. Link it from the footer of every page.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do tracking tags have visible privacy controls?
rows.answer: It looks for a consent banner and privacy policy alongside detected tracking.
rows.why: What this observes is between tracking code and the controls or policy the site exposes. A presence test can flag a missing piece for review, while the behaviour of that control still needs to be checked directly.

condition.text: Detected advertising pixels or the recognised session-recording tools trigger the banner-presence condition. If none of the successful pages has a saved consent-banner flag, a medium finding is emitted. Any detected analytics or advertising tracking also prompts a privacy-policy presence check, with another medium finding when the policy is not found. Legal requirements for each visitor need a separate review.

pages.text: The check reads detected trackers, banner detections and the privacy-policy lookup. Code waiting for consent and a tracker already running describe different states. Review how each tag loads when a visitor makes a choice.

reports.text: Both findings are medium severity. A detected banner does not prove that it blocks the right tags, records a valid choice or satisfies any particular law. The check's title must not be mistaken for a legal compliance opinion.

fix.text: List the tracking tools you intend to run. Review their loading against the consent choices you offer and make the privacy explanation accurate. Test acceptance, refusal and later changes of choice using suitable tools. Seek jurisdiction-specific advice where needed instead of treating an installed banner as proof of compliance.

rows.guide_title: Marketing tag audit

review.text: Inspect the behaviour behind the banner, not only its visible presence. A policy link and an accept button do not show which scripts load before a choice. Keep the stated privacy practices aligned with actual tracking. Review the site with the people responsible for those practices, and test changed choices as well as the initial visit before treating a configuration update as a complete resolution of the concern.

faq.question: Which tracking tools trigger the consent-banner presence check?
faq.answer: Detected advertising pixels or recognised session-recording tools trigger it. Missing banner flags across successful pages can then produce a finding.

faq.question: Does finding a banner prove that tracking waits for consent?
faq.answer: No. Banner detection cannot establish that the right tags wait for a choice. Its behaviour needs separate review.

faq.question: Does analytics tracking also trigger a privacy-policy check?
faq.answer: Yes. A privacy-policy presence check also follows detected analytics or advertising tracking. Missing policy wording produces a medium result.
