findings.title: f'No email capture {scope.where()}'
findings.detail: 'Most visitors are not ready to buy on their first visit, and once they leave with no way to reach them again, that acquisition cost is spent. An email list is the only marketing channel you own outright: it does not depend on an algorithm or an ad auction.'
findings.fix: "Add a single email capture with a real reason to subscribe: a useful guide, a price list, an availability alert. A bare 'subscribe to our newsletter' converts poorly; offering something specific converts well."

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Can visitors choose to hear from you again?
rows.answer: It looks for recognised email tools, signup forms or invitation wording.
rows.why: Visitors may want updates without making an enquiry. This test looks for a route that appears to support that choice, while leaving the business to decide whether an email list fits its service.

condition.text: The check needs a supported prose language. A recognised email-platform tracker ends the test without a finding. Otherwise it reads up to 40 readable pages for a signup-form flag or signup wording. Text searches use up to 8000 characters plus action labels. At least 5 indexable pages with no signup signal produce a low finding. For example, a site with 5 indexable pages can receive the finding when no signup signal is found.

pages.text: The check reads detected email tools, form types, text and action labels. It does not submit an address. Test the signup route and confirm that it reaches the intended list.

reports.text: The finding is low severity. A recognised tool or invitation can satisfy the presence condition without proving that the form works, and a business may deliberately choose not to run a mailing list.

fix.text: If updates are useful to your visitors, provide a clear invitation and explain what they will receive. Check that the form reaches the intended list and honours the choices you state. Keep enquiry forms separate where their purpose differs. Do not add a mailing platform solely because the audit reports an optional opportunity.

rows.guide_title: Email capture audit

review.text: Follow a signup invitation through to the intended list and confirm what a subscriber is told. A recognised phrase can be present in a discussion rather than a working invitation. Keep subscription choices clear and distinct from a service enquiry where their purposes differ. If the business deliberately does not send updates, record that choice instead of adding an unwanted workflow merely to remove an optional finding.

faq.question: How many pages are needed for a missing-signup finding?
faq.answer: The sample needs 5 indexable pages or more without a signup signal. This is a low-priority presence finding.

faq.question: Can a recognised email-platform tracker satisfy the capture check?
faq.answer: Yes. The presence of a recognised email-platform tracker clears this test. It does not establish that a signup form works.

faq.question: How much page text is searched for an email signup invitation?
faq.answer: The text window reaches 8000 characters. Action labels and a saved signup-form flag provide additional clues.

findings.detail: detail
findings.fix: fix

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Which marketing tools appear on your pages?
rows.answer: It inventories detected tools and raises severity when a page carries many of them.
rows.why: An inventory makes old or overlapping installations easier to review. The page maximum matters because a large site-wide list can be spread across separate page types rather than loaded together on every visit.

condition.text: The check lists tools found on each successful page, including available browser output. No detected tools means no inventory finding. Otherwise it names the tools and the largest count on a page. A page carrying at least 8 tools changes the result from a notice to medium severity. That page count is separate from the site's total number of different tools. For example, a page with 8 detected tools reaches medium severity even if other pages carry fewer.

pages.text: Tracker signatures in saved served or rendered pages supply the inventory. It does not measure each vendor's account status, invoice, usefulness or contribution to page loading time.

reports.text: An ordinary inventory is a notice. A page with the larger tool count produces medium severity. Check whether each detected tool still serves a business purpose and sends the expected data.

fix.text: Match each listed tool to a current business purpose and owner. Remove abandoned installations through the template or tag manager that supplies them. Keep tools required for real workflows and test those workflows after changes. Review consent and loading separately instead of assuming that a smaller list alone proves a faster or compliant site.

rows.guide_title: Marketing tag audit

review.text: Match detected labels to the installation that supplies them. A shared tag manager and a page template can both introduce tools, so removing a visible script may leave another copy. Keep needed workflows in view during cleanup. Ask the responsible person which tools remain active, then verify the relevant events after removing abandoned code rather than treating a smaller detected inventory as proof that every remaining tool works.

faq.question: How many tools on one page raise the marketing-stack severity?
faq.answer: A page reaches medium severity at 8 detected tools. The threshold concerns the largest page count rather than the site's whole inventory.

faq.question: Does an audit with no detected tools get a stack inventory finding?
faq.answer: No. When there are no detected tools, the inventory finding is omitted. That result does not establish which tools may exist outside the observations.

faq.question: Is an ordinary marketing-tool inventory an error?
faq.answer: The ordinary inventory gets only a notice. Use the named tools to review purpose and expected data collection.

rows.title: UTM tagging hygiene

findings.title: f"{total} internal link{plural_s(total)} {verb('carry', total)} UTM parameters"
findings.detail: f'Links from one page of the site to another are tagged with campaign parameters. In GA4 this starts a brand new session and re-attributes it to that campaign, so the campaign gets credit for traffic it never sent and the original source is erased. It also creates duplicate URLs for search engines to index. Example: {offenders[0].internal_utm_links[0][:110]}'
findings.fix: 'Strip UTM parameters from all internal links. UTMs are for traffic arriving from outside only. To track internal clicks, use GA4 events or a dedicated internal link parameter that analytics ignores.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do internal links carry campaign tags?
rows.answer: It reports indexable pages linking within the site with UTM parameters.
rows.why: Campaign labels describe where a visit came from. Applying those labels to a route inside the site creates a different tracking statement from an ordinary internal destination, which is why the audit keeps this pattern separate.

condition.text: The check selects pages intended for search with recorded internal links carrying UTM parameters. Any such links produce a medium finding. It totals the recorded links, with no minimum share or page-count cutoff. For example, a menu link with utm_source is an internal campaign-tagged link. The check counts the crawler's recorded links and leaves the effect on analytics data unmeasured.

pages.text: Saved internal link lists show which pages qualify and supply the reported total. External campaign links are outside this test because its subject is navigation within the same site.

reports.text: The finding is medium severity. It can establish that the links carry campaign parameters, but it does not read analytics reports or calculate a resulting attribution error.

fix.text: Remove campaign parameters from ordinary internal navigation and use clean destination URLs. Keep campaign tags on the external links where they serve their intended purpose. If you need to measure an internal action, review a suitable event instead. Check shared templates so that a repeated tagged link is corrected at its source.

rows.guide_title: How common are internal links with UTM parameters?

review.text: Inspect a tagged internal destination alongside the reason the tag was added. Ordinary navigation and an external acquisition link have different tracking roles. Keep public internal addresses clean where campaign attribution is unnecessary. Review menu builders, banners and stored article links as separate sources, then test any replacement event tracking independently because this check identifies tagged links without reading the resulting analytics session records.

faq.question: How many internal campaign-tagged links trigger the UTM finding?
faq.answer: Any recorded internal campaign link can qualify. The page-count cutoff and minimum-share limits used elsewhere do not apply here.

faq.question: Does the UTM check include campaign links to other sites?
faq.answer: No. External campaign links belong to a different scope. This test concerns internal navigation on the audited site.

faq.question: Does an internal UTM finding calculate an analytics attribution error?
faq.answer: No. It has medium severity and identifies parameters on links. Analytics reports are not read to quantify an effect.

rows.title: Internal link anchor text

findings.title: f"{len(vague)} link{plural_s(len(vague))} {verb('use', len(vague))} non-descriptive anchor text"
findings.detail: 'Anchor text tells search engines what the linked page is about. Most common here: ' + ', '.join((f'"{t}" ({c}x)' for (t, c) in common))
findings.fix: 'Replace with the destination\'s topic: "Read more" becomes "our drain cleaning service".'

findings.title: f'{empty_links} link{plural_s(empty_links)} {has_have(empty_links)} no anchor text at all'
findings.detail: 'Links wrapping only an icon or an image with no alt text carry no meaning for search engines or screen reader users.'
findings.fix: 'Add alt text to the wrapped image, or an aria-label on the link.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do your link labels explain the destination?
rows.answer: It finds vague link text and a larger set of links with no text.
rows.why: Link labels help a reader decide whether a destination is useful before opening it. Counting labels without context cannot judge every design, but it can point to links that deserve a direct inspection.

condition.text: The check reads link labels on pages intended for search. It skips page fragments, script links, email links and phone links. A plain Download label is allowed when it points to a recognised file or download route. Other labels are checked against a list of vague wording. Empty labels produce a finding only when there are more than 3 empty labels. A vague label can be reported whenever one is found. For example, exactly 3 empty labels stay within the empty-label count limit.

pages.text: The check reads link destinations and their labels. It does not click them or assess the whole surrounding paragraph. Review each label in the interface where it appears.

reports.text: Both vague and empty-label findings are low severity. A recognised download destination has a different purpose from an ordinary content link, which is why its short label is not automatically treated as vague.

fix.text: Replace unclear labels with words describing the destination or action. Give icon-only controls an appropriate accessible name in the interface that owns them. Keep a concise Download label where the destination is genuinely a file. Review repeated card and menu templates if the same empty label appears across the site.

rows.guide_title: How to fix vague and empty link text

review.text: Read the label without relying on nearby visual placement. A person reviewing a list of links may not have the same surrounding cues as someone looking at the whole layout. Keep destination text specific enough to choose the right page. For file links, preserve the useful download meaning, and inspect icon controls through their actual accessible names rather than adding visible words that duplicate an existing label unnecessarily.

faq.question: How many empty link labels trigger a finding?
faq.answer: More than 3 empty labels are needed. Exactly that count stays within the empty-label limit.

faq.question: Is a Download link label always considered vague?
faq.answer: No. A download route or recognised file can justify a plain Download label. Its destination changes the interpretation.

faq.question: Are email and phone links tested for vague labels here?
faq.answer: No. Email links and phone links are skipped along with fragments and script links. Other contact tests handle different concerns.

rows.title: Meta descriptions

findings.title: f'{len(missing)} page{plural_s(len(missing))} {has_have(len(missing))} no meta description'
findings.detail: 'The description is the sales pitch under the headline in search results. Without one Google extracts an arbitrary sentence from the page, often a cookie notice or a nav label.'
findings.fix: 'Write a 120–155 character description per page: what the page offers and why to click.'

findings.title: f"{len(long_)} meta description{plural_s(len(long_))} {verb('exceed', len(long_))} {DESC_MAX} characters"
findings.detail: 'The tail gets truncated with an ellipsis, so any call to action at the end is lost.'
findings.fix: f'Trim to under {DESC_MAX} characters with the key message first.'

findings.title: f'{len(short)} meta description{plural_s(len(short))} {is_are(len(short))} very short'
findings.detail: 'Short descriptions leave free advertising space unused in the search result.'
findings.fix: 'Expand to 120–155 characters and include a reason to click.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Are your page descriptions missing or too long?
rows.answer: It checks whether descriptions exist and fit the engine's display-width range.
rows.why: A description is a short account of a particular page. Presence and width checks can expose an empty or unwieldy summary, while the wording still needs a person to decide whether it accurately describes the destination.

condition.text: The check trims surrounding spaces from descriptions on pages intended for search. Empty descriptions produce a medium finding. Display width below 70 half-width character units produces a low short-description finding. Width above 165 half-width character units produces a low long-description finding. Widths at the limits pass. The engine counts wide and fullwidth Unicode characters twice and all other characters once. For example, a description with measured display width exactly 165 half-width character units stays within the long-description limit.

pages.text: The check reads each page's meta description. It does not compare descriptions for duplication or ask a search service which snippet it displayed. Review those questions separately.

reports.text: Missing descriptions are medium. Short and long ones are low. The thresholds are the engine's review limits, not a promise that a search service displays an exact number of characters or uses your description unchanged.

fix.text: Write a concise, specific summary of what the page gives a visitor. Remove template filler and keep the useful point early. Review pages with the shortest and longest values before applying a shared fix. Do not pad a clear summary merely to hit a number or promise content the page does not contain.

rows.guide_title: How to write meta descriptions

review.text: Compare the description with the content it summarises. A technically present value can still be copied, stale or vague. Keep the useful point early and avoid adding claims simply to fill space. After editing a shared description template, inspect pages with different subjects so that a fix for an empty value does not replace accurate page-specific summaries with the same generic statement across the site.

faq.question: What counts as a short meta description?
faq.answer: A description is short under 70 half-width character units. Wide and fullwidth characters count twice, and other characters once.

faq.question: Is a description width of 165 units too long?
faq.answer: No. At 165 half-width character units, the value passes. This approximates text width without measuring pixels.

faq.question: Is a missing meta description worse than a long one?
faq.answer: Yes. Missing descriptions are medium, while long descriptions are low. Review the actual summary as well as its width.

rows.title: Heading structure

conditions.expression: page.word_count >= SUBSTANTIAL_WORDS and (not page.headings.get('h2')) and (not deeper)

findings.title: f'{len(no_h1)} page{plural_s(len(no_h1))} {has_have(len(no_h1))} no H1 heading'
findings.detail: 'The H1 states what the page is about, in the page itself. It is a strong relevance signal and the anchor AI answer engines use when extracting a summary.'
findings.fix: 'Give each page exactly one H1 naming its topic in plain language. If the tag is already there but empty, put the text inside it. An H1 with no text counts as no H1.'

findings.title: f'{len(multi_h1)} page{plural_s(len(multi_h1))} {has_have(len(multi_h1))} more than one H1'
findings.detail: 'Multiple H1s blur what the page is primarily about. HTML5 permits it, but in practice it usually means the template is using H1 for styling.'
findings.fix: 'Keep one H1 for the page topic and demote the rest to H2.'

findings.title: f'{len(no_h2)} substantial page{plural_s(len(no_h2))} {has_have(len(no_h2))} no subheadings'
findings.detail: 'Long pages with no H2s are a wall of text. Subheadings are also what AI answer engines use to locate the section that answers a specific question.'
findings.fix: 'Break the content into sections with descriptive H2s, ideally phrased as the questions customers ask.'

findings.title: f"{len(skipped)} page{plural_s(len(skipped))} {verb('skip', len(skipped))} a heading level"
findings.detail: 'H3s appear with no H2 above them, which breaks the document outline for screen readers and parsers.'
findings.fix: 'Use heading levels in order: H1, then H2, then H3.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do your headings give the page a clear outline?
rows.answer: It checks missing main headings, distinct repeated main headings and gaps in the outline.
rows.why: Heading levels describe relationships between parts of a page. Visual styling alone does not provide that structure, so the check looks at actual markup rather than assuming large text is a main heading.

condition.text: Pages with readable content are checked for a missing main heading or multiple different main headings. Capitalisation and extra spaces are ignored when comparing heading text. A page with at least 300 words and no deeper subheadings can produce a missing-subheading finding. Using a third-level heading with no second-level heading produces a skipped-level notice. The check reads the heading markup. For example, a 300-word article with only a main heading can reach the missing-subheading finding.

pages.text: The check reads headings and word counts on pages with usable content. Repeated copies of the same main-heading text receive different treatment from different main headings. Inspect the outline before changing shared headers.

reports.text: Missing main headings are medium, multiple distinct main headings and absent subheadings low, and the skipped-level case a notice. A clean result does not establish that each heading accurately names its section.

fix.text: Give the page a clear main subject and use subheadings to divide substantial content where helpful. Keep levels in a sensible order and style them through CSS. Review repeated header furniture before removing an intentional content heading. Check the resulting outline as well as the rendered appearance after updating a template.

rows.guide_title: How to fix heading structure

review.text: Read the outline independently of font size and colour. A styled paragraph does not become a heading merely because it looks prominent. Keep the structure tied to the relationships between sections. When a shared header supplies a repeated heading, distinguish that furniture from the main subject before editing, and inspect the final markup so that a visual adjustment does not leave the document hierarchy harder to follow.

faq.question: How much text can trigger the missing-subheading finding?
faq.answer: The test can apply from 300 words when deeper subheadings are absent. It reads markup rather than visual text size.

faq.question: Are identical repeated main headings treated like different main headings?
faq.answer: No. Copies containing the same main-heading text are handled differently. Review the actual outline before removing template elements.

faq.question: How serious is skipping straight to a third-level heading?
faq.answer: A third-level heading without a second-level heading can produce a skipped-level notice. Missing main headings have a separate result.

rows.title: Image optimisation

conditions.expression: len(imgs) >= 8 and (not any((i.lazy for i in imgs)))

findings.title: f'{len(missing_alt)} image{plural_s(len(missing_alt))} {has_have(len(missing_alt))} no alt attribute'
findings.detail: f'Across {len(pages_missing_alt)} page{plural_s(len(pages_missing_alt))}. Alt text is how screen readers describe images, how Google Images understands them, and a genuine accessibility requirement. Note: alt="" on a purely decorative image is correct and is not counted here.'
findings.fix: 'Describe what the image shows, in a short phrase. For decorative images, add an explicit empty alt="" so assistive tech skips them.'

findings.title: f'{len(no_dims_pages)} page{plural_s(len(no_dims_pages))} {has_have(len(no_dims_pages))} images without width/height'
findings.detail: 'Images with no declared dimensions cause the page to jump as they load. This is measured directly as Cumulative Layout Shift, one of the three Core Web Vitals Google uses in ranking.'
findings.fix: "Add width and height attributes to every , matching the file's real pixel dimensions."

findings.title: f'{len(no_lazy_pages)} image-heavy page{plural_s(len(no_lazy_pages))} {does_do(len(no_lazy_pages))} not lazy-load'
findings.detail: 'Every image downloads before the page finishes loading, including ones the visitor may never scroll to.'
findings.fix: 'Add loading="lazy" to images below the fold. Leave the main hero image eager so it is not delayed.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do your images have the markup they need?
rows.answer: It checks missing alternative text, dimensions and lazy loading on image-heavy pages.
rows.why: Image markup can supply a text alternative and reserve space before loading. Those jobs differ from choosing when to fetch an image, which is why the code reports them separately rather than describing every image issue as a single optimisation.

condition.text: The test reads image resources on indexable pages and excludes detected beacons. An absent alt attribute with a nonempty image URL enters the missing-alt finding. Intentionally empty alt text is allowed by this presence test. At least 3 images without saved dimensions marks a page for the dimensions finding. A set of at least 8 images with none marked lazy produces the lazy-loading finding. These are separate conditions with separate affected page sets. For example, 3 images with no recorded dimensions are enough for the dimensions finding.

pages.text: The check reads image addresses and markup. It does not look at the picture to identify its subject. Review the image's purpose before deciding what alternative text it needs.

reports.text: Missing alt attributes and dimensions are medium severity. Lack of lazy loading on image-heavy pages is low. A present attribute does not prove that its text is useful or that an image's dimensions are correct.

fix.text: Give meaningful images useful alternative text and decorative images the appropriate empty attribute. Set correct dimensions or a suitable reserved aspect ratio. Apply lazy loading to images that should wait, reviewing prominent content separately. Check a real page after editing shared image components so that the fix does not hide useful descriptions or delay an important image.

rows.guide_title: How to fix image SEO problems

review.text: Inspect the image's purpose before writing alternative text. A decorative element and an informative picture require different treatment. Keep the reserved dimensions consistent with the image actually delivered, including responsive variants. Review loading choices against where the picture is needed, and check a representative page after editing the component rather than assuming that adding attributes everywhere makes every image's text, size and loading priority correct.

faq.question: How many images without dimensions trigger the image-markup finding?
faq.answer: At least 3 images lacking saved dimensions are enough. This count is separate from the lazy-loading test.

faq.question: Does an intentionally empty alt attribute count as missing alternative text?
faq.answer: No. Intentionally empty alt text passes the presence test. A person still needs to decide whether the image is decorative.

faq.question: How many images are needed before absent lazy loading is reported?
faq.answer: The page needs 8 images or more, without any marked lazy. Review prominent images before delaying their loading.

rows.title: Language and viewport declarations

findings.title: f'{len(no_lang)} page{plural_s(len(no_lang))} {does_do(len(no_lang))} not declare a language'
findings.detail: 'Without a lang attribute, screen readers guess the pronunciation and browsers offer the wrong translation.'
findings.fix: 'Set the language on the html element.'

findings.title: f'{len(no_viewport)} page{plural_s(len(no_viewport))} {has_have(len(no_viewport))} no mobile viewport tag'
findings.detail: 'Without a viewport meta tag, mobile browsers render the page at desktop width and zoom out. Google indexes the mobile version of every site first, so this affects rankings directly, and most local searches are on a phone.'
findings.fix: 'Add the viewport meta tag to the head of every page.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your page declare language and viewport?
rows.answer: It checks for a language value and a mobile viewport declaration.
rows.why: Language and viewport declarations give readers' software basic information about the document. Presence is a useful first check, but the page still needs a real language review and a layout check in the environments it serves.

condition.text: The check builds separate lists of indexable pages with no saved language and with no saved viewport. A missing language produces a low-severity finding, while a missing viewport produces a high-severity finding. There is no sample-size or percentage cutoff in this test. A nonempty value passes the presence test even though its accuracy must be reviewed elsewhere.

pages.text: The check reads language and viewport declarations on pages intended for search. A separate test compares the declared and detected languages. You need a browser to review the narrow-screen layout.

reports.text: Results identify absence rather than validating every possible value. A viewport declaration can exist while the layout still has mobile problems, and a language attribute can exist while naming the wrong language.

fix.text: Set the document language to the page's actual main language. Add a suitable viewport declaration through the shared head template. Review the existing values before inserting duplicates. Test representative pages at a narrow viewport and read the language markup after the change rather than treating the presence check as a full mobile audit.

rows.guide_title: Mobile SEO: what a crawl can and cannot check

review.text: Read the declaration values as statements about the document, rather than merely checking that tags exist. A language attribute can be nonempty and wrong, while a viewport can be present on an unusable narrow layout. Keep the presence result separate from those broader reviews. Update the shared head carefully, then inspect generated pages in different languages or templates so that a common fix does not overwrite valid distinctions.

faq.question: Is a missing viewport treated more seriously than a missing language value?
faq.answer: Yes. A missing viewport gets a high-severity finding. Missing language has a low result in this presence check.

faq.question: Does a nonempty language declaration prove it names the right language?
faq.answer: No. Presence of a nonempty value clears this test. Text-language clues are compared by another check.

faq.question: Can viewport markup be present while mobile layout is still broken?
faq.answer: Yes. A viewport declaration can exist despite mobile problems. Review the narrow-screen layout in a browser.

rows.title: Title tags

conditions.expression: words and max((words.count(w) for w in set(words))) >= 4

findings.title: f'{len(missing)} page{plural_s(len(missing))} {has_have(len(missing))} an empty title tag' if empty_tag and len(empty_tag) == len(missing) else f'{len(missing)} page{plural_s(len(missing))} {has_have(len(missing))} no title tag'
findings.detail: 'The title is the single strongest on-page ranking signal and the clickable headline in every search result. With none, Google invents one from the page text.' + (f' On {len(empty_tag)} of them the <title> element is there and empty. The tag exists, so it is easy to look straight past.' if empty_tag and len(empty_tag) != len(missing) else ' The element is present and empty, which is why it does not show up as absent in your template.' if empty_tag else '')
findings.fix: 'Add a unique title to each page: the primary topic first, the business name last.'

findings.title: f'{len(long_)} title{plural_s(len(long_))} {is_are(len(long_))} too long for the search result'
findings.detail: f'Long titles get cut off in search results, so the end is invisible to searchers. Longest found ({display_width(example.title)} wide): {example.title[:110]}…'
findings.fix: 'Trim so the distinctive words come first. Search results cut off at roughly 580 pixels, which is about 65 Latin characters or 33 East Asian ones.'

findings.title: f'{len(short)} title{plural_s(len(short))} {is_are(len(short))} very short'
findings.detail: 'Very short titles waste the most valuable space in the search result and usually omit the terms people actually search for.'
findings.fix: 'Expand each to describe the specific offer and, for a local business, the location it serves.'

findings.title: f"{len(stuffed)} title{plural_s(len(stuffed))} {verb('repeat', len(stuffed))} the same keyword excessively"
findings.detail: 'Repeating a keyword in the title reads as spam to both search engines and searchers, and depresses click-through rate.'
findings.fix: 'Use the keyword once, and spend the remaining characters on what makes the page worth clicking.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do your page titles fit and describe the page?
rows.answer: It checks missing titles, display width and excessive repeated keywords.
rows.why: A title states what a page is about in a small space. Missing or repetitive wording gives little guidance, while a long value can bury the useful distinction between this page and another.

condition.text: Pages with readable content are checked for missing titles, including an empty title element. Display width below 25 half-width character units is short and above 65 half-width character units is long. A title such as 'Home' falls below the short limit. The engine counts wide and fullwidth Unicode characters twice and all other characters once. For the keyword test, the engine removes recognised brand text, then keeps words of at least 4 letters. A word repeated at least 4 times is flagged. Repeated brand fragments at the end can also be removed before counting.

pages.text: The check reads title text, whether the title element exists, and the business name. A separate check compares titles across pages. Review both results to give each page a clear, distinct name.

reports.text: Missing titles are high severity, short and keyword-repeating titles medium, and long titles low. The width limits are review thresholds rather than a guarantee of how much a search result will display.

fix.text: Write a specific title that names the page's job. Keep the main subject early and a useful brand suffix concise. Remove repeated keywords without erasing necessary meaning. Review the page itself before shortening a title so that the edit preserves the information a visitor needs to choose the right destination.

rows.guide_title: How to write title tags that fit

review.text: Read the title as a compact promise about the destination. A useful distinction can disappear when an overlong value is cut without understanding the page. Keep necessary product or topic details and remove redundant wording first. Compare the revised title with related pages as well, because satisfying width and repetition limits does not establish that each page now has its own accurate, distinct title.

faq.question: What counts as a short page title?
faq.answer: A title is short under 25 half-width character units. Wide and fullwidth characters count twice, with other characters counted once.

faq.question: Is a title width of 65 units too long?
faq.answer: No. Exactly 65 half-width character units passes. A plain character count can differ when the title includes wide characters.

faq.question: Is a missing page title worse than a long one?
faq.answer: Yes. Missing titles are high severity; a long title has low severity. A short title or repeated keyword gets medium severity.

rows.title: Layout shift risk

conditions.expression: len(without) / len(imgs) > 0.6 and any((i.url not in template for i in without))

findings.title: f'{len(risky)} page{plural_s(len(risky))} {is_are(len(risky))} at high risk of layout shift'
findings.detail: f'Most images have no declared size. The worst is {risky[0][1]} of {risky[0][2]} on {risky[0][0].url}. The browser cannot reserve space, so content jumps as images arrive. This is measured directly as Cumulative Layout Shift, a Core Web Vital. (this audit infers the risk from the markup; confirm the actual CLS score in PageSpeed Insights or Search Console.)'
findings.fix: 'Add width and height attributes to every image, or set an explicit aspect-ratio in CSS.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Could your image markup cause layout shifts?
rows.answer: It identifies image patterns associated with shifting layout, rather than measuring a browser score.
rows.why: Dimensions can reserve space before an image arrives. The check looks for missing space in image markup and accounts for shared template images. Use a browser to see the movement a visitor actually experiences.

condition.text: A page needs at least 3 images with URLs, excluding detected tracking images. More than a 0.6 share must lack recorded dimensions. At least one image missing dimensions must be outside the shared template. An image counts as shared only with at least 5 successful pages and presence on at least a 0.6 share. These limits keep repeated logos alone from triggering the same risk on every page. For example, a missing-dimensions share of exactly 0.6 does not exceed the risk threshold.

pages.text: The check reads image markup from successful pages. It does not measure movement in a browser. Use a browser measurement when you need an actual layout-shift score.

reports.text: The finding is medium severity. It reports a markup risk, not a measured Core Web Vitals result or a prediction of the exact amount a page moves during loading.

fix.text: Set correct image dimensions or reserve the intended aspect ratio in the relevant component. Review content images as well as repeated logos. Test the page visually while images load and use suitable browser measurements for an actual layout-shift result. Keep the source fix tied to the missing space rather than claiming a numerical score improvement from this check alone.

rows.guide_title: How to fix layout shift

review.text: Inspect the space reserved before content images load. A template logo and a large article image can have different roles in the reported pattern. Keep the source diagnosis separate from a measured browser shift. After reserving the intended dimensions, review the layout while loading and confirm that the image still fits its container, rather than assuming any numeric width and height will preserve the desired space.

faq.question: How many images are needed for the markup-based layout-shift risk check?
faq.answer: The minimum is 3 images with URLs after tracking-image exclusions. Missing dimensions must also pass the share and template guards.

faq.question: Does a missing-dimensions share of 0.6 trigger layout-shift risk?
faq.answer: No. The share must be greater than 0.6. A qualifying image outside the shared template is also required.

faq.question: Does the image layout-shift check measure a browser CLS score?
faq.answer: No. It reports a medium severity markup risk. Actual movement and the browser score need separate measurement.

rows.title: Compression and caching headers

findings.title: f'{len(uncompressed)} page{plural_s(len(uncompressed))} {is_are(len(uncompressed))} served without compression'
findings.detail: 'These pages arrived uncompressed at a client asking for `Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate`. Compression typically cuts HTML transfer size by 70–80%, which is one of the largest single speed wins available.\n\n' + ('This audit also asked for Brotli, and that came back uncompressed too.' if probe == '' else 'One case this cannot distinguish: this audit does not ask for Brotli, so a server that offers ONLY Brotli is required to answer uncompressed and appears here while working correctly for every browser.')
findings.fix: "Check which it is before changing anything: `curl -sI -H 'Accept-Encoding: br,gzip' <url> | grep -i content-encoding`. If that returns `br`, compression is already on and there is nothing to fix. If it returns nothing, enable gzip or Brotli for text/html, text/css, application/javascript and application/json."

findings.title: 'Pages are served with no caching headers'
findings.detail: 'No Cache-Control, ETag or Last-Modified. Browsers and CDNs cannot cache efficiently, and crawlers cannot use conditional requests to save bandwidth.'
findings.fix: 'Set Cache-Control on HTML responses and make sure ETag or Last-Modified is present.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Are your HTML responses compressed and cacheable?
rows.answer: It checks response headers for missing compression and caching settings.
rows.why: Compression and caching answer different delivery questions. The probe guard matters because a server can support an encoding that the initial request did not obtain, making a direct absence claim too broad.

condition.text: A successful page with more than 20000 HTML bytes and no content-encoding header can enter the compression finding. Any nonempty separate compression result suppresses that finding. This accounts for servers that use compression only when another encoding is requested. Pages missing cache-control, etag and last-modified are reported when they exceed a 0.5 share of successful pages. These header tests check presence. For example, a response of exactly 20000 HTML bytes stays outside the compression size test.

pages.text: The check reads response headers, HTML size and the separate compression test. It cannot estimate savings from those fields alone. Review the response your server sends for each requested encoding.

reports.text: Missing compression is high severity. Absent cache headers across the larger share produce low severity. A present cache header does not establish that its policy is useful, and a separate encoding probe can change what an apparently uncompressed response means.

fix.text: Inspect the response and the requested encoding. Enable suitable HTML compression where needed. Set caching rules for the content's update needs. Keep private or changing responses safe when editing shared rules. Request the same URL again and review the new headers.

rows.guide_title: How to fix compression and caching headers

review.text: Inspect the encoding negotiation and response headers on the affected route. A separate probe can explain why an initially plain response did not justify a missing-compression claim. Keep cache validators separate from cache lifetime choices. Test dynamic and stable page types appropriately after changing server configuration, because a header appearing on the homepage does not establish that every route receives the same delivery policy.

faq.question: How large must HTML be for the missing-compression finding?
faq.answer: The successful response must exceed 20000 HTML bytes. Missing encoding alone is not enough if a separate compression result exists.

faq.question: Can a separate encoding probe prevent a false missing-compression claim?
faq.answer: Yes. Any nonempty separate compression result prevents that finding. The server may compress only for a different requested encoding.

faq.question: Is absent compression as minor as missing cache headers?
faq.answer: No. Missing compression is high severity. Widespread absent cache headers receive low severity.

rows.title: Image formats

findings.title: f"{legacy_count} image{plural_s(legacy_count)} {verb('use', legacy_count)} JPEG/PNG instead of a modern format"
findings.detail: f'Across {len(legacy_pages)} page{plural_s(len(legacy_pages))}. WebP and AVIF are typically 25–50% smaller at the same visual quality, and every current browser supports WebP.'
findings.fix: 'Convert images to WebP (or AVIF with a WebP fallback). Most CMS platforms and CDNs can do this automatically on upload.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Are image-heavy pages using older formats?
rows.answer: It counts pages with several JPEG or PNG images lacking a modern source alternative.
rows.why: An image-heavy page offers a concrete place to inspect format choices. The check uses that concentration as a review cue, while leaving the actual tradeoff between quality, compatibility and file size to the owner.

condition.text: The test reads successful pages and selects image resources whose URL path ends in JPEG or PNG after the query string is removed. A saved modern-source flag excludes an image from the legacy set. At least 4 remaining images on a page are needed for that page to enter the finding. The count is then totalled across qualifying pages, rather than reporting every isolated older-format image. For example, 4 JPEG images with no recognised newer-format alternative can qualify a page for review.

pages.text: The check reads image addresses and whether a newer-format alternative was found. It does not measure visual quality, transfer size or the browser's actual choice. Review the delivered picture before converting files.

reports.text: The finding is low severity. A newer format alternative can satisfy the check while the delivered image still needs a quality or size review, and a valid older-format file is not automatically broken.

fix.text: Compare suitable modern encodings with the current images using the same visual content. Provide source alternatives where needed and keep a working fallback for your audience. Check the actual chosen source in a browser. Avoid replacing images blindly when a conversion loses useful detail or does not reduce the delivered file.

rows.guide_title: How to serve images in modern formats

review.text: Compare encodings using the actual picture and the resolution needed on the page. A file extension is only the selection signal here, not a measurement of quality or transfer cost. Keep responsive alternatives and fallbacks working after conversion. Check which source a browser chooses, then review the delivered file separately instead of assuming that a modern-source flag proves the visitor received the smallest suitable image.

faq.question: How many older-format images trigger the modern-image check?
faq.answer: The minimum is 4 remaining images after checking for newer alternatives. Fewer qualifying images do not reach the page finding.

faq.question: Can a JPEG image with a newer source alternative be excluded?
faq.answer: Yes. A JPEG or PNG image can be left out when a modern alternative is recognised. Review the actual delivered picture separately.

faq.question: Does the image-format check calculate the bytes a conversion would save?
faq.answer: No. Transfer size is not measured. Image URLs and newer-format alternatives supply the comparison.

rows.title: Page weight

findings.title: f"{len(heavy)} page{plural_s(len(heavy))} {verb('send', len(heavy))} more than {kb(HTML_VERY_HEAVY)} KB of HTML"
findings.detail: f"Largest: {('at least ' if worst.body_truncated else '')}{kb(worst.html_bytes)} KB on {worst.url}. That is the HTML document alone, before images, CSS or JavaScript. On a phone connection this delays the first paint by seconds."
findings.fix: 'Usually caused by inlined CSS/JS or an entire product catalogue rendered into one page. Move inline blocks to cached external files and paginate long listings.'

findings.title: 'HTML documents are larger than they need to be'
findings.detail: f'{len(moderate)} pages exceed {kb(HTML_HEAVY)} KB of HTML.'
findings.fix: 'Check for large inline styles or scripts that could be external and cached across pages.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Is your HTML document unusually large?
rows.answer: It compares decompressed HTML bytes with the engine's document-size cutoffs.
rows.why: A large document can contain repeated markup or extensive inline data. Its byte count identifies something concrete to inspect, while a separate resource review is needed to understand the weight of the whole page.

condition.text: Successful pages above 400000 HTML bytes join the larger-document group. Pages above 150000 HTML bytes and at or below 400000 HTML bytes join the moderate group. Larger documents are reported first. If none exist, a moderate group above a 0.5 share of successful pages can produce the lower-severity finding. This measures the HTML document alone. Images and separate files need their own size measurements. For example, a document of exactly 400000 HTML bytes stays in the moderate size group.

pages.text: The check reads HTML sizes from successful responses. A capped response gives only the amount retained. Keep the size unit and any read limit beside the result.

reports.text: The larger-document finding is medium severity. Widespread moderate documents produce low severity. Browser loading time, script execution and page painting need separate measurements.

fix.text: Inspect the largest served documents and identify what fills them. Remove unused inline data and repeated markup, or split long listings when that suits the content. Move reusable assets only where the resulting requests and caching make sense. Compare decompressed HTML after the change and preserve the useful content the page was meant to deliver.

rows.guide_title: Page weight: how heavy is too heavy?

review.text: Inspect what the HTML contains before moving or deleting large blocks. Embedded state, repeated listings and inline assets have different purposes. Keep required content readable while reducing avoidable duplication. Compare the same document measurement before and after editing, and record a truncated read as a lower bound, since the bytes retained by a capped fetch cannot establish how much unseen HTML remains beyond it.

faq.question: What counts as a very large HTML document in this audit?
faq.answer: A successful page above 400000 HTML bytes enters the larger-document group. Separate page resources are outside this HTML-size measure.

faq.question: Is an HTML document of exactly 400000 bytes in the larger group?
faq.answer: No. Exactly 400000 HTML bytes stays moderate. The larger group requires a strict excess over the limit.

faq.question: How small can HTML be and still enter the moderate-weight group?
faq.answer: Moderate documents must exceed 150000 HTML bytes. A qualifying site's share of moderate pages can affect the lower-severity result.

rows.title: Redirect latency

findings.title: f'{len(redirected)} of {len(ctx.pages)} crawled URLs went through a redirect'
findings.detail: 'Each redirect is an extra round trip before any content arrives, typically 100–300ms on mobile, and it is pure waste when the links could point at the final URL directly.'
findings.fix: 'Update internal links, the sitemap and any hardcoded URLs to the final destinations.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do many crawled addresses need a redirect?
rows.answer: It checks how much of the crawled URL set travelled through a redirect.
rows.why: Many redirects can indicate that the site still advertises old addresses. The useful follow-up is to identify the sources of those requests, rather than removing valid redirects that protect visitors arriving through older links.

condition.text: The check selects crawled pages with a nonempty saved redirect chain. Their count must exceed the larger of 5 pages or a 0.25 share of all crawled pages before the finding appears. The comparison is strict, so equality does not trigger it. This check uses redirect volume as the measured signal. It does not add network timings to calculate a total delay. For example, exactly 5 redirected pages cannot exceed a threshold that is at least 5 pages.

pages.text: The full crawl's request history supplies the counts, including pages outside the successful content set. It is distinct from the check for a particular loop or a chain containing several hops.

reports.text: The finding is low severity. A redirected address can be a correct legacy route, and a large share can reflect how the crawl was seeded rather than proof that every internal link is wrong.

fix.text: Update internal links and sitemaps to the final intended addresses where you control them. Keep redirects that support old external links. Check for loops and unnecessary intermediate moves. Measure response times separately when you need to quantify delay.

rows.guide_title: How to fix redirect problems

review.text: Trace why the crawl requested old addresses in the first place. A sitemap or internal template may still publish them, while an externally discovered legacy URL can correctly rely on a redirect. Keep necessary old-address support. Update controlled sources to final destinations and compare another crawl, using actual response timing separately when the question is how much delay visitors experience rather than how often a redirect appeared.

faq.question: Can exactly five redirected pages trigger the redirect-volume finding?
faq.answer: No. The count must exceed a threshold of at least 5 pages. Larger crawls can raise the limit through the share rule.

faq.question: Does the redirect-cost check add up network delay?
faq.answer: No. It counts the saved redirect chain entries rather than adding network timings. Measure response time separately to quantify delay.

faq.question: How serious is a high volume of redirected crawl requests?
faq.answer: It has low severity. A high count can reflect the crawl's starting addresses as well as outdated links.

rows.title: Render-blocking resources

findings.title: f"{len(worst)} page{plural_s(len(worst))} {verb('load', len(worst))} 5+ render-blocking files"
findings.detail: f'Worst: {worst[0][1]} blocking stylesheets/scripts on {worst[0][0].url}. The browser cannot paint anything until each one downloads and parses, which is a direct hit to Largest Contentful Paint.'
findings.fix: 'Add defer to scripts that are not needed for first paint, load non-critical CSS with media="print" onload, and merge the small files that remain.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your page load many blocking files?
rows.answer: It counts resources marked as blocking the initial render.
rows.why: Resources needed before a page can paint occupy a different place in loading from optional enhancements. The check makes that distinction visible through saved flags, while the correct loading order still depends on what the page needs to show.

condition.text: Successful pages are scanned for resources whose saved render-blocking flag is true. A page enters the finding when it has at least 5 such resources. Qualifying pages are sorted by count, and the report gives the worst count with a limited URL sample. It does not time each request or decide that every script and stylesheet should be delayed regardless of its role. For example, a page with exactly 5 blocking resources qualifies for this finding.

pages.text: The check uses the crawler's recorded blocking-resource types on successful pages. It cannot measure every file's effect on display time. Review which files the first view needs before delaying them.

reports.text: The finding is medium severity. A blocking resource can be necessary for initial display, so the count points to a review rather than proving that every listed file is wasteful.

fix.text: Inspect the files and identify which are required for the first useful view. Defer scripts and delay nonessential styles only where the page continues to work correctly. Combine files when that is useful, then test loading and interaction. Measure the browser result separately instead of translating a lower count into an invented time saving.

rows.guide_title: How to fix render-blocking resources

review.text: Review the role of each blocking file before changing its loading order. A stylesheet needed for the first view and an optional enhancement should not be treated identically. Keep dependencies intact when deferring scripts. After editing, test the initial display and later interactions together, because a lower resource count cannot establish that the page still paints correctly or that an action remains available when needed.

faq.question: How many blocking files trigger the resource-count finding?
faq.answer: At least 5 blocking resources on a successful page qualifies. Saved flags determine which files enter that count.

faq.question: Does a blocking-resource finding mean every listed file should be delayed?
faq.answer: No. Some blocking files are needed for initial display. Review the first useful view before changing their loading order.

faq.question: Does the blocking-file check time the delay from each request?
faq.answer: No. Display time is not measured for each file. The medium result uses saved blocking flags as a review prompt.

rows.title: Server response time

conditions.expression: med > TTFB_POOR and warm is not None and (warm <= TTFB_GOOD)

findings.title: f'Pages are slow the first time they are requested (median {med:.2f}s); repeated, {warm:.2f}s'
findings.detail: f'This audit is the first visitor to most pages it reads, and the median first response was {med:.2f}s against a {TTFB_GOOD}s target. Asked again, the slowest pages answered in {warm:.2f}s: a cache in front of a slow server. Visitors who reach a page the cache already holds get it fast; the first visitor after it expires, and search engine crawlers working through pages nobody else has asked for lately, wait for the server.'
findings.fix: 'Keep pages in the cache longer, warm it after publishing or clearing it, and speed up the origin itself: slow database queries on the main templates are the usual cause.'

findings.title: f'Server responses are slow across the site (median {med:.2f}s)'
findings.detail: f'Median time to first byte is {med:.2f}s against a {TTFB_GOOD}s target. TTFB is the floor for Largest Contentful Paint: no amount of front-end optimisation can produce a fast page on top of a slow server.'
findings.fix: 'In order of typical payoff: enable full-page caching, put a CDN in front of the site, check for slow database queries on the main templates, and move off shared hosting if the host is the bottleneck.'

findings.title: f'Server response time is above target (median {med:.2f}s)'
findings.detail: f"Median TTFB {med:.2f}s; Google's guidance is under {TTFB_GOOD}s."
findings.fix: 'Add page caching and a CDN. This is usually a configuration change, not a rebuild.'

findings.title: f'{len(slow)} page{plural_s(len(slow))} {is_are(len(slow))} much slower than the rest of the site'
findings.detail: f'The site is generally fast (median {med:.2f}s) but these pages take over {TTFB_POOR}s. That pattern usually means one uncached template or an expensive query on a specific page type.'
findings.fix: 'Profile these specific templates. The rest of the site is already fast, so the cause is local to them.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Is your server slow to start responding?
rows.answer: It compares first-response samples, repeat requests and slower-page outliers.
rows.why: The first byte is an early part of delivering a page. Comparing cold and repeated requests can help distinguish a cache effect from a broader response problem, without claiming that the test observed a particular visitor's connection.

condition.text: The check needs at least 3 positive response-time samples from successful pages. It compares the median with 0.8 seconds and 1.8 seconds. Above 1.8 seconds is medium severity when the repeat-request median is at most 0.8 seconds. Otherwise it is high. A median above 0.8 seconds and at most 1.8 seconds produces medium severity. At a median of 0.8 seconds or less, pages above 1.8 seconds can produce a low outlier finding when their share is below 0.3. For example, a slow first request followed by a repeat median of 0.8 seconds meets the warm-cache limit.

pages.text: The check uses recorded first-response times and any positive repeat-request times. It compares the sampled requests. Review their timing and cache state before drawing conclusions about a visitor's experience.

reports.text: Severity depends on the measured pattern. A fast repeat can point to a cache effect. Consistently slow medians call for a different review. Keep the first and repeat measurements together when reading the result.

fix.text: Inspect slow templates and compare repeat requests before choosing a fix. Review server work, cache setup and cache expiry where the measurements point to them. Measure representative URLs again after changes. Check browser rendering and resource loading separately when reviewing the complete page experience.

rows.guide_title: How to reduce server response time (TTFB)

review.text: Compare first and repeat requests for the same page types. A warm result may reveal a cache effect that varies between visits. Check how many positive samples were available before relying on the median. Review server work and cache behaviour for slow templates. Repeat comparable measurements after editing.

faq.question: Is a first-response median of 0.8 seconds too slow?
faq.answer: No. At 0.8 seconds, the site median stays within the fast group. Individual slower pages can still qualify for an outlier result.

faq.question: When can a slow first response get medium rather than high severity?
faq.answer: A first median exceeding 1.8 seconds gets medium severity if the repeat median does not exceed 0.8 seconds. Otherwise it gets high.

faq.question: How many response-time samples does the TTFB check need?
faq.answer: The minimum is 3 positive response-time samples. They must come from successful pages; zero or missing timings do not fill the sample.

rows.title: Incomplete structured data

conditions.expression: prop and prop not in all_missing
not isinstance(ident, str) or ident not in by_id
not isinstance(ident, str) or not ident
any((k not in ('@type', '@id', '@context') for k in raw))
any((k not in ('@type', '@context') for k in known))
written and written != prop and _has_prop(node, written)

constants.name: VALUABLE_TYPES
constants.expression: {'Organization': "defines the business as an entity in Google's Knowledge Graph", 'LocalBusiness': "drives the local pack, map results and 'near me' searches", 'BreadcrumbList': 'replaces the raw URL in search results with a readable path', 'FAQPage': 'marks up Q&A content for AI answers, though Google retired the FAQ rich result in 2026', 'Product': 'enables price, availability and review stars in results', 'Service': 'clarifies what you sell for both search and AI answers', 'WebSite': 'enables the sitelinks search box and site-name display'}

findings.title: f'{len(pages)} page{plural_s(len(pages))} {has_have(len(pages))} incomplete {type_name} markup'
findings.detail: f'{lead}{near_note} ' + _why_so_many(type_name, nodes, len(pages), [d for d in entry.get('dangling', []) if d]) + (f'Google has retired the {type_name} rich result, so completing this will not produce a search feature, but incomplete markup still describes the page wrongly to anything that reads it, including AI answer engines.' if no_feature else 'Google requires these properties before it will show a rich result, so the markup currently validates but produces nothing.')
findings.fix: fix_text

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your structured data have useful values?
rows.answer: It checks required properties by type, including empty fields and unresolved references.
rows.why: A key can be present while holding no usable value. References can also look complete while naming a definition absent from the document, so the check inspects more than whether the expected words occur in source.

condition.text: The check walks supported types on indexable pages and compares each node with the source's required-property table. Same-page identifier definitions are resolved before testing fields. Empty strings, lists and objects do not count as useful values. Case errors, unresolved references, review snippets, service offers and organisation-shaped product blocks affect the explanation or required set. Findings are grouped by type and missing-field combination rather than treating every node as a separate page.

pages.text: The check reads structured objects on each page intended for search. Empty fields and references to missing objects can leave gaps. Confirm the type and the subject before filling them.

reports.text: Incomplete-type findings are medium severity. A required-property table is the engine's coverage, not an exhaustive validation of every schema vocabulary or search feature. Correctly filled fields can still contain inaccurate claims.

fix.text: Read the reported node and the type it claims. Fill applicable fields with real values and define referenced objects on the page where needed. Correct property casing and remove misleading types instead of inventing data to complete them. Use the guide to review empty fields before assuming the template omitted a key entirely.

rows.guide_title: When a field is there and still missing

review.text: Inspect the declaration and any referenced object on the same served page. A pointer can look substantial in source while contributing no local definition. Keep the type's purpose clear before filling fields. Where a value is genuinely unknown or inapplicable, review whether the node should make that claim at all, rather than inserting plausible-looking data solely to complete the engine's required-property list.

faq.question: Can a schema property be present and still count as missing?
faq.answer: Yes. Empty strings, lists and objects leave a required field unfilled. A property name cannot provide the missing value.

faq.question: Does the incomplete-schema check resolve same-page identifier references?
faq.answer: Yes. The check resolves same-page identifier definitions first. A reference with no definition can still leave a required-field gap.

faq.question: How serious is an incomplete supported schema type?
faq.answer: It receives medium severity. The required-property table covers supported types rather than every schema vocabulary or display feature.

rows.title: Invalid JSON-LD

conditions.expression: whole or (field in _IDENTITY_FIELDS and len(text) <= 300 and _TEMPLATE_TAG.search(text))

constants.name: _JSON_ERROR_REMEDY
constants.expression: {'Invalid control character': 'a literal newline, tab or carriage return inside a string value. JSON forbids them unescaped, so write them as \\n and \\t, or strip them. This is almost always a CMS writing multi-line HTML into a field', 'Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes': 'a trailing comma before a closing brace or bracket, or a key quoted with apostrophes instead of double quotes', "Expecting ',' delimiter": 'an unescaped double quote inside a string value: write it as \\"', 'Expecting value': 'an empty field emitted with nothing after the colon, or HTML entities such as " that the CMS encoded into the script block', 'Extra data': 'two JSON documents in one script block.
