findings.evidence: {'fields': [{'page': p.url, 'field': f, 'value': v} for (p, hits) in tagged[:5] for (f, v) in hits[:3]]}

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Can software read your JSON-LD correctly?
rows.answer: It reports parsing errors, CDATA wrappers and unfilled template values.
rows.why: Structured content must be readable before its fields can be interpreted. A saved parser error gives a concrete starting point for repair, while template placeholders need a different fix in the code that supplied the value.

condition.text: The check groups recorded JSON-LD errors from successful pages. It explains the most common error and a matching repair. CDATA wrappers are reported separately. Readable blocks are searched for unfilled template tags, including short identity fields. That identity-field test has a 300-character limit. Longer strings with braces are left out of that short-field test. For example, a short identity field containing an unfilled template tag can be checked up to the 300-character limit.

pages.text: The check reads JSON-LD blocks, recorded errors and wrapper detections. It does not repair JSON or verify the truth of a readable value. Review the declared facts after fixing syntax.

reports.text: Parsing failures are high severity. CDATA wrappers and unfilled template tags are medium. A block can be valid JSON yet still carry a literal template value, which is why the check includes a separate case after parsing.

fix.text: Use the reported error and location to inspect the original block. Fix quoting, commas or leftover wrappers as appropriate, and ensure templates fill values before serving the page. Generate structured JSON through a serializer where possible. Parse the final served block again and check its factual content after syntax is repaired.

rows.guide_title: Read the JSON-LD error, not the guess

review.text: Copy the exact served block into a parser before changing surrounding page content. A template may generate valid local data and still escape it incorrectly in the final document. Keep syntax repair separate from factual review. After resolving a parser error, inspect literal template values and wrapper output too, because a block can become parseable while still describing an unfinished or inaccurate business field.

faq.question: Are JSON-LD syntax errors more serious than leftover CDATA wrappers?
faq.answer: Yes. Syntax failures get high severity. Leftover CDATA wrappers and template tags receive medium results.

faq.question: How long can an identity field be for the unfilled-template check?
faq.answer: The identity value can reach a 300-character limit in that test. Longer brace-containing strings are left out of this comparison.

faq.question: Can valid JSON-LD still contain unfinished template values?
faq.answer: Yes. Readable blocks are checked for unfilled template tags. Syntax validity alone does not ensure the declared value was filled.

rows.title: Structured data vs visible content

conditions.expression: rendered is None or not rendered.html

findings.title: f"{len(offenders)} page{plural_s(len(offenders))} {verb('mark', len(offenders))} up ratings that are not shown on the page"
findings.detail: "AggregateRating markup is present but the page displays no reviews or ratings. Google's policy requires structured data to reflect visible content; violations can trigger a manual action that removes all rich results for the site."
findings.fix: 'Either display the reviews and rating on the page, or remove the AggregateRating markup.'

findings.title: f'{len(unconfirmable)} page{plural_s(len(unconfirmable))} with rating markup could not be checked for visible ratings'
findings.detail: f"These pages carry AggregateRating markup. Google's policy is about what a visitor actually sees, and a rating widget is very often drawn by JavaScript, so the served HTML cannot settle it either way, and nothing is being alleged here. This audit renders a sample of pages; these were not in it."
findings.fix: 'Open one of these pages and check whether a visitor actually sees the star rating the markup claims. If they do not, remove the AggregateRating: Google treats invisible rating markup as a structured-data violation, and a manual-action risk.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does rating markup match what readers can see?
rows.answer: It checks whether declared ratings have visible reviews or rating text.
rows.why: Declared ratings and visible reviews should describe the same thing. The check uses browser output when available to review a possible mismatch. Without that output, it leaves the result unknown.

condition.text: The check reads aggregate-rating markup on pages intended for search. It leaves out recognised off-page rating arrangements for supported software types. Page text is searched for stored rating words. If none match, saved browser output is checked when available. Without that output, the result stays unknown. A loaded page still lacking the wording can produce the stronger finding.

pages.text: The check reads rating objects, visible prose and any saved browser output. It compares the declared rating with words it can find on the page. You need to confirm that they describe the same subject.

reports.text: Confirmed nonvisible ratings are high severity. A visibility result that cannot be established is a notice. The distinction matters on pages where scripts add reviews that were absent from the initial document.

fix.text: Confirm the subject and values of each declared rating. Compare them with the public page and any recognised off-page rating arrangement. Show the supporting review or remove an unsupported declaration. When browser output was unavailable, inspect the loaded page before deciding whether the rating is hidden.

rows.guide_title: Structured data that says what the page does not

review.text: Compare a declared rating with the visible material that belongs to it. A review word elsewhere may concern another subject. Keep track of which pages had a loaded-browser comparison. Inspect any recognised off-page arrangement before removing it. Use only ratings you can verify against their source.

faq.question: Can the rating-visibility check use saved browser output?
faq.answer: Yes. The check can search saved browser output when initial text has no rating wording. That can reveal reviews supplied by scripts.

faq.question: Is a rating definitely hidden if browser output was never obtained?
faq.answer: No. The result stays unknown when loaded output is unavailable. A notice preserves that limit instead of confirming hidden ratings.

faq.question: How serious is a confirmed rating absent from the loaded page?
faq.answer: The result gets high severity when the loaded comparison confirms the absence. Also verify that the rating describes the right reviewed item.

rows.title: Missing structured data

conditions.expression: 'BreadcrumbList' not in all_types | scripted and total >= 5

findings.title: 'The site has no structured data at all'
findings.detail: 'No JSON-LD, microdata or RDFa was found on any crawled page. Structured data is how you tell search engines what the business is, where it operates and what it sells. Without it they have to guess from prose, and AI answer engines have nothing authoritative to cite.'
findings.fix: 'Start with Organization (or LocalBusiness if you serve customers at a location) on the homepage, then BreadcrumbList site-wide.'

findings.title: f'Your {named} markup is added by a script, not served in the HTML'
findings.detail: f"No page's HTML as served declares who the business is, but in a browser {named} markup appears: a script writes it into the page after it loads ({scripted_pages[0]}). Google runs the script and reads it. Crawlers that read only the HTML your server sends, which includes the AI crawlers, see no business markup at all, so they cannot tie the site to a real-world entity from it."
findings.fix: "Write the JSON-LD block into the page's HTML (the theme template, or your SEO plugin's schema settings) instead of building it in a script. Then open the page source, not the browser inspector, and confirm it is there."

findings.title: 'No breadcrumb markup'
findings.detail: 'Breadcrumb structured data replaces the raw URL in search results with a readable hierarchy, which measurably improves click-through rate.'
findings.fix: 'Add BreadcrumbList markup to section and detail page templates.'

findings.title: f'Only {coverage:.0%} of pages carry structured data'
findings.detail: f'{pages_with_schema} of {total} indexable pages have any markup. Schema belongs in the shared template, not on individual pages.'
findings.fix: 'Move the markup into the base template so every page inherits at least Organization and BreadcrumbList.'
findings.urls: ctx.urls_of([p for p in ctx.indexable if not ctx.json_ld_types(p)])

findings.title: 'No Organization or LocalBusiness markup'
findings.detail: 'The site uses structured data but never declares who the business is. This is the single most valuable piece of schema for a business site: it connects the website to a real-world entity, which is the precondition for a Knowledge Panel and for being cited by name in AI answers.'
findings.fix: 'Add Organization (or LocalBusiness) markup to the homepage.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your site serve structured data?
rows.answer: It checks for schema coverage, business identity and breadcrumb markup.
rows.why: Coverage and correctness are separate questions. Knowing where markup appears helps locate a template gap, while the type and completeness checks still need to establish whether the declarations fit the content.

condition.text: Pages intended for search are checked for JSON-LD, microdata and recognised script-built types. No detected markup produces high severity. Missing identity and identity built only by scripts get different explanations. At least 5 indexable pages without breadcrumb markup produce a low finding. Coverage above zero but below 0.4 produces another low finding. With no indexable pages, coverage stays unknown. For example, markup coverage of exactly 0.4 stays outside the partial-coverage finding.

pages.text: The check reads structured types in server responses and types known to be built by scripts. Objects it cannot read remain unknown. Review coverage before treating an apparent gap as a reason to add duplicate markup.

reports.text: No schema and absent identity can be high, script-only identity medium, and breadcrumb or coverage gaps low. Presence of a type is not proof that all required properties exist or that a particular rich result is available.

fix.text: Choose markup that accurately describes the business and page. Add it to the appropriate shared template and serve important identity in readable HTML where practical. Keep breadcrumb declarations aligned with the visible route. Check several page types after editing, then validate values and ownership instead of stopping at a presence result.

rows.guide_title: How to fix structured data errors

review.text: Inspect several page templates to see where declarations originate. A shared business object and a page-specific content object describe different things, even when both count toward coverage. Keep their roles accurate when extending markup. After adding a type, review its properties and visible subject separately, because a presence result can improve while the new node still contains empty fields or describes another organisation.

faq.question: Can missing breadcrumbs be reported on a small schema sample?
faq.answer: The count must reach 5 indexable pages lacking breadcrumbs. Smaller sets do not reach that finding.

faq.question: Does markup coverage of 0.4 trigger the partial-coverage finding?
faq.answer: No. The partial-coverage comparison applies below 0.4 and above zero. Equality stays outside that result.

faq.question: Is identity markup built only by scripts treated like served identity?
faq.answer: No. The report rates script-only identity medium, with a separate explanation for absence. Served JSON-LD and microdata are also recognised.

rows.title: Rich result opportunities

findings.title: f'{len(faq_candidates)} page{plural_s(len(faq_candidates))} {has_have(len(faq_candidates))} Q&A content with no FAQ markup'
findings.detail: 'These pages already answer questions in their headings, and FAQPage markup labels that structure for anything parsing the page. Be clear about what it no longer buys: Google retired FAQ rich results on 7 May 2026, so this will not produce an expandable answer in the result any more, and Google states no special structured data is needed for its AI features. The value left is entity clarity and machine-readable Q&A: real, and smaller than it was.'
findings.fix: 'Wrap the existing questions and answers in FAQPage markup if you want the structure declared. Do not expect a result feature from it. The question-shaped headings themselves are doing most of the work here.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Do your real answers have FAQ markup?
rows.answer: It finds pages with several qualifying question headings and no FAQPage declaration.
rows.why: Structured declarations should follow the content the reader can actually use. Counting locally answered questions protects that relationship and keeps an index of links from being described as a complete answer page.

condition.text: Pages already declaring FAQPage are excluded. A remaining page needs at least 3 headings recognised as questions. Heading text and linked destinations are checked. A question that sends readers elsewhere may be navigation. Review the local answer before adding markup. The count does not verify facts or promise a search display feature. For example, 3 accepted question headings can qualify a page that has no FAQPage declaration.

pages.text: The check reads headings, question links and structured types. It looks for a page's own questions and answers. A complete factual and editorial review still needs a person.

reports.text: The opportunity finding is low severity. It describes possible markup for existing answers rather than a requirement to manufacture questions or a claim that adding the type will produce a rich result.

fix.text: Review the qualifying questions and confirm that the page provides their answers. Add matching question-and-answer markup only for that content. Keep the visible wording and declared answers aligned when editing. Do not add filler questions simply to reach the count or promise a search appearance that this test does not measure.

rows.guide_title: How to fix structured data errors

review.text: Read each qualifying question with its answer before adding structured declarations. A heading linked to another page may be navigation rather than a locally answered question. Keep the visible answers and declared text aligned during later edits. Review the existing page's purpose first, and leave out invented questions or unsupported claims about search appearance. This opportunity identifies content shape rather than an assured display feature.

faq.question: How many question headings suggest an FAQ markup opportunity?
faq.answer: At least 3 headings must be recognised as questions. Their answers should already belong to the page before markup is added.

faq.question: Are pages that already declare FAQPage included in the opportunity check?
faq.answer: No. Declaring FAQPage takes a page out of the sample. Remaining pages are checked for potential declarations.

faq.question: Can a question linked elsewhere be navigation rather than an FAQ answer?
faq.answer: Yes. An onward question link may be navigation. Confirm that the answer really belongs to this page before adding FAQ markup.

rows.title: Schema price vs visible price

conditions.expression: rendered is None or not rendered.html
not any((_amounts(p) & visible for p in priced))

findings.title: f"{len(offenders)} page{plural_s(len(offenders))} {verb('mark', len(offenders))} up a price that is not shown on the page"
findings.detail: f"Offer markup states a price ({shown}) that appears nowhere in the page's visible text. Google may show that price in search results, so a visitor arrives expecting it. Structured data must reflect what the page shows; a mismatch risks a manual action that removes every rich result for the site, not just this one."
findings.fix: 'Show the same price on the page, or correct the markup to the price you charge. If the page does not sell anything (an article carrying sitewide Offer markup, say), remove the Offer from it rather than restating the price.'

findings.title: f'{len(unconfirmable)} page{plural_s(len(unconfirmable))} with price markup could not be checked against the visible price'
findings.detail: f'These pages state a price in their markup. Whether a visitor sees the same number is a question about the rendered page, and a price is very often drawn by JavaScript from a variant picker, so the served HTML cannot settle it either way, and nothing is being alleged here.'
findings.fix: 'Open one of these pages and compare the price a visitor sees with the one in the markup. A mismatch is what Google penalises here, and a variant picker that changes the visible price without updating the markup is the usual cause.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your marked-up price appear on the page?
rows.answer: It compares nonzero declared price amounts with visible and saved rendered text.
rows.why: Markup prices are claims about an offer. Comparing them with readable content can expose stale or hidden values, while a person still needs to check that the amount and the offer belong together.

condition.text: The check reads price, low-price and high-price fields from supported offer and price objects. Zero-only declarations are excluded. A matching amount in the page text can pass the comparison. Otherwise saved browser text is checked after removing tags, scripts and styles. Without browser output, the result stays unknown. No matching amount after that comparison produces a high finding.

pages.text: The check reads price declarations, page text and saved browser output. It recognises different punctuation in amounts. You still need to confirm the currency, billing period and offer. It performs no currency conversion.

reports.text: Confirmed absent price text is high severity. Unconfirmable visibility is a notice. Review the whole offer after finding a matching amount. Check currency, availability and any terms attached to the price.

fix.text: Compare the declared amount with the actual offer shown to visitors. Update stale values and show relevant prices clearly, or remove declarations that no longer describe the page. Check script-rendered offers before treating them as absent. Review currency and pricing conditions separately because a shared number alone cannot validate them.

rows.guide_title: Structured data that says what the page does not

review.text: Compare the numeric match with the exact offer and its conditions. A number elsewhere in prose may coincide with the declared amount without being its price. Keep currency, billing period and the subject of the offer clear in your manual review. When scripts supply the visible price, inspect that output before editing the declaration, and preserve uncertainty when the audit never obtained a rendered comparison.

faq.question: Are zero-only price declarations included in the visible-price test?
faq.answer: No. Zero-only declarations are excluded. The comparison uses supported price and offer objects with qualifying amounts.

faq.question: Can browser text satisfy the declared-price visibility check?
faq.answer: Yes. The comparison searches saved browser text if page text has no matching amount. Missing browser output leaves visibility unknown.

faq.question: Does a matching price amount prove the whole offer is accurate?
faq.answer: No. Currency, availability and any terms still need review. A numeric match does not establish the complete offer's accuracy.

rows.title: Security headers

findings.title: f'No HSTS header needed: .{tld} is HTTPS-only in every major browser'
findings.detail: f'This site sends no Strict-Transport-Security header, and on .{tld} that costs nothing. The whole .{tld} domain is on the HSTS preload list built into Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge, so a browser never makes an http:// request to any site under it, not even on the first visit, which is the one gap the header exists to close. Other security scorecards check for the header by name and will still report it missing.'
findings.fix: 'Nothing to do. Adding the header is harmless, and changes nothing a visitor can see.'

findings.title: f'Missing {len(missing_basics)} baseline security header{plural_s(len(missing_basics))}'
findings.detail: f"Not set: {', '.join(missing_basics)}. These are low-risk to add and are checked by most security scorecards."
findings.fix: 'Add them at the web server or CDN. If your host cannot send headers (GitHub Pages cannot), then Referrer-Policy can be set in the page itself with a meta tag, which browsers honour. There is no meta equivalent for X-Content-Type-Options, so on such a host that one cannot be set at all and is not worth chasing.'

findings.title: 'No HSTS header'
findings.detail: 'Strict-Transport-Security tells browsers to use HTTPS for this site from now on, closing the window where a first visit over http:// could be intercepted.'
findings.fix: 'Add the header at your web server or CDN: start with a short max-age, confirm nothing breaks, then raise it. If your host cannot send headers (GitHub Pages cannot), HSTS cannot be set at all. Unlike Referrer-Policy there is no meta tag browsers honour for it, so on such a host this one waits until you move somewhere that can send it.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your secure site send baseline headers?
rows.answer: It checks selected response headers and recognises some equivalent protections.
rows.why: Equivalent protections can live in different places. Recognising a browser-enforced suffix or an HTML referrer declaration avoids asking for a duplicate solely because a particular response-header key was absent.

condition.text: The check runs on HTTPS sites. Missing strict-transport-security produces a low finding unless the final host's suffix is in the source's preload list, in which case the code reports a pass for that case. It also checks x-content-type-options and referrer-policy. A nonempty meta referrer declaration in the first 25 successful pages can satisfy the referrer-policy presence test. Missing baseline headers produce a notice. For example, a nonempty meta referrer value in the first 25 successful pages can satisfy that header-presence test.

pages.text: The check reads saved security headers, the final host and sampled meta declarations. It checks presence and recognised alternatives. Review each value to see whether the policy suits the site.

reports.text: HSTS absence is low, recognised suffix coverage a pass and missing baseline headers a notice. The report is a focused configuration check, not a complete security assessment of the application.

fix.text: Inspect the live response configuration through your normal server tools. Add appropriate baseline values and review HSTS carefully for all hosts it would cover. Keep a valid meta referrer policy where that is the intended configuration. Test representative responses after editing shared server rules, including pages served through another proxy layer.

rows.guide_title: How to fix missing security headers

review.text: Inspect header values after confirming their presence. A key can exist while applying an unsuitable policy, and a shared proxy can supply values independently of the page template. Keep the recognised equivalent cases in view before adding duplicates. Review representative responses after configuration changes and check the hosts covered by a transport policy, rather than assuming that a presence-only result completes a broader application security review.

faq.question: Can a meta referrer declaration satisfy the referrer-policy check?
faq.answer: Yes. The first 25 successful pages are searched for a nonempty meta referrer value. That can satisfy the policy-presence test.

faq.question: Is missing HSTS always reported when no header is saved?
faq.answer: No. A final-host suffix in the source's preload list gets a pass for that case. Check the actual host and policy separately.

faq.question: Does passing the header check mean the application is fully secure?
faq.answer: No. It is a focused configuration check. The result cannot complete a broader application security assessment.

rows.title: HTTPS

conditions.expression: not ctx.site.http_redirects_https and 'http' not in ctx.site.robots_skipped
days is not None and days < 21

findings.title: 'The site is not served over HTTPS'
findings.detail: "HTTPS has been a Google ranking signal since 2014, and browsers now label plain HTTP pages as 'Not secure' in the address bar. Any form on the site sends its data in the clear."
findings.fix: "Install a TLS certificate (Let's Encrypt issues them free and most hosts provide one-click setup), then redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS."

findings.title: f'The certificate for {cert_host} could not be checked'
findings.detail: f'{message}. That is a fact about this connection, not about your certificate. No chain was evaluated, so this audit will not say whether it is valid. A slow link, a proxy, or rate limiting all look like this.'
findings.fix: f"Check it yourself: `curl -sI https://{(ctx.site.final_origin or ctx.site.origin).split('://')[-1].rstrip('/')}/` should return a status line rather than an error."

findings.title: f'http://{probed_host} answers {status} instead of redirecting to https://'
findings.detail: f'The plain-http address answers {status}, so it neither redirects nor serves the site. Nothing insecure is indexable, but anyone who types the bare domain, follows an old link, or uses a client that defaults to http lands on an error page rather than on the site.'
findings.fix: f'Add a site-wide 301 from http://{probed_host} to https://, preserving the path.'

findings.title: f'The TLS certificate for {cert_host} is not valid'
findings.detail: f'{message}. Browsers show a full-page security warning before the site loads, which stops effectively all traffic.'
findings.fix: 'Reissue or reinstall the certificate. Check that the full chain (including intermediates) is served, and that it covers every hostname in use.'

findings.title: f'http://{probed_host} does not redirect to https://'
findings.detail: f'The site has a certificate, but http://{probed_host} answered {status} and stayed on http. That leaves two indexable copies of every page and lets visitors land on the unencrypted one. This is about {probed_host} only. Another spelling of the host can be configured differently, and this audit did not check one.'
findings.fix: f'Add a site-wide 301 from http://{probed_host} to https://, preserving the path.'

findings.title: 'Whether http:// redirects could not be checked'
findings.detail: f"The plain-http address answered with {status or 'no response at all'}, which is what a site does when it blocks automated requests, not evidence about redirects. This audit will not claim a missing redirect it did not observe."
findings.fix: f'Check it by hand: `curl -sI {probed}` should answer 301 with a Location on https://.'

findings.title: f'The TLS certificate for {cert_host} expires in {days} day{plural_s(days)}'
findings.detail: f'The certificate served by {cert_host} expires in {days} day{plural_s(days)}. Once it expires, every visitor sees a security warning instead of the site.'
findings.fix: 'Renew now, and enable automatic renewal so it cannot lapse again.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your site serve secure working responses?
rows.answer: It checks HTTPS, the plain-HTTP route and certificate validity.
rows.why: Secure delivery and a consistent plain-HTTP route are different configuration tasks. Keeping uncertainty separate helps avoid changing a correct redirect because a network refusal prevented this particular audit from observing it.

condition.text: A site not served over HTTPS produces a critical finding and ends this check. Otherwise the plain-HTTP probe is reviewed unless skipped by policy. Refusals, zero statuses and server errors produce uncertainty rather than a definite redirect fault. Other client errors and nonredirecting responses have separate cases. Certificate validity is checked separately. Expiry below 21 days is reported, with high severity below 7 days and medium otherwise. For example, a certificate with exactly 7 days left stays in the medium expiry group.

pages.text: Site-level scheme and saved redirect-probe results are combined with a certificate check against the final origin. The final origin is used for the certificate host, avoiding an assumption that the starting address remained the destination.

reports.text: Missing HTTPS and invalid certificates are critical. Redirect problems can be high or medium, unknown results notices, and expiry high or medium. A certificate test that cannot run is not silently treated as valid or invalid.

fix.text: Use a valid certificate for the final host and review its renewal setup. Redirect the intended plain-HTTP routes to their secure equivalents where appropriate. Investigate probe failures before declaring the route broken. Test the affected host and path after changes, checking both the response destination and certificate rather than only the browser's final appearance.

rows.guide_title: How to redirect http:// to https://

review.text: Compare the starting address, final host and certificate details as separate parts of delivery. A host move can make the final certificate the relevant one even when the original name appears in the audit setup. Keep unknown probes distinct from invalid results. After changing renewal or redirect configuration, test the affected route again without treating a successful final browser view as proof that every intermediate response behaved as intended.

faq.question: How soon before certificate expiry does the HTTPS check report a finding?
faq.answer: It reports fewer than 21 days remaining. Expiry with fewer than 7 days left is high, with the remaining reported window medium.

faq.question: Is a certificate with seven days left in the high-expiry group?
faq.answer: No. Exactly 7 days remaining stays medium. The high group requires less time than that.

faq.question: Does an unavailable certificate probe mean the certificate is invalid?
faq.answer: No. The report calls unknown results notices. An uncompleted test does not establish validity or invalidity.

rows.title: Mixed content

findings.title: f"{len(blocking)} page{plural_s(len(blocking))} {verb('load', len(blocking))} {what} over http://"
findings.detail: f'Browsers block active mixed content outright, so these {what} never load. The page will be visibly broken or missing functionality' + (' (an embedded frame shows as an empty box)' if 'iframe' in kinds else '') + f', usually without any error the site owner notices.\n\nExample: {first_rs[0].url} on {first_page.url}'
findings.fix: 'Change these resource URLs to https:// (or protocol-relative //) and confirm the origin serves them over TLS.'

findings.title: f"{len(image_only)} page{plural_s(len(image_only))} {verb('load', len(image_only))} images over http://"
findings.detail: 'Insecure images downgrade the padlock indicator and may be blocked outright by stricter browser settings.'
findings.fix: 'Update the image URLs to https://.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your HTTPS page load insecure resources?
rows.answer: It separates insecure active resources from pages with insecure images only.
rows.why: A secure document can refer to resources through a different scheme. Separating executable or embedded content from images keeps the report tied to the types of resources that actually produced the finding.

condition.text: The check runs on HTTPS sites. It scans successful pages for HTTP images, scripts, stylesheets and frames. Insecure scripts, styles or frames produce high severity. Image-only cases produce medium severity. A page counted in the active group is counted there once, even if it also has an insecure image.

pages.text: The check reads resource addresses and types from successful pages. It does not test every feature in a browser. Review the actual file response before changing its URL.

reports.text: Active mixed content is high severity and image-only mixed content medium. The report describes the resource addresses observed in markup rather than claiming to have measured every resulting browser error.

fix.text: Replace insecure resource addresses with working secure equivalents and verify that the resource exists there. Update shared templates or stored content that supplies the old addresses. Remove an obsolete resource when it has no useful role. Check the browser for loading errors after editing, since changing the scheme text alone does not guarantee that the remote server supports it.

rows.guide_title: How to redirect http:// to https://

review.text: Inspect the resource target as well as the page that names it. An HTTPS address needs to serve the file the page actually uses. Prioritise insecure scripts, styles and frames when reviewing the report. Find old addresses in shared templates and stored content. After updating them, test page loading and interactions in a browser.

faq.question: Are insecure scripts treated more seriously than insecure images?
faq.answer: Yes. Scripts and other active resources get high severity. An image-only case receives medium.

faq.question: Which resource types are checked for mixed content?
faq.answer: The scanned types are images, scripts, stylesheets and frames using HTTP addresses on successful secure pages. Saved markup supplies the resource addresses.

faq.question: Does the mixed-content check also run on an HTTP-only site?
faq.answer: No. Only HTTPS sites enter the check. It looks for insecure resources within that secure-page context.

rows.title: Favicon

findings.title: 'No favicon found'
findings.detail: "Google shows a site's favicon next to its name in mobile search results. Without one you get a generic globe icon, which reads as less established than the competitors around you."
findings.fix: 'Add a favicon at /favicon.ico plus a 180x180 apple-touch-icon, and declare them in the head.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Can your site's favicon be found?
rows.answer: It reports a confirmed missing favicon from the saved site probe.
rows.why: The icon is a small part of the site's public identity. A presence probe can identify a delivery problem, while appearance and suitability still need a visual check in the places the icon is meant to be used.

condition.text: The check needs a final or starting origin. It emits a low-severity finding only when the saved icon result is false and the saved unknown flag is also false. An unknown result is therefore not turned into a missing-icon claim. Browser tabs, icon formats and article text are outside this missing-file test.

pages.text: The check uses the saved icon request result. It cannot judge the artwork, branding or every cached browser tab. Review the served icon yourself.

reports.text: A confirmed missing favicon is low severity. No finding under an unknown result does not prove that the icon exists or that every browser will display the intended artwork.

fix.text: Check the icon declaration and the file it names. Serve a valid icon from a working address and keep the declaration in the shared head template. Review fallback paths where relevant. Request the file again after publishing through your normal workflow, then inspect its appearance separately from the probe's limited existence result.

rows.guide_title: How to fix a favicon not showing in search results

review.text: Inspect the icon request independently of a cached browser tab. A tab can retain earlier artwork even after the served file changes, while a successful probe says little about how the icon looks. Keep the file's existence and visual identity as separate checks. Review the declaration generated by the shared head and request the intended resource again before treating a missing result as a reason to redesign the artwork.

faq.question: Does an unknown favicon probe mean the icon is missing?
faq.answer: No. An unknown result is kept separate from a confirmed absence. The missing-icon finding needs both saved flags to support that claim.

faq.question: How serious is a confirmed missing favicon?
faq.answer: It receives low severity. Check the actual icon request separately from a cached tab image.

faq.question: Does the icon check inspect the artwork shown in my browser tab?
faq.answer: No. Browser tabs and icon formats are outside this file-presence test. A successful probe does not judge the design.

rows.title: Open Graph tags

conditions.expression: not any((k.startswith('og:') and v for (k, v) in og.items()))

findings.title: f'{len(untitled)} page{plural_s(len(untitled))} {has_have(len(untitled))} Open Graph tags but no og:title'
findings.detail: 'These pages carry some Open Graph tags (' + ', '.join(sorted((k for (k, v) in untitled[0].open_graph.items() if k.startswith('og:') and v))[:4]) + " on the first) and no og:title, so a shared link's headline is whatever the platform takes from the page's <title> tag, brand suffix and all."
findings.fix: 'Add og:title (and og:description) to the template beside the tags it already has.'

findings.title: f'{len(no_og)} page{plural_s(len(no_og))} {has_have(len(no_og))} no Open Graph tags'
findings.detail: 'When these URLs are shared on LinkedIn, Facebook, WhatsApp, Slack or iMessage, the preview is assembled by guesswork: often the wrong image and a fragment of navigation text. A bare link gets a fraction of the clicks a proper card does.'
findings.fix: 'Add Open Graph tags to the base template so every page gets a correct preview.'

findings.title: f'{len(no_image)} page{plural_s(len(no_image))} {has_have(len(no_image))} Open Graph tags but no image'
findings.detail: 'Shared links show as a plain text row rather than a card, which is far less noticeable in a feed.'
findings.fix: 'Add an og:image of at least 1200x630px. A single branded default for the whole site is better than none.'

findings.title: f"{n} page{plural_s(n)} {('gives its' if n == 1 else 'give their')} share image only as og:image:url"
findings.detail: 'The Open Graph protocol lists og:image as one of four properties every page needs, and og:image:url as an optional detail of it. The same URL, meant to sit beside og:image rather than replace it. These pages have the detail and not the tag, so any platform that reads only og:image shares them with no picture.'
findings.fix: 'Add og:image with the same URL the page already gives in og:image:url.'

findings.title: f'The og:image on {len(dead_image)} page{plural_s(len(dead_image))} does not exist'
findings.detail: 'The tag is there and the file is not, so every share of these URLs, on any platform, renders as a plain text row with a blank space where the card should be. This is worse than having no image tag at all, because it looks deliberate and nothing warns you: the markup validates and the page is fine.'
findings.fix: 'Upload the image at the URL the tag names, or point the tag at one that exists. Then check it resolves rather than assuming: that is the whole failure mode here.'

findings.title: f'{len(no_desc)} page{plural_s(len(no_desc))} {has_have(len(no_desc))} no og:description'
findings.detail: 'The share card shows a title and image but no supporting line.'
findings.fix: 'Add og:description. It can reuse the meta description.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Will shared links have useful preview metadata?
rows.answer: It checks Open Graph identity, images, descriptions and measured image failures.
rows.why: A shared URL can carry its own title, image and description. Checking those fields separately helps locate whether an incomplete preview comes from missing metadata or a measured problem fetching the named picture.

condition.text: Pages with readable content are checked for Open Graph values. Missing tags and tags without a title receive different explanations. A missing primary image is separate from an image supplied only through an image-URL subproperty. Measured image responses with HTTP status 400 or above are treated as dead after refusals are excluded. Missing descriptions are reported separately when the whole set of tags has not already been reported absent. For example, a measured image response with HTTP status 400 can be treated as dead after refusal handling.

pages.text: The check reads Open Graph fields and saved image responses. A refused or unmeasured image stays uncertain. Check the served image before replacing its declaration.

reports.text: Most missing fields are low severity, dead images medium and missing descriptions notices. Valid-looking metadata does not prove that every sharing service uses it or that a cached preview has refreshed.

fix.text: Add accurate preview fields through the appropriate page template. Use a working image URL and confirm that the image is the one you intend to share. Keep page-specific titles and descriptions where useful. Review a sharing service's cached preview separately after fixing the source, since this check reads the page and saved response rather than clearing external caches.

rows.guide_title: How to fix a broken link preview

review.text: Compare preview metadata with the actual page and named image. A title can be useful while the picture address is stale, and an unmeasured image response remains uncertain. Keep the primary image property distinct from its subproperties during repair. After updating a shared template, inspect pages with different content so that every preview does not inherit a generic or misleading summary simply because the tags are now present.

faq.question: Can an Open Graph image error be reported without a dead page?
faq.answer: Yes. HTTP status 400 or higher can establish a dead preview image once refusals are excluded. Its page can still respond successfully.

faq.question: Are missing Open Graph descriptions as serious as dead preview images?
faq.answer: No. The report rates dead images medium. Missing descriptions receive notices, and most other missing fields are low.

faq.question: Does finding Open Graph tags guarantee the current sharing preview?
faq.answer: No. A cached preview can be stale despite correct metadata. The check cannot promise a service's current display.

rows.title: Twitter/X card

findings.title: f'No {what}' if every_page else f'{len(missing)} of {len(ctx.indexable)} pages have no {what}'
findings.detail: ('X falls back to Open Graph, so this is minor, but a declared card type gives you control over the layout.' if every_page else f'X falls back to Open Graph, so this is minor, but a declared card type gives you control over the layout. {len(ctx.indexable) - len(missing)} of your pages already have one, so this is a template that missed it rather than a setting you have never used.') + has_tags
findings.fix: 'Add the card type. X will use your existing og:title, og:description and og:image.'

presentation.scope: shared UI only, not check thresholds

rows.question: Does your site declare a Twitter card type?
rows.answer: It checks widespread missing card-type declarations on sites with Open Graph titles.
rows.why: Related metadata can be partly present while a type declaration is missing. Naming the actual gap gives a clearer template fix than replacing the whole preview setup based on an overly broad absence claim.

condition.text: The check builds a missing set from indexable pages without twitter:card. It proceeds only when some indexable page has an Open Graph title and the missing set is greater than a 0.5 share. Pages carrying other Twitter fields are distinguished from pages with no such markup, so the wording can identify a missing card type rather than falsely saying all card tags are absent. For example, a missing-card share of exactly 0.5 does not exceed the finding threshold.

pages.text: The check reads card metadata and Open Graph titles. It does not ask a social platform to refresh its cache. Review the live page tags before testing an external preview.

reports.text: The finding is a notice. A nonempty card-type value satisfies this presence condition without establishing that every other preview field is valid or that a particular platform will display the card.

fix.text: Review the intended preview style and add an appropriate card-type declaration where missing. Keep its title, description and image consistent with the page. Inspect existing fields before inserting duplicates through another plugin or template. Test the source output and any platform preview separately, recognising that external caches can preserve earlier metadata.

rows.guide_title: How to fix a broken link preview

review.text: Inspect which card fields already exist before adding another declaration. A page may have a useful preview title and picture while lacking only the type value. Keep the type consistent with the intended preview and avoid competing values supplied by different templates. Review the served metadata first, then check any platform preview separately, because a cached external result cannot establish exactly what the current page source publishes.

faq.question: Does a missing-card share of 0.5 trigger the Twitter card finding?
faq.answer: No. The missing-card share must exceed 0.5. An indexable page with an Open Graph title is also required.

faq.question: Can a page have Twitter preview fields but still lack a card type?
faq.answer: Yes. The check distinguishes other Twitter fields from a missing card type. That allows a narrower explanation without claiming all preview tags are absent.

faq.question: Is a missing twitter:card declaration treated as a serious error?
faq.answer: It is only a notice. A card-type value that is nonempty clears the presence comparison. Other preview details still need review.
